> **Try this:** Before reading on, take one minute. Sit still and notice: what's the strongest sensation in your body right now? Where is it? Is it warm, cool, tight, loose, still, moving? That noticing is where all energy work begins.

docs.title: Breath awareness
docs.summary: The foundation of every practice in this course: resting your attention on your breath, step by step, with timings, common difficulties and how to know it's working.
docs.body:
## Why start with the breath?

Every energy practice you'll learn begins with the breath, in nearly every tradition that does this kind of work. There are good reasons:

- **It's always with you.** You can practise anywhere, without tools.
- **It's both automatic and controllable.** You can let it happen or change it, which makes it a bridge between what your body does and what you choose.
- **It changes your state.** Slow, steady breathing tends to calm the nervous system and steady the mind. This is well established.
- **It trains attention.** Learning to rest your attention on one thing, notice when it wanders, and bring it back is the core skill behind feeling, raising and directing energy.

In many languages the words for breath and spirit are linked: Latin *spiritus*, Greek *pneuma*, Hebrew *ruach*. People have long felt that breath is where body and spirit meet.

## Getting ready

- **Where:** somewhere you won't be interrupted for ten minutes. Silence your phone or put it in another room (log the session afterwards).
- **Position:** sit on a chair with your feet flat on the floor and your back upright but not stiff, hands resting on your thighs. You can also sit on a cushion, or lie down if sitting is uncomfortable (though lying down makes it easier to fall asleep).
- **Eyes:** closed, or open and resting softly on a spot on the floor about a metre ahead.
- **Timer:** set a gentle timer so you're not checking the clock. Start with five minutes.

## The practice: counting the breath

1. Settle into your position. Let your shoulders drop. Unclench your jaw. Rest your tongue on the floor of your mouth.
2. Take three slightly deeper breaths than usual, in through the nose and out through the mouth, as if sighing. Let each out-breath release a little tension.
3. Now let your breath return to its own pace, breathing through your nose if you can. Don't try to control it.
4. Notice where you feel the breath most clearly: the cool air at your nostrils, the rise and fall of your chest, or your belly moving. Choose one of these places and rest your attention there.
5. Silently count each out-breath: in... "one"; in... "two"; up to five. Then start again at one.
6. When you notice you've lost count, or are thinking about something else (you will, again and again), gently note "thinking", and go back to "one". No frustration needed: noticing that your mind wandered **is** the practice.
7. When the timer sounds, stop counting. Sit for a few more breaths and notice how you feel. Then open your eyes, wiggle your fingers and toes, and get up slowly.
8. Log the session and write a line or two in your journal.

## The practice: the four-count breath

Once counting feels familiar, try gently shaping the breath. This is a simple, slow rhythm many traditions use to steady themselves before ritual.

1. Settle as before, with three sighing breaths.
2. Breathe in through your nose for a slow count of **four**.
3. Pause, without straining, for a count of **two**.
4. Breathe out through your nose or mouth for a count of **four**, or six if that's comfortable. A longer out-breath tends to calm.
5. Pause for a count of **two**.
6. Repeat for five minutes. Count at whatever speed feels easy; the rhythm matters more than the length.
7. Let the breath return to normal for a minute before you finish.

> **Safety:** Never hold your breath until it's uncomfortable, and never breathe fast or deeply enough to feel dizzy or tingly around the lips: that's over-breathing, and it can bring on panic. If you have a heart or lung condition, anxiety or panic attacks, epilepsy, or are pregnant, skip the pauses and keep the breath natural. Stop at once if you feel faint, and breathe normally.

## What you may notice

During and after breath practice, people commonly notice:

- the breath slowing and deepening on its own
- warmth spreading through the body, or the hands and feet warming
- tingling, especially in the hands and face
- a heavy, settled feeling, or a light, floating one
- the mind quietening for a few seconds at a time, then racing again
- emotions rising: relief, sadness, restlessness
- sleepiness

All of these are normal. If you notice warmth or tingling, especially in your hands, make a note: this is often the first sensation that practitioners call energy. Whether it's subtle energy, blood flow or attention (see the previous lesson), it's the raw material you'll be working with.

## Common difficulties

**"My mind won't stop."** Nobody's mind stops. The skill isn't having no thoughts; it's noticing when you've drifted and coming back. If you come back fifty times in five minutes, that's fifty repetitions of the exercise. Some people find it helps to say "in" and "out" silently instead of counting.

**"I keep controlling my breath and it feels unnatural."** Very common. Try watching the breath as if watching waves on a shore. Or try the four-count breath instead, where control is the point.

**"I fall asleep."** Sit up straighter, open your eyes, practise earlier in the day, or practise after a short walk.

**"I feel anxious when I focus on breathing."** For some people, attention on the breath raises anxiety. Rest your attention on your feet on the floor or your hands on your thighs instead, and breathe naturally. Tell your mentor.

**"I'm bored."** Boredom is a sensation too. Notice where you feel it. It often passes after the first two or three weeks.

**"I feel nothing."** That's fine. You're building a skill, not waiting for an event.

## How you'll know it's working

Not by dramatic experiences. Signs of progress are quieter:

- you notice you've drifted sooner than you used to
- you can settle in fewer breaths
- you start to notice your breath at other times of day, and can slow it when stressed
- you feel a little steadier after practice than before
- sensations you'd never noticed become noticeable

Most people notice some of these within two to three weeks of daily practice.

## Making it a daily habit

Five minutes every day does far more than half an hour once a week. Tie it to something you already do: after brushing your teeth, before your morning drink, when you get into bed. Log each session with its number of minutes. If you miss a day, just carry on the next.

> **Try this:** Tonight, do five minutes of counting the breath. Afterwards, write three things in your journal: how you felt before, what you noticed during, and how you felt after.

docs.title: The body scan
docs.summary: Moving your attention slowly through your body to notice sensation, the skill that lets you feel energy in yourself, with full step-by-step instructions.
docs.body:
## Learning the map

Before you can notice changes in your body during ritual (warmth rising, a buzz in the hands, heaviness after grounding), you need to know what your body normally feels like. Most of us live "in our heads" and notice the body only when something hurts. The **body scan** is a practice of moving your attention slowly through your body, part by part, noticing what's there without trying to change it.

It's used in many meditation traditions and in modern mindfulness courses. In magical practice, it's the way you learn to perceive energy in yourself: where you feel tense or loose, warm or cool, heavy or light, buzzing or still.

## What you're looking for

As you scan each part of the body, you're simply asking: **what can I feel here?** Possible answers include:

- temperature: warm, cool, neutral
- contact: the chair, the floor, clothing, air
- tension or ease: tight, clenched, loose, soft
- movement: pulsing, throbbing, tingling, the breath moving
- weight: heavy, light, sinking
- aliveness: buzzing, fizzing, vibrating, or still and quiet
- discomfort: aches, itches, pain
- nothing in particular

"Nothing in particular" is a perfectly good answer. Some parts of the body feel blank for most people at first. Over time, more becomes noticeable.

## The practice: a fifteen-minute body scan

Set a timer for fifteen minutes. Sit in a chair with your feet flat, or lie on your back with a pillow under your knees.

1. **Settle (one minute).** Close your eyes or soften your gaze. Take three sighing breaths. Then let your breath be natural.
2. **Feel the whole body (one minute).** Notice your whole body at once: its weight on the chair or floor, the points of contact. Notice where the body meets the world.
3. **Feet (one minute).** Bring your attention to your left foot: the toes, the sole, the heel, the top of the foot. What can you feel? Then the right foot. Then both together.
4. **Legs (two minutes).** Move slowly up through the ankles, shins and calves, knees, thighs. Notice where the legs meet the chair or floor.
5. **Hips and belly (one minute).** Notice the pelvis, the lower back, the belly rising and falling with the breath.
6. **Chest and back (two minutes).** Notice the chest moving with the breath, the heartbeat if you can feel it, the upper back, the shoulder blades.
7. **Hands and arms (two minutes).** Bring your attention to your fingertips, one hand and then the other. Hands are often where people first notice tingling, warmth or pulsing. Linger here. Then move up the wrists, forearms, elbows, upper arms.
8. **Shoulders, neck and throat (one minute).** These hold a lot of tension. Just notice.
9. **Face and head (two minutes).** The jaw, the mouth, the tongue, the cheeks, the eyes and the muscles around them, the forehead, the scalp, the top of the head.
10. **The whole body again (one minute).** Feel your body as one whole, breathing.
11. **Finish (one minute).** Wiggle your fingers and toes. Open your eyes. Look around the room and name three things you can see. Sit for a moment before you stand.

At each part, if you notice tension, you can breathe into it and let it soften on the out-breath. But don't force anything. The main skill is noticing.

## A five-minute version

For daily use, try a quick scan: feet and legs, belly and back, hands and arms, shoulders and face, the whole body. About a minute each. This is also how you'll check in with yourself before and after ritual.

## Other ways to scan

People differ. If the standard scan doesn't suit you, try one of these:

- **Visual:** imagine a slow band of soft light, like a photocopier's light, moving up from your feet to your head. Notice what each part feels like as the light passes.
- **Physical:** with your eyes open, touch each part of your body lightly with your hand as you scan it: tap your feet, press your thighs, rest a hand on your belly, your chest, your face. Touch gives attention something to hold.
- **Movement:** tense each part gently for a count of three, then release it, from feet to face. The contrast between tension and release makes sensation easier to notice. (Skip any part that hurts.)
- **Verbal:** name each part silently or aloud as you go: "left foot... warm... right foot... tingling."

## Common difficulties

**"I can't feel anything in some parts."** Very common, especially the back, the thighs and the scalp. Try touching the part, or tensing and releasing it, and notice the after-feeling. Blank spots usually fill in with practice.

**"Paying attention to my body makes me uncomfortable."** For some people, especially those who've experienced trauma or chronic pain, focusing on the body brings up difficult feelings. Keep your eyes open, keep the scan short, skip any area that's distressing, and focus on contact points (feet on the floor, hands on the chair) instead. Tell your mentor. You can learn energy work in other ways.

**"I notice pain."** Note it without dwelling on it, and move on. If you have chronic pain, scan the parts that are comfortable and acknowledge the painful places briefly.

**"I fall asleep."** Sit up, open your eyes, or scan earlier in the day. Many people use the body scan to fall asleep at night; that's a good use for it, just not for this course's practice sessions.

**"My mind wanders."** As with the breath, notice and come back to the part you were on.

> **Safety:** If a body scan brings up strong emotion, memories, panic, or a sense of being outside your body, stop. Open your eyes, press your feet into the floor, look around and name what you see, have a drink of water, and talk to your mentor. These reactions aren't your fault and don't mean you can't practise; they mean this method needs adapting for you.

## Connecting it to energy

Once you've done the body scan a few times, start to notice patterns:

- Where do you usually hold tension? (Shoulders, jaw and belly are common.)
- Which parts feel most alive or "buzzy"? (Often the hands, face and chest.)
- How does your body feel different on a calm day and a stressed day?
- What changes after the scan compared to before?

This is your baseline: what normal feels like for you. In the next module you'll learn to ground and centre, and you'll be able to feel the difference it makes. In the module after that, when you raise energy, you'll recognise the changes because you know where you started.

> **Your coven:** Many covens begin rituals with a short body scan or a breath practice to help everyone arrive. Ask your mentor how your coven helps its members settle before ritual.

## How you'll know it's working

- you can feel more parts of your body than you could at first
- you notice tension sooner, in everyday life, and can let it go
- the hands and face start to feel more vivid when you attend to them
- you can tell, roughly, how your body feels without needing to scan every part

> **Try this:** Do the fifteen-minute body scan tonight. Afterwards, write in your journal which parts felt most vivid, which felt blank, and where you noticed warmth or tingling.

docs.title: Sensing with your hands
docs.summary: The classic first exercise in feeling energy: noticing what happens between your palms, around your body and near objects, with several methods and honest notes on what's going on.
docs.body:
## Why the hands?

Your hands are among the most sensitive parts of your body, packed with nerve endings for touch, warmth and pressure. They're also the part of the body most traditions use to work with energy: blessing, healing, charging objects, casting circles. So the hands are where most people first notice what practitioners call energy.

This lesson teaches several hand-sensing exercises. Try them all over a week or two, and keep the ones that work for you.

## Before you start: wake up your hands

1. Sit comfortably and do two minutes of breath awareness, as you learned in the breath lesson.
2. Rub your palms together briskly for about fifteen seconds, until they're warm.
3. Shake your hands loosely from the wrists for a few seconds.
4. Rest them palms up on your thighs. Breathe slowly and notice how they feel: warmth, tingling, pulsing, heaviness.

That simple sequence already gives most people some sensation. You'll build on it.

## Exercise 1: between the palms

1. After waking up your hands, hold them in front of your chest, palms facing each other, about thirty centimetres (a foot) apart. Keep your elbows and shoulders relaxed.
2. Close your eyes or soften your gaze. Breathe slowly: in for four, out for four.
3. Very slowly, over about ten seconds, bring your palms closer together until they're two or three centimetres (an inch) apart. Don't let them touch.
4. Slowly move them apart again, to about thirty centimetres.
5. Repeat this slow in-and-out movement for two or three minutes. Pay close attention to the space between your palms.
6. Notice: is there a point where you feel something? Warmth? Pressure, as if pushing on a soft balloon? A magnetic pull or push? Tingling? Does it change with distance? With your breath?
7. Finish by resting your hands on your thighs and taking three breaths. Then shake your hands loosely.

Many people feel warmth, a springy pressure or a tingling at some distance, often between five and fifteen centimetres. Some feel it at once; some after a few sessions; some not at all at first.

## Exercise 2: the energy ball

This builds on the first exercise using imagination, which many traditions treat as a key part of working with energy.

1. Start with your palms facing each other, about fifteen centimetres apart, as if holding a ball.
2. As you breathe in, imagine drawing breath and warmth down your arms into your hands. As you breathe out, imagine it flowing from your palms into the space between them.
3. Picture a ball of soft light forming there. Choose any colour that comes to mind. With each breath, it grows a little brighter and denser.
4. Gently "squeeze" the ball by moving your hands slightly closer, and let it expand by moving them apart. Notice any feeling of resistance, warmth or springiness.
5. After three to five minutes, decide what to do with the ball. For now, simply press it into your belly, just below your navel, and let it settle there. Or press your palms flat on the floor and let it go into the ground.
6. Shake your hands. Write down what you noticed.

> **Note:** If you can't "see" pictures in your mind (some people can't, a trait called aphantasia, and plenty of practitioners have it), skip the picture. Instead, focus on a felt sense of warmth gathering, or say silently "gathering... gathering" with each breath. Energy work doesn't depend on visualisation.

## Exercise 3: sensing your own body

1. Wake up your hands.
2. Hold one palm about five centimetres above your other forearm, not touching.
3. Very slowly, move it from your wrist up to your elbow and back.
4. Notice any warmth, tingling or sense of contact, even though you're not touching.
5. Try the same over your knee, your belly, your face (hold the palm a few centimetres away, eyes closed).
6. Notice if some areas feel different from others: warmer, cooler, "thicker", "thinner".

## Exercise 4: sensing an object

1. Gather three or four objects with different characters: a stone, a houseplant, a glass of water, a piece of metal, a piece of jewellery you wear often, an object you've had since childhood.
2. Wake up your hands.
3. Hold your dominant hand (the one you write with) palm down about five centimetres above the first object. Don't touch it. Close your eyes.
4. Breathe slowly and notice anything: temperature, tingling, pressure, a pull, an image, a mood, a memory.
5. After a minute, write down what you noticed in a word or two.
6. Shake your hand, and repeat with each object.
7. Now compare. Were some objects "louder" than others? Did the plant feel different from the stone? Did the old object have a particular feeling?

You can make this more interesting by having someone else set out objects under a cloth so you don't know which is which, and seeing if your impressions are consistent. Treat it as play, not a test of your worth.

## Exercise 5: with a partner (optional, with consent)

If someone in your coven or a willing friend would like to try with you:

1. Ask before you start, and agree that either of you can stop at any time.
2. Sit facing each other. Both wake up your hands.
3. Hold your palms facing theirs, about ten centimetres apart, not touching.
4. Breathe slowly together. Notice what you feel. After two minutes, tell each other.
5. Try one person "sending" (imagining warmth flowing out from their palms) and the other just noticing, without saying who's doing what. Then swap.

## What's actually going on?

Be honest with yourself about this, as you learned in the first lesson of this module. When your palms come close, you can feel the warmth of your own skin; that's a real physical effect. Relaxing and breathing slowly increases blood flow to the hands, which can feel like tingling or pulsing. Attention makes subtle sensations vivid. Tiny, unconscious movements can create a sense of push or pull.

None of this rules out a subtle-energy explanation, and none of it makes the experience less useful. Whatever the cause, you're learning to notice and work with sensations that are the raw material of energy work. Your journal will help you see what's consistent.

## Common difficulties

**"I feel nothing."** Try warming your hands longer, slowing down, practising after the body scan, or practising at a different time of day. Cold hands make it harder. Keep at it for two weeks before deciding it's not for you, and if it still isn't, notice what you **do** perceive: images, moods, a sense of knowing. Not everyone perceives through the hands.

**"I think I'm imagining it."** You might be, in part. Imagination is one of the faculties energy work uses. Write down what you noticed and keep practising; consistency over time will tell you more than any one session.

**"My arms get tired."** Rest your elbows on a table or cushions.

**"It feels too strong or uncomfortable."** Stop, press your palms flat on the floor or a table, and breathe out slowly. Shake your hands. Eat something. The next module teaches grounding, which helps.

## How you'll know it's working

- sensation in your hands appears sooner and more reliably
- you notice differences between objects, places and people that you can describe
- your impressions are somewhat consistent from day to day
- you can tell when your hands feel "ordinary" and when they feel "charged"

> **Try this:** Do Exercise 1 every day for five days, three minutes each time. On the last day, write a short note: did anything change between the first day and the fifth?

docs.title: Sensing places and objects
docs.summary: Turning your attention outward: how to feel the character of a room, an outdoor place or an object, step by step, and how to tell perception from assumption.
docs.body:
## Places have character

You've probably walked into a room and felt that something was off: an argument had just happened, or someone was grieving. Or you've stood in a woodland, a church, a stone circle or by the sea and felt a hush, a lift, a presence. Practitioners say places have **energy**: a character, mood or presence that can be sensed.

How you understand that (subtle energy left by people and events, the spirits of a place, or your mind reading a thousand small cues) is up to you, as you learned in the first lesson. Many traditions give great importance to it. Ancient Greeks and Romans spoke of the **genius loci**, the spirit of a place; Norse and Germanic traditions of **landvættir**, land spirits; many modern pagans simply of "the land". Learning to sense a place is the beginning of relating to it respectfully.

## The practice: sensing a room

Choose a room in your home. Set aside fifteen minutes.

1. **Arrive.** Stand or sit just inside the door. Do one minute of breath awareness. Do a quick body scan: how do you feel right now? This is your baseline.
2. **Look.** With your eyes open, slowly take in the room: light, colour, clutter, order. Notice what your eyes are drawn to.
3. **Listen.** Close your eyes. What sounds are there? What's the quality of the silence?
4. **Feel the air.** Notice temperature, draughts, smells, the feel of the air on your skin.
5. **Feel the room as a whole.** With your eyes still closed, ask yourself: if this room had a mood, what would it be? Calm, busy, heavy, bright, stuck, welcoming, sad? Don't think hard; notice the first impression.
6. **Notice your body.** Has anything changed since step 1? Tighter, looser, heavier, lighter, more alert, sleepier?
7. **Use your hands.** Wake up your hands as in the previous lesson. Walk slowly around the room with one palm held out, facing the walls, the corners, the furniture. Notice any changes in sensation from place to place. Corners, doorways, windows and cluttered spots are interesting to compare.
8. **Record.** Write down what you noticed at each step, in plain words.
9. **Close.** Shake your hands, press your feet into the floor, and take three slow breaths.

Repeat with two or three different rooms, and with the same room at different times of day.

## The practice: sensing a place outdoors

Choose somewhere safe and reasonably quiet: a park, garden, wood, beach or churchyard. Tell someone where you're going if it's somewhere remote, and check the weather.

1. **Approach slowly.** As you arrive, notice how you feel. Some practitioners pause at the edge of a place, as if at a threshold, and say quietly, "Hello. I've come to listen." This is a courtesy many traditions share; you can do it whether or not you believe a spirit hears it.
2. **Settle.** Stand or sit. Do two minutes of breath awareness with your eyes open.
3. **Use each sense in turn,** a minute each: what you see, hear, smell, feel on your skin, feel under your feet.
4. **Feel the place.** Ask yourself: what's this place like? Old, young, busy, sleepy, welcoming, wary, joyful, sorrowful? Notice the first impression without arguing with it.
5. **Move and compare.** Walk slowly. Notice if the feeling changes near a particular tree, a stream, a path, a boundary, a building.
6. **Notice anything that draws you.** A stone, a tree, a spot where you'd like to sit. Go there and notice what you feel.
7. **Leave with courtesy.** Say thank you, aloud or silently. Don't take anything away, except litter you pick up. Some people leave a small, harmless gift (a little clean water poured on the ground, a song); never leave food that harms wildlife, candles, glitter, plastic or anything that won't break down.
8. **Record it** as soon as you can.

> **Safety:** Outdoors, your physical safety comes before any practice. Keep your eyes open in public places, stay aware of people around you, don't trespass, don't light fires, and leave if you feel unsafe, whether for a magical or an ordinary reason. Gut feelings of danger deserve respect either way.

## The practice: reading an object

Objects, especially old, handmade or much-loved ones, are often said to carry the energy of their makers, owners and history. Practitioners use this when choosing tools, cleansing second-hand items, and making charms.

1. Choose an object: something you own with a known history is a good start, then try something second-hand or unfamiliar.
2. Sit and do one minute of breath awareness.
3. Hold the object in both hands, or hold your palm just above it.
4. Close your eyes and notice: weight, temperature, texture first. Then any sensation in your hands, any mood, image, memory, colour or word that comes to mind.
5. After two or three minutes, put it down, shake your hands, and write it all down.
6. If it's a second-hand object with a known history, check your impressions against what you know afterwards. Don't look for proof; just notice.

> **Your coven:** Many covens teach members to sense a ritual space before working there, and some ask permission of the land, the household spirits or the gods first. Ask your mentor how your coven approaches a new place.

## Perception or assumption?

This is the hard part, and the most important. When you sense a place, your mind draws on everything it already knows: the room is messy, so it feels "stuck"; the church is old, so it feels "holy"; you know someone died here, so it feels "sad". These are **assumptions**. They're not wrong, and they're part of how intuition works, but they're not the same as fresh perception.

Ways to tell the difference over time:

- **Notice first, explain later.** Write the raw impression before you think about why.
- **Watch for surprise.** Impressions that surprise you, or go against what you expected, are worth paying special attention to.
- **Check consistency.** Visit the same place on different days and in different moods. What stays the same?
- **Compare with others.** In your coven, sense a space separately and compare notes before discussing. Agreement you didn't plan is interesting; disagreement is normal.
- **Account for your state.** If you're tired, sad or anxious, everything can feel heavy. Your baseline (from the body scan) helps you tell what's you and what's the place.

## Common difficulties

**"Every place feels the same."** Try places that are very different: a busy supermarket and a quiet wood, a hospital waiting room and your bedroom. Contrast helps.

**"I only get thoughts, not feelings."** That's fine. Thoughts, words and images are also perceptions. Write them down.

**"Some places make me uneasy."** Leave, ground yourself, and note it. You don't need to "fix" a place, and you shouldn't go poking at somewhere that feels wrong. Tell your mentor.

> **Try this:** This week, sense three rooms in your home and one place outdoors. For each, write one sentence: "This place feels..." and one sentence: "I noticed this in my body..."

docs.title: Keeping a perception journal
docs.summary: How to record what you perceive so that, over weeks and months, you can see what's real, consistent and useful for you, with a simple format to follow.
docs.body:
## Why a separate kind of note

In the welcome module you started a practice journal. For energy work, it helps to keep your notes in a particular way, so that over time you can answer questions like: Do I feel more than I used to? Are my impressions consistent? What helps me perceive, and what gets in the way? Is what I notice real for me, or wishful thinking?

A **perception journal** is simply a practice journal with a steady format, used every time you do an energy practice. You can keep it in the answer box of each step, in your Grimoire, or on paper.

## A simple format

For each session, write:

1. **Date, time, place.**
2. **Practice.** Which one, for how long. ("Hand-sensing, Exercise 1, three minutes.")
3. **Before.** Your state in a few words: energy level, mood, anything going on. ("Tired after work, a bit anxious.")
4. **Sensations.** What you noticed in your body, in plain words, with where and how strong. A simple scale helps: 0 nothing, 1 faint, 2 clear, 3 strong. ("Warmth in both palms, 2. Tingling in fingertips, 1. Pressure between palms at about ten centimetres, 1.")
5. **Other impressions.** Images, colours, moods, words, memories, a sense of presence. ("A pale blue colour. Felt calmer.")
6. **After.** How you felt when you finished. ("Calmer, hands warm, a bit spacey.")
7. **Interpretation (optional).** What you think it might mean, kept separate. ("Maybe what my mentor calls energy gathering.")
8. **Questions.** Anything to ask your mentor.

Most entries will take two or three minutes to write. Don't make it a chore.

## An example entry

Here's what a typical beginner's entry might look like:

"Tuesday, 9.40pm, bedroom, sitting on the bed. Hand-sensing, Exercise 1, about four minutes, after two minutes of breath. Before: tired, a bit wound up after a long day. Sensations: warmth in both palms, 2. Faint tingling in the fingertips, 1, stronger on the right. A soft springy feeling between the palms at about a hand's width, 1, came and went. Other: nothing much; kept thinking about work. After: calmer, hands warm. Interpretation: maybe the springiness is what the lesson means by pressure. Question: is it normal for one hand to feel more than the other?"

Notice that it's short, plain and honest, and that the question at the end gives your mentor something to answer.

## Plain words first

Practitioners have a lot of vocabulary: chakras, auras, astral, vibrations, frequencies. These words come from particular systems (chakras, for instance, come from Indian tantric and yogic traditions, and the familiar Western seven-chakra-and-rainbow model is a twentieth-century blend). Avoid using them in your journal for now unless your coven teaches them. Plain words keep you honest:

- not "my aura expanded", but "I felt warmth spreading out from my chest and a sense of being larger"
- not "the room had bad vibes", but "my shoulders tightened when I walked in and I wanted to leave"
- not "a spirit was present", but "I had a strong sense of someone standing behind me, and the back of my neck prickled"

Later, you and your mentor can decide what these experiences mean in your tradition's language.

## Looking back

Every two weeks or so, read back through your entries and ask:

- **What's changed?** Do sensations come sooner, stronger, or in new places?
- **What's consistent?** Do the same objects, places or practices produce similar impressions?
- **What helps?** Time of day, mood, place, warming the hands, breath first?
- **What hinders?** Tiredness, phone nearby, rushing, a busy mind?
- **What surprised me?**

Write a short summary. These summaries are what you'll share with your mentor at the end of this module.

## The honest middle

As you look back, you'll probably find three kinds of entry:

- **Clear and consistent:** "My palms warm and tingle every time I do the breath first." Good. This is your foundation.
- **Interesting but uncertain:** "I saw an image of a door when I held my grandmother's ring." Keep it, hold it lightly, and see if anything comes of it.
- **Probably me:** "The room felt heavy, but I was exhausted." That's not failure; it's what the journal is for.

Neither dismiss everything as imagination nor accept everything as real. That middle way, sometimes called **discernment**, is one of the most valuable skills in the craft, and you'll keep developing it for as long as you practise.

> **Note:** Some practitioners never feel strong physical sensations, but perceive through images, emotions or a quiet sense of knowing. If that's you, your journal will show it. It's a valid way to perceive, and your mentor can help you work with it.

## Sharing with your mentor

At the end of this module, you'll write a summary of your perception journal in the answer box. Include:

- which practices you did and roughly how often
- what you noticed most often
- what changed over the weeks
- what was difficult
- any questions or experiences you'd like to talk about

Your mentor isn't grading your sensitivity. They're looking at how honestly and carefully you observe, and whether anything needs support.

> **Your coven:** Some covens keep shared records of what members perceive during group ritual, to compare afterwards. Ask your mentor whether yours does, and how members share experiences in a way that respects everyone's privacy.

## Privacy and kindness to yourself

Your perception journal is private unless you choose to share it. Write freely, including the sessions where nothing happened and the times you felt silly. You're learning to pay a new kind of attention, and that takes time.

> **Try this:** Use the format above for your next three energy practices. After the third, read them together and write one sentence about what you notice.

docs.title: Grounding and centring
docs.summary: What grounding and centring are, why every practitioner needs them, the signs you need them, and several step-by-step methods for each.
docs.body:
## The first skills of safe practice

If you learn only two skills from this whole course, make them grounding and centring. They're what keep energy work, ritual and magic safe and steady. Experienced practitioners use them before and after every working, and in daily life whenever they feel scattered.

**Grounding** means settling yourself: bringing your attention fully into your body and the present moment, and (in energy terms) connecting with the earth so that excess or unwanted energy drains away and steady energy flows in. A grounded person feels solid, calm, present and clear-headed.

**Centring** means gathering yourself to your own middle: drawing your attention and energy in from wherever they've scattered (worries, other people, the screen) to a still point in your body. A centred person feels collected, balanced and themselves.

They're closely linked, and most people do them together: first grounding (down and settled), then centring (gathered and balanced). Your coven may treat them as one practice.

## Why they matter

However you understand energy (see the energy module), these practices do something real:

- **Before practice,** they help you arrive: leaving the day behind, steadying your breath and attention, so you can perceive clearly.
- **After practice,** they help you come back: settling any buzz, spaciness or emotion, so you can drive, cook and talk to people normally.
- **In daily life,** they help with stress, overwhelm and being pulled in all directions.

In the energy view, grounding stops raised energy from building up in you with nowhere to go, which practitioners say causes headaches, jitteriness or exhaustion. In the psychological view, grounding techniques are well-known ways to calm the nervous system and come back to the present; similar methods are used to help people with anxiety. Either way, it works.

## Signs you need grounding

- feeling spacey, floaty or "not quite here"
- light-headedness or dizziness after practice
- buzzing, jittery or restless energy you can't settle
- racing thoughts, or not being able to focus
- clumsiness: dropping things, bumping into furniture
- feeling overwhelmed by noise, people or emotions
- difficulty sleeping after evening practice

## Method 1: roots (visual)

The classic method taught in many covens.

1. Sit on a chair with your feet flat on the floor, or stand with your feet hip-width apart, knees soft. Close your eyes or lower your gaze.
2. Take three slow breaths, in for four and out for four.
3. Bring your attention to the soles of your feet. Feel their contact with the floor.
4. Imagine roots growing from the soles of your feet (or from the base of your spine if you're sitting). With each out-breath, they grow downward: through the floor, through the foundations, into the soil, between stones, down into the cool, dark earth.
5. Let them go as deep as feels right. Some people imagine them reaching a core of warm stone or water.
6. On each out-breath, imagine anything you don't need (tension, jitteriness, worry, excess energy) draining down the roots into the earth, which can take it without harm.
7. On each in-breath, imagine steady, calm strength rising up through the roots into your body. Many people imagine it as a colour: deep green, brown or gold.
8. Continue for two to five minutes, until you feel settled and heavier.
9. You can leave the roots in place (many people keep a light connection all day) or draw them gently back up. Open your eyes. Press your feet into the floor.

## Method 2: physical grounding

Uses your body and senses, with no imagery. Excellent if visualisation isn't for you, and the fastest method when you're very spacey.

1. Stand or sit with your feet flat. Press them firmly into the floor for a count of five, then release. Repeat three times.
2. Press your palms together hard for five seconds, then release. Or press them flat on a table or the floor.
3. Stamp your feet gently, or walk slowly, feeling each step: heel, sole, toes.
4. Name, aloud or silently: five things you can see, four you can feel touching your body, three you can hear, two you can smell, one you can taste.
5. If you can, go outside and stand barefoot on grass, soil or sand for a few minutes, or put your hands on a tree or a stone.
6. Eat something, especially something substantial like bread, nuts, cheese or a root vegetable, and drink a glass of water. Eating is one of the most widely used groundings after ritual, and many covens share food at the end of a rite for exactly this reason.

## Method 3: breath and words (verbal)

1. Sit or stand comfortably.
2. Breathe in slowly for four counts, and as you breathe out for six, say aloud or silently a grounding phrase. For example: "I am here. My feet are on the earth." Or simply: "Down... down... down."
3. Repeat for one to three minutes.
4. If your tradition has a short prayer or a name of a deity of the earth or home, you can use it here.

## Method 4: lying on the earth

When you feel very overwhelmed or drained, lie on your back on the floor or on the ground outside, arms by your sides, palms down. Let your whole weight sink. Breathe slowly and let the floor or earth hold you. Stay for five to ten minutes. Get up slowly, rolling onto your side first.

## Centring: finding your middle

Once grounded, centre yourself. Most traditions place the "centre" in one of two places: the belly, a couple of fingers below the navel, or the heart, in the middle of the chest. Choose whichever feels more natural. (The belly is often easier for beginners, because it's where breath and balance are felt most.)

### Method A: gathering in (visual)

1. Grounded, sit or stand still, breathing slowly.
2. Place one hand over your centre. Feel the warmth of your hand and the breath moving under it.
3. Imagine all the threads of your attention, scattered across the day (the inbox, the argument, tomorrow's worries), being gently drawn back in, like a spider gathering its threads, to that point under your hand.
4. Picture your centre as a small, steady light or flame. With each in-breath, it gathers; with each out-breath, it settles and steadies.
5. Continue for two minutes. Notice when you feel collected.

### Method B: balance (physical)

1. Stand with your feet hip-width apart.
2. Slowly sway forward and back, then side to side, making the movements smaller and smaller until you come to stillness at the point of balance.
3. Rest your attention on your belly. Notice how your body holds itself upright from this point.
4. Breathe here for a minute.

### Method C: words

Say slowly, with a breath for each line: "I gather myself. I am whole. I am here." Or your own words. Some people simply say their own name.

## Grounding and centring together: the two-minute sequence

This is the sequence you'll use before and after every practice in this course.

1. Three slow breaths (in for four, out for four).
2. Feel your feet; send roots down, or press your feet into the floor (thirty seconds to a minute).
3. Let tension and excess drain down on the out-breath; draw steadiness up on the in-breath (thirty seconds).
4. Hand on your centre; gather your attention in (thirty seconds).
5. One last breath. Notice how you feel compared with before.

## How you'll know it's working

- you feel heavier, steadier, calmer, more present
- your breath slows on its own
- thoughts slow down; the room seems clearer
- after practice, the buzz or spaciness settles within a few minutes
- with practice, you can ground in under a minute, and eventually in a few breaths

## Common difficulties

**"I can't imagine roots."** Use physical grounding or words. They work just as well.

**"I feel too heavy or sleepy afterwards."** You may have overdone it. Stand up, stretch, look around, and next time draw your roots back up a little at the end.

**"I don't feel any different."** Try grounding when you're obviously ungrounded (after a stressful call, a busy shop, too much coffee). The difference is easier to notice.

**"It makes me feel trapped or heavy in a bad way."** Some people dislike the sense of being rooted. Try lighter imagery, such as resting your weight on a friendly floor, or a purely physical method.

> **Safety:** If you remain dizzy, faint or detached after grounding, eating and drinking, or if such feelings keep coming back, stop practising and seek medical advice. Grounding helps with ordinary after-practice spaciness, but it isn't a treatment for medical symptoms.

> **Your coven:** Your coven probably has its own way of grounding and centring before ritual, sometimes led by one person for everyone. Ask your mentor to show you, and add it to your Grimoire.

docs.title: Shielding
docs.summary: What practitioners mean by shielding, when it helps, several step-by-step methods, and what a shield can't do.
docs.body:
## What is shielding?

**Shielding** is setting a protective boundary around yourself, so that you can be open to the world without being overwhelmed by it. Practitioners describe it as an energetic boundary that filters what comes in: other people's moods, the noise of a crowded place, the intensity of a ritual, or unwanted influences.

As with energy itself, people understand it in different ways:

- **Energy view:** a real field around you that you can strengthen and shape.
- **Spirit view:** asking for protection from your gods, ancestors or guardian spirits, or wearing a protective charm that they bless.
- **Psychological view:** a focused intention and image that helps you hold a boundary, stay calm and not absorb others' emotions.

All three lead to similar practices.

## When to shield

- in crowded or noisy places: shops, public transport, festivals
- before difficult conversations or meetings
- when you work with distressed people (in health care, teaching, customer service)
- when you feel easily drained by other people
- before ritual or energy work, especially in a new group or place
- when you notice you're "picking up" other people's moods and carrying them home

## Signs you might need a shield

- feeling drained or tired after being around certain people or places
- taking on others' moods: coming home anxious after time with an anxious friend
- feeling raw, jumpy or overwhelmed in busy places
- finding it hard to tell your own feelings from other people's

> **Safety:** These signs can also come from ordinary causes: tiredness, being an introvert in an extrovert's world, depression, anxiety, or physical illness. Shielding is a useful tool, but if you feel drained or overwhelmed much of the time, talk to a doctor as well as your mentor.

## Before you shield: ground and centre

A shield works best around a grounded, centred self. Always do the two-minute grounding and centring sequence first, at least until you can shield quickly.

## Method 1: the sphere of light (visual)

The most common method.

1. Ground and centre.
2. Bring your attention to your centre, the steady light in your belly or chest.
3. As you breathe out, imagine that light expanding outward through your body and beyond your skin, until it forms a sphere or egg shape all around you, about an arm's length from your body in every direction: above your head, below your feet, behind your back.
4. Make the edge of the sphere clear and firm, like a soap bubble that won't burst, or a wall of soft glass. Choose a colour that feels protective to you: many use white, gold, blue or silver.
5. Set its purpose. Silently or aloud: "Only what is good for me may enter. All else is turned away." Or "I am open to love and closed to harm."
6. Breathe into it for a minute, feeling it steady around you.
7. Then let it fade from your active attention, trusting it to stay. Open your eyes.

## Method 2: the mirror

For when you're dealing with hostility or intense emotions you don't want to absorb.

1. Ground and centre.
2. Imagine the outside of your sphere becoming mirrored, facing outward. What comes towards you is reflected back, without harm, to its source or into the earth.
3. Keep the inside warm and soft, so you're comfortable within it.

> **Note:** Some practitioners prefer a mirror that sends things down into the earth rather than back at people, so that nothing is returned to anyone with force. That's in keeping with the ethics of most covens: protect yourself, but don't send harm back.

## Method 3: the cloak (physical and visual)

1. Ground and centre.
2. Stand, and with your hands, make the gesture of putting on a cloak: reach behind your shoulders, draw it around you, fasten it at your chest. Pull up an imagined hood.
3. Feel it as heavy, warm and close. Choose its colour and texture.
4. When you no longer need it, make the gesture of taking it off and hanging it up.

The physical gesture makes this easy to remember, and easy to do discreetly in a much smaller form (a touch at the collarbone) in public.

## Method 4: the filter

A shield doesn't have to block everything. In this version, your boundary is a fine net or a living hedge: it lets in what's good (warmth, friendship, information) and catches what isn't (hostility, others' distress). This suits people who find solid shields make them feel cut off.

## Method 5: words and prayer

Speak a short protective phrase or prayer, perhaps calling on a deity, ancestor or guardian. For example, "I stand within the protection of my gods and ancestors. Nothing ill may cross." Your tradition may have its own: many traditions have protective prayers and gods of the threshold.

## Method 6: a physical object

Many people carry a protective object: a piece of jewellery, a stone, a small pouch, a holy symbol. To use one as a shield:

1. Ground and centre, holding the object.
2. Imagine your shield forming as in Method 1, and imagine it bound into the object.
3. Say what it's for: "While I wear this, my boundary holds."
4. Each time you put it on, touch it and briefly remember the shield.

The object becomes a reminder, and in many traditions it's understood as a blessed or charged thing in its own right. You'll learn more about charging objects in the raising energy module.

## What a shield can't do

A shield is a practice for your own steadiness. It isn't:

- **physical protection.** It doesn't replace locking your door, staying out of dangerous situations, or calling for help.
- **a replacement for boundaries in real life.** If someone is draining or mistreating you, the most powerful shield is often saying no, leaving, or limiting contact.
- **a wall to hide behind forever.** Constant heavy shielding can leave you feeling cut off and numb. Use lighter shields day to day and stronger ones when needed.
- **a cure for anxiety, depression or trauma.** It can help alongside proper care, not instead of it.

## Checking and taking down

Once a day, or after a difficult situation, briefly check your shield: imagine it, notice if it feels thin or damaged, and breathe it back to strength. At the end of the day, or when you're safe at home, you can let it soften or fade, or keep a light one while you sleep. Some people "wash" their shield at the end of the day, imagining it rinsed clean, which links to the next lesson on cleansing.

## How you'll know it's working

- you feel steadier in places that used to overwhelm you
- you come home less drained after difficult days
- you can tell your own moods from other people's more easily
- with practice, you can set a shield in a few breaths

> **Your coven:** Some covens teach a particular shield, or ask members to shield before group workings. Others, especially in traditions that work closely with gods and spirits, rely more on purification and the gods' protection. Ask your mentor what your coven uses.

> **Try this:** Set a sphere-of-light shield each morning for a week, and check it each evening. Note in your journal whether you notice any difference in how drained or steady you feel.

docs.title: Cleansing yourself
docs.summary: Why practitioners cleanse themselves, signs you need it, and safe step-by-step methods with water, salt, smoke, sound, breath and movement.
docs.body:
## What is cleansing?

**Cleansing** (also called purification or clearing) means removing what you don't want to carry: stale or unwanted energy, the residue of a hard day, someone else's mood, the after-effects of a difficult ritual, or (in many religious traditions) ritual impurity. It leaves you clear, fresh and ready.

Cleansing yourself is one of the oldest religious practices there is. Ancient Greeks washed their hands in lustral water (**khernips**) before approaching the gods. Romans purified with water and fire. Many traditions use salt, water, smoke, sound or breath. Modern witches cleanse before and after ritual.

How cleansing differs from grounding and shielding:

- **Grounding** settles you and connects you to the earth.
- **Shielding** keeps unwanted things out.
- **Cleansing** clears away what's already clinging to you.

In practice, they go together: cleanse, ground and centre, shield.

## Signs you need cleansing

- feeling heavy, grimy or "sticky" in a way a nap doesn't fix
- carrying a mood that isn't yours after a difficult encounter
- feeling unsettled after visiting a hospital, funeral, crowded place or argument
- before ritual, to arrive fresh
- after ritual or energy work, especially if it was intense
- after illness, a breakup, a move, or any big transition

## Method 1: water (the shower or bath)

The simplest and most universal cleansing.

1. Before you begin, ground and centre for a minute.
2. Take a shower or bath as normal. As the water runs over you, imagine it washing away everything you don't need: tension, other people's moods, the day's residue. Some people imagine the water glowing with light.
3. Start at the head and move down. Pay particular attention to your hands, the back of your neck and your feet.
4. As the water drains away, imagine everything you've released going with it, down into the earth to be cleansed.
5. You can say a few words: "Water, wash me clean. Take what's not mine. Leave me clear."
6. Finish with a moment of gratitude and dry off.

## Method 2: hand-washing (quick and traditional)

Washing the hands and face is a cleansing in many religious traditions. It's quick, and you can do it anywhere.

1. Fill a bowl with clean, cool water, or use a tap.
2. Breathe slowly and set your intention: "I wash away what I don't need, to come clean to my practice."
3. Wash your hands slowly, and splash or touch water to your face.
4. Shake or pat your hands dry.

> **Your coven:** In Hellenic practice, purification before ritual uses **khernips**: water into which a burning twig or match has been plunged, used to wash the hands and sometimes sprinkled on the participants and space. This is taught in full in the Hellenic tradition module. Other traditions have their own forms; your mentor will show you yours.

## Method 3: salt

Salt has been used to purify for thousands of years, in many cultures. It's often used dissolved in water.

1. Dissolve a pinch of salt (ordinary table or sea salt) in a bowl of water. Stir it clockwise (the direction the sun moves across the sky in the Northern Hemisphere; many in the Southern Hemisphere stir anticlockwise for the same reason) while saying what it's for.
2. Dip your fingers and touch the salt water to your forehead, hands and feet, or sprinkle a little over yourself.
3. Or add a handful of salt to your bath.

> **Safety:** Salt water can sting cuts and irritate sensitive skin or eczema; use plain water if so. Rinse salt off your skin afterwards if it dries tight. Never put salt on plants or soil you care about: it kills them. Don't use salt baths if you've been told to avoid them for a medical reason.

## Method 4: smoke

Passing smoke from incense, resin or dried herbs around the body is a cleansing used in many cultures.

1. Open a window. Light a stick of incense, or put a little resin (such as frankincense) on a lit charcoal disc in a heat-proof dish of sand.
2. Hold it safely and let the smoke pass around you: from your feet up to your head, front and back, under your arms, around your hands. Or stand still and waft the smoke towards yourself.
3. Imagine the smoke carrying away what you don't need as it rises and drifts out of the window.
4. Put out the incense or let the charcoal burn out safely in its dish. Never leave it unattended.

> **Safety:** Smoke can trigger asthma and other breathing problems, harm birds and small pets, and set off smoke alarms. Always ventilate, use small amounts, and choose another method if anyone present has breathing problems. Charcoal discs get extremely hot: use a heat-proof dish with sand, and handle with tongs.

> **Note:** Burning herbs is often called "smudging", but smudging is a particular practice of some Indigenous nations of North America, and the white sage often sold for it is being overharvested from the wild. Call it smoke cleansing, and use herbs grown in your own region or garden (garden sage, rosemary, lavender, mugwort, juniper, bay) or resins from reliable sources. The Living Library's notes on closed traditions and sourcing explain more.

## Method 5: sound

Sound is a smoke-free, water-free method that suits shared homes and people with breathing problems.

1. Use a bell, singing bowl, drum, rattle, or simply clap your hands.
2. Ring or clap around your body: above your head, by each ear, around your shoulders, hands and feet.
3. Imagine the sound shaking loose and scattering anything clinging to you.
4. Finish with silence for a few breaths.

You can also hum or sing a long note, feeling the vibration in your chest.

## Method 6: breath and brushing (visual and physical)

No tools needed.

1. Ground and centre.
2. Breathe in deeply and imagine fresh, clean light filling you.
3. Breathe out through your mouth with a sigh, imagining everything stale leaving with the breath.
4. With your hands held just above your body, or lightly touching, brush down from the top of your head to your feet, front and back, as if brushing off dust. Flick your hands towards the floor after each stroke.
5. Repeat the breath and brushing three to seven times.
6. Shake your hands vigorously at the end and wash them if you can.

## Method 7: movement and the outdoors

- **Shaking:** stand and shake your whole body loosely for a minute: hands, arms, shoulders, legs. Many people find this surprisingly effective at shifting a stuck mood.
- **Wind and rain:** stand in a breeze, or in light rain, and imagine it blowing or washing you clean.
- **Moving water:** dip your hands in a stream or the sea (safely). Many traditions regard running water as cleansing.

## Before and after ritual

Before ritual, cleansing marks the change from everyday life to sacred time. Many practitioners bathe, put on clean clothes, and wash their hands. After ritual, a light cleansing (washing the hands, shaking off) helps close the work. Your coven will have its own customs.

## How you'll know it's working

- you feel lighter, fresher, clearer
- a mood that wasn't yours lifts or fades
- you feel ready to begin practice, or ready to return to ordinary life
- over time, you come to recognise the "after cleansing" feeling and can call it up quickly

> **Try this:** Try three different methods this week: water, one of the smoke-free methods (sound, breath and brushing, or shaking), and one more of your choice. Note in your journal how each felt.

docs.title: Quick versions for daily life
docs.summary: Short forms of grounding, centring, shielding and cleansing that take seconds to a minute, a simple daily routine, and what to do when they aren't enough.
docs.body:
## Practice that fits real life

The full methods in the last three lessons take a few minutes each and are best learned at home, in quiet. But the point of learning them is to use them when you need them: on the bus, before a meeting, in a queue, after a difficult phone call. With practice, each can shrink to a few breaths, and you can do them without anyone noticing.

Quick versions work because you've practised the long versions. The full practice builds the feeling; the quick version calls it back. So keep doing the full forms regularly while you use the short ones day to day.

## The one-breath ground

1. Feel your feet on the floor.
2. Breathe in, and on a long out-breath, imagine everything you don't need draining down through your feet.
3. Press your feet down slightly as you do it.

Use it: before you speak in a meeting, when you notice your shoulders creeping up, before you answer a call.

## The thirty-second ground and centre

1. Three slow breaths, feet on the floor.
2. On the first, send roots down (or press your feet down).
3. On the second, let tension drain.
4. On the third, touch your centre (belly or chest), or just bring your attention there, and gather yourself in.

Use it: when you sit down at your desk, before ritual, when you come home.

## The quick shield

1. Touch your collarbone, or a protective object you wear.
2. On one breath, imagine your sphere, cloak or filter around you.
3. Silently say your shield phrase: "Only good may enter."

Use it: walking into a crowded place, before a hard conversation, on public transport.

## The ten-second cleanse

Choose one:

- wash your hands slowly with intention: "I wash away what isn't mine"
- breathe out with a sigh and brush down your arms with your hands
- shake your hands hard for five seconds
- step outside into the air for a few breaths

Use it: after a difficult encounter, between tasks, after leaving a hospital or a busy shop.

## The pocket version for public places

All of these can be made invisible: pressing your feet into the floor, a slow out-breath, a hand resting on your belly, touching a necklace, washing your hands in a public washroom. No one needs to know you're doing anything.

## A simple daily routine

Here's a routine that takes about five minutes a day. Try it for two weeks and adapt it.

**Morning (two to three minutes):**

1. Before you look at your phone, sit on the edge of your bed with your feet on the floor.
2. Ground and centre (the two-minute sequence from the first lesson).
3. Set a light shield for the day.

**During the day (seconds each):**

- one-breath grounds whenever you notice tension
- a quick shield before demanding situations
- a ten-second cleanse after hard encounters

**Evening (two to three minutes):**

1. Cleanse: a shower with intention, washing your hands and face, or breath and brushing.
2. Check and soften your shield.
3. Ground: press your feet into the floor, or lie down and let the bed hold you, letting the day drain away.
4. A breath or two of gratitude for anything good in the day.

## Before and after any practice

From now on in this course, begin and end every practice with grounding and centring, and use cleansing and shielding when it suits. Your mentor will expect this, and so will your coven in ritual. It becomes automatic surprisingly quickly.

## Signs you need more than a quick version

- you've used quick versions several times and still feel spacey, drained or jittery
- the feeling has lasted more than a day
- it's after an intense ritual or energy working

Then do a full practice: the long grounding, a proper cleansing bath or shower, food, water, rest, time outdoors. And if that doesn't help, read the next section.

## When it isn't enough

Grounding, shielding and cleansing are practices for everyday wellbeing and for safe energy work. They aren't treatments. If you notice any of the following, stop magical practice for a while and talk to your mentor, and to a doctor or mental health professional:

- feeling drained, flat or overwhelmed most days for two weeks or more
- persistent anxiety or panic
- feeling detached from yourself or the world much of the time
- feeling that you're under constant psychic or spiritual attack, so that you're spending more and more time on protection
- your protective practices growing into rituals you feel you must do, or something bad will happen

These are signs that something else needs care. They're common, treatable, and nothing to be ashamed of. A good coven will support you in getting help.

> **Safety:** If protection practices start to take over your day, or you feel frightened without them, that's a reason to pause and talk to someone, not to shield harder.

> **Your coven:** Covens often have a short grounding that everyone does at the start and end of a gathering, or a habit of sharing food afterwards. Learn your coven's versions and you'll always have them to hand.

## Recording it

For the next two weeks, log your daily grounding and centring in the app. Note in your journal which quick versions you used, when, and whether they helped. After two weeks, look back and see what you reach for most. That's the start of your own toolkit.

> **Try this:** Choose one quick version and attach it to something you do every day: grounding as you unlock your front door, shielding as you step onto the bus, cleansing as you wash your hands after work. Do it every time for a week.

docs.title: The arc of a working
docs.summary: What it means to raise, direct and release energy, the seven parts of every energy working from preparation to grounding, and why you decide your purpose first.
docs.body:
## What "raising energy" means

So far you've learned to **feel** energy (the energy module) and to **steady** yourself (grounding, centring, shielding and cleansing). This module teaches the next three verbs: **raise**, **direct** and **release**.

- **Raising energy** means deliberately building up a heightened state of force, feeling and focus, using breath, sound, movement, rhythm and imagination. It usually feels like rising warmth, tingling, a racing heart, intensity, excitement, or a sense of pressure building.
- **Directing energy** means focusing that heightened state on a purpose: into a candle, an object, a symbol, or towards a goal.
- **Releasing energy** means letting it go, all at once, to do its work: the moment the working is "sent".
- Then **grounding** settles whatever is left in you.

How you understand this depends on your view of energy (see "What is energy?"):

- In the **subtle energy** view, you're generating and gathering a real force, and sending it into the world to influence events.
- In the **spirit and relationship** view, you're offering devotion, attention and power to gods and spirits, and asking their help.
- In the **psychological** view, you're bringing your whole self (body, emotion, imagination and will) to a peak of focus on one purpose, then letting go, which changes how you feel, what you notice, and what you do next.

The steps are the same in every view. That's why covens with members who hold different views can work together.

> **Your coven:** Not every tradition "raises energy" in these words. Hellenic and Roman practice centre on prayer, offering and libation to the gods; Heathen practice on blót and sumbel; Christian folk magic on prayer and psalms. But the underlying skills here (building intensity through voice, rhythm and focus, directing it to one purpose, and letting go) appear in almost every tradition's prayer, song and ritual. Your tradition module will show you how your coven uses them.

## The seven parts of a working

Every energy working, whether five minutes alone or an hour with your coven, follows the same arc. Learn it now and you'll recognise it everywhere.

### 1. Decide the purpose

Before you raise anything, know exactly what it's for, in one sentence. "To bring calm and focus to my week of exams." "To bless this pendant as a protective charm." "To give thanks for the harvest." Energy raised without a purpose tends to leave you buzzing and unsettled, with nowhere for it to go.

Check the purpose against your ethics:

- Is it for yourself, or for someone who has **asked** for it or agreed to it?
- Could it harm anyone, or take away anyone's free choice?
- Is it paired with practical action? (A working for a new job goes with sending applications.)

### 2. Prepare

Cleanse yourself and your space, then ground and centre. Many people also set sacred space at this point (the next module teaches how). Have everything you need within reach: candle, matches, the object, water. Turn off your phone.

### 3. Raise

Use one or more methods (breath, chant, movement, rhythm, visualisation, taught in the next lesson) to build intensity. Start slowly and build.

### 4. Focus and hold

As the energy builds, keep your purpose in mind: see it, feel it, say it. This is what turns raw intensity into a working. Many people repeat a short phrase of intent throughout.

### 5. Direct and release

At the peak, when you feel the energy is as strong as it will usefully get, send it into its target in one decisive moment: push it from your hands into the candle, breathe it into the object, shout the final word, drop to the floor. Then **let go**, of the energy and of the outcome.

### 6. Ground the excess

Ground and centre thoroughly. Press your palms to the floor and let any remaining buzz drain into the earth. Eat and drink something.

### 7. Record

Write down what you did, what you felt, and how you feel afterwards. Later, note any results.

## Why release matters

Beginners often find raising easier than releasing. You build a wonderful intensity and then hold on to it, unsure if you've done it right. Practitioners teach that holding on does two things: it leaves you jittery, headachy or unable to sleep, and it keeps the working "tied" to you, so you keep checking on it, worrying at it, which many traditions say weakens it.

Releasing is an act of trust: you've done your part, now you let it go. In the psychological view, it's the difference between obsessing about a goal and doing your best and moving on. Either way, practise letting go.

## How you'll recognise the peak

There's no meter for this, and it varies from person to person. Common signs:

- the chant or movement reaches a natural fullest point and wants to change
- a feeling of fullness, pressure or "now"
- your heart is beating faster and your skin is warm or tingling
- an emotional crest: joy, power, tears
- in a group, everyone seems to rise together

At first you'll miss it, go too early, or go too late. That's fine. It's like learning when to laugh at a joke: you get better by doing it.

## What results look like

Be honest with yourself here, too. Magic as this course teaches it is a practice, not a guarantee. Results, when they come, often look ordinary: you feel calmer during your exams; an opportunity appears and you're ready to take it; you notice something you'd have missed. Sometimes nothing seems to happen. Record your workings and look back after a few months: the spellcraft module will teach you how to evaluate results fairly.

> **Safety:** Raising energy can bring strong emotions and physical sensations. If it ever feels frightening, out of control, or leaves you unwell, stop, ground thoroughly, eat and drink, and talk to your mentor. Don't raise energy when you're ill, exhausted, drunk, or in a very distressed state.

> **Try this:** Think of a small, kind purpose for yourself that you'd like to work on in this module, such as calm, focus, courage or rest. Write it as one sentence in your journal. You'll use it in your first working.

docs.title: Ways to raise energy
docs.summary: Five methods of raising energy, each step by step: breath, chant and voice, movement and dance, drumming and rhythm, and visualisation, with seated and quiet versions and safety notes.
docs.body:
## Many ways up the same hill

People raise energy in different ways, and most traditions use several together. Try each method in this lesson at least once. You'll probably find one or two that suit you. Whatever you do, always ground and centre first, and always ground afterwards.

In every method, the pattern is the same: **start slowly, build gradually, reach a peak, release, ground.**

## Method 1: breath

The quietest method, good for small spaces and shared homes.

1. Sit upright, feet on the floor. Ground and centre.
2. Breathe slowly and naturally for a minute, attention on your centre (belly or chest).
3. Begin to deepen the breath, gently. On each in-breath, imagine drawing warmth and strength up from the earth through your feet and in from the air around you, gathering in your centre.
4. On each out-breath, don't let it go; imagine it settling into your centre, which grows a little warmer, brighter or fuller with each breath.
5. Continue for three to five minutes. Let the sense of fullness build. Some people feel heat, tingling, pressure in the chest or belly, or a slight rush.
6. When you feel full, move your attention from your centre up through your chest, along your arms and into your hands. Feel your palms grow warm and charged.
7. Now direct and release (see the next lesson), then ground.

> **Safety:** This is not fast or forced breathing. Keep the pace slow and comfortable; deepen the breath only a little. If you feel dizzy, tingly around the lips, or panicky, you're over-breathing: stop, breathe normally, and ground. If you have a heart or lung condition, panic attacks or epilepsy, or are pregnant, keep the breath completely natural and use imagery to build instead.

## Method 2: chant and voice

Voice is one of the most powerful ways to raise energy, and it's used in nearly every religion on earth: hymns, mantras, chants, keening, war cries.

### Toning (a single sound)

1. Stand or sit upright. Ground and centre.
2. Take a comfortable breath, and on the out-breath sing a long, steady vowel sound: "Ahhh", "Ohhh" or "Oooo". Let it come from your belly. Feel it vibrate in your chest.
3. Take another breath and tone again, a little louder or with a little more feeling.
4. Continue for three to five minutes. Let the sound grow in strength and let yourself feel it in your whole body.
5. At the peak, let the last tone rise and end sharply, or fall into silence, as your release.

### A simple chant

A chant is a short phrase repeated over and over. You can write your own: four to eight words, simple rhythm, saying what you're working for. For example:

"Calm and clear, calm and clear,
Peace within and courage here."

1. Ground and centre. Hold your purpose in mind.
2. Begin to chant slowly and quietly, spoken or sung on two or three notes.
3. With each repetition, let it grow a little faster, louder or stronger. Feel the words. Add clapping or swaying if you like.
4. Build for three to ten minutes. You'll feel the chant gather momentum, often a sense of being carried by it.
5. At the peak, end on a final shout of the key word, or stop abruptly, and release.
6. Sit in the silence afterwards for a few breaths, then ground.

If you live with others and need to be quiet, whisper the chant, or chant silently in your head while moving your lips. It's less intense but still works.

> **Your coven:** Covens often have their own chants, some very old (or claimed to be), many written by members. Hymns to the gods are central in Hellenic practice; Heathens may use galdr, chanted runes and verse. Ask your mentor for one of your coven's chants and learn it by heart.

## Method 3: movement and dance

Movement brings the whole body into the working. It's one of the oldest methods of all: circle dances appear in folk customs across Europe and the world.

### Walking the circle

1. Clear a space. Ground and centre.
2. Begin walking slowly in a circle, clockwise (sunwise in the Northern Hemisphere; many in the Southern Hemisphere walk anticlockwise for the same reason). Keep your purpose in mind.
3. With each round, walk a little faster. Add a chant or a rhythm if you like.
4. Let the walk become a trot, a skip or a dance, as your body allows. Feel energy and warmth rising.
5. When you reach the peak, stop suddenly and throw your arms up or out, or drop to the floor, releasing the energy to its purpose.
6. Ground: kneel or sit, palms on the floor, breathe slowly.

### Seated and gentle movement

Movement doesn't need to be vigorous. You can:

- sway from side to side in your chair, gradually wider and faster, then come to stillness
- rock forward and back in rhythm with a chant
- move your arms in circles, building speed
- tap your thighs or clap in a rising rhythm

> **Safety:** Clear the floor, keep candles well out of the way of moving bodies and loose clothing, and stop if you're dizzy, short of breath or in pain. Spinning can cause falls; walk rather than spin. Adapt freely to your body: seated movement is fully valid.

## Method 4: drumming and rhythm

Rhythm synchronises bodies and minds, and steady drumming has been used for focus and trance in many cultures.

1. Use a drum, a rattle, a tabletop, a book, your thighs, or your hands.
2. Ground and centre. Hold your purpose in mind.
3. Begin a slow, steady beat, about one beat per second, like a slow heartbeat.
4. Keep it steady for a minute or two, letting your breath and attention settle into it.
5. Gradually speed up, over three to five minutes. Let it become louder and more intense. Add your voice if you like.
6. At the peak, finish with a rapid roll and one final strong beat, or stop dead, and release.
7. Sit in the silence. Ground.

> **Safety:** Steady drumming can bring on trance-like states in some people. Keep sessions short at first, keep your eyes open if you prefer, and stop if you feel disoriented. If you have epilepsy, avoid rapid rhythmic drumming and flashing light, and check with your doctor. Protect your hearing and your neighbours: drum softly or use your hands on a cushion.

## Method 5: visualisation

Imagination is the inner engine of most energy work. It can be used alone, or added to any of the methods above.

1. Ground and centre. Close your eyes or soften your gaze.
2. Imagine a small flame, coal or light in your centre.
3. With each breath, it grows: a candle flame, then a fire, then a blaze of light. Feel its warmth spreading through your body.
4. Let it fill you from feet to head. Imagine it in a colour that suits your purpose: gold for success, green for growth, blue for calm, red for courage (or your own choice; correspondences come in a later module).
5. When you feel full, draw it into your hands, or gather it in your chest.
6. Direct and release it, then ground.

If you can't picture images (aphantasia), use felt sense ("warmth spreading") or words ("rising... rising... rising") instead.

## Combining methods

Most rituals combine methods: breath to begin, then a chant with clapping, then a dance, all with visualisation behind it. Start with one at a time, then try two together.

## Common difficulties

**"I feel self-conscious."** Very common, especially with voice and movement. Practise alone first. Start quietly. Remind yourself that every practitioner has felt silly. It gets easier.

**"I don't feel anything rise."** Try a more physical method (movement or rhythm), go a little longer, or practise at a time you have more energy. Notice subtle changes: warmth, a faster heart, a lift in mood.

**"It builds and then falls away."** You may be losing focus or going too long. Try a shorter build with a clear release, and repeat a phrase of intent throughout.

**"I feel overwhelmed."** Stop, release whatever's there into the earth through your palms, and ground. Next time, build more slowly and stop sooner.

> **Try this:** Over the next week, try three methods, one each session, using your purpose sentence from the last lesson. Just raise and release into the earth for now; the next lesson teaches you to direct it.

docs.title: Directing, releasing and grounding
docs.summary: How to send raised energy into a candle, an object, a sigil or a goal; the moment of release; grounding the excess; the signs of overdoing it; and a complete first working, step by step.
docs.body:
## Giving it somewhere to go

Raising energy is only half the work. A working needs a **target**: something the energy goes into or towards. This lesson teaches four common targets, how to release, how to ground afterwards, and how to tell when you've overdone it. It ends with a complete first working you can do at home.

## Directing into a candle

Candle magic is one of the simplest and most popular forms of working. The candle holds the purpose, and as it burns, practitioners say, it releases the working into the world; in the psychological view, it's a focus and a visible reminder.
