## The anniversary

Mark the day each year with a short rite of thanks:

1. Purify and light Hestia's flame.
2. Read your words of dedication aloud.
3. Pour a libation to the gods you dedicated to.
4. Tell them, honestly, how the year has gone.
5. Give a small offering, perhaps something you made.
6. Hestia last, and close.

## The path ahead

After dedication, many devotees continue as devotees for a long time, and that is a full and honourable practice. Most Hellenic polytheists in history lived and died as faithful household worshippers.

Some feel called, after a while, to seek initiation: a year and a day of deeper craft, the full festival year, service, an oath and the coven's rite of initiation. If you feel that pull, talk to your mentor. There is no hurry, and no expectation.

## If the path proves not to be yours

Sometimes, after dedicating, people find that the coven or the tradition is not right for them after all. Circumstances change; understanding grows; a different path calls. This is not failure, and it is not oath-breaking. Your dedication was a commitment to walk this path in good faith; when you find you must leave it, good faith means leaving well.

### Leaving well

1. **Talk to your mentor or High Priestess** honestly about what has changed.
2. **Take time** to be sure, unless you are leaving because of harm, in which case go at once and seek support outside the coven.
3. **Keep confidential** what members shared with you in trust.
4. **Return or give back** anything that belongs to the coven.
5. **Thank the gods** at your shrine: pour a last libation as a devotee, and tell them you are taking a different road. Your anathema can stay with them, or be buried with thanks.
6. **Part with kindness.** A good coven will let you go with goodwill.

You can keep Hestia's flame and honour the Greek gods on your own, or in another community, for the rest of your life.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what your coven expects of devotees after dedication: which roles you might take, how often to check in, and how the coven marks the anniversary of members' dedications.

## Common questions

**I missed a week of devotion straight after dedicating. Have I broken my word?** No. Return to your shrine, light Hestia's flame, and say simply that you have come back. A dedication is kept by returning, not by never faltering.

**Do I have to tell people outside the coven?** No. Whom you tell about your religion is your own choice.

**Can I change my anathema?** Once given, it belongs to the gods. You can always give another gift; you don't take the first one back.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** household worship as a full life of piety, offerings of thanks, anathemata kept by the gods.
- **Modern:** aftercare, anniversaries, the freedom to leave well, and the path from devotee to initiate.

quizzes.title: Welcome: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on how the course works, what a coven is, consent, safety, looking after yourself and red flags. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: You sat for a breathing practice for ten minutes and noticed nothing in particular. What should you write in the answer box?
options: Nothing; leave it blank until something happens
What you did and that you noticed nothing much, honestly
A description of what you think you were supposed to feel
Skip logging it, since it didn't work
questions.explanation: Honest notes, including "nothing much happened", are what let you and your mentor see real patterns. Most practitioners' early journals are full of quiet sessions.

questions.prompt: To pass a module's test, you need 80 per cent of the points.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each module's test needs 80 per cent. Choice questions are marked at once and written answers are scored by your mentor. If you don't pass, look at the questions you missed, go back over the lessons and talk to your mentor about trying again. The right answers and explanations show once you've passed.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to separate noticing from concluding in your journal?
options: "I felt energy between my hands."
"Noticed: my palms tingled and grew warm as I breathed slowly. I think this may be what my coven calls energy."
"My spirit guide touched my hands."
"Nothing; I don't write conclusions."
questions.explanation: Write what you noticed in plain words first, then your interpretation, kept apart. The noticing is the evidence; the conclusion may change as you learn.

questions.prompt: Modern covens, and Wicca in particular, are an unbroken continuation of an organised pagan religion that survived the witch trials.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. That was Margaret Murray's 1920s theory, which historians have rejected. Wicca was made public in the 1950s by Gerald Gardner and others, drawing on older sources. Modern practice is meaningful without needing to be ancient.

questions.prompt: Which of these respect consent? Choose all that apply.
options: Asking "Is it all right if I anoint your hands?" before doing so
Doing a healing working for a friend who asked you to
Doing a working to make a particular person fall in love with you
Stepping out of a ritual partway through because you're uncomfortable
questions.explanation: Consent means free, informed agreement that can be withdrawn. Asking before touch, working only for those who've asked, and being free to step out all respect it. A love spell aimed at a particular person tries to change their feelings without their agreement.

questions.prompt: You can't safely use a naked flame where you live. What should you do?
options: Use one anyway, but only for short rituals
Use a battery candle; it's perfectly acceptable
Give up on candle practices
Light it outside your door
questions.explanation: Battery candles are fully acceptable and many experienced practitioners use them. Safety always comes first: never leave a flame unattended or use one where it isn't safe.

questions.prompt: Which of these are safe practice with herbs and oils? Choose all that apply.
options: Diluting essential oils in a carrier oil and patch-testing before they touch skin
Drinking a herbal tea from a spell book to make the spell stronger, without asking anyone
Checking every herb and oil with a professional if you're pregnant
Keeping oils away from cats, dogs and birds
questions.explanation: Never ingest a herb or oil for magical purposes without expert advice: many interact with medicines. Dilute and patch-test oils, check everything in pregnancy, and keep oils away from pets, some of which are poisoned by them.

questions.prompt: Libations must be alcoholic to be acceptable.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Alcohol is always optional. Water, juice, milk or tea are acceptable offerings in every tradition this course teaches, and no one should pressure you to drink.

questions.prompt: After a week of evening meditation you've been sleeping badly and feel detached from your surroundings much of the day. What's the right first step?
options: Meditate longer to push through it
Stop the practice, ground yourself, tell your mentor, and see a doctor if it continues
Keep it to yourself so you don't look weak
Stop taking any medication that might be interfering
questions.explanation: These are signs to pause. Stop, ground (food, water, feet on the floor, something ordinary), tell your mentor, and get medical help if it doesn't settle. Never change medication because of a spiritual practice.

questions.prompt: Which of these are red flags in a spiritual group? Choose all that apply.
options: Being told you must pay the leader to be initiated
Being asked to share the cost of candles and room hire, with the costs shown openly
Being told not to talk to former members
Being told sex with the leader is part of advancement
questions.explanation: Open sharing of costs is normal. Paying for advancement, being cut off from people outside the group, and any suggestion that sex is required are serious warning signs.

questions.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between confidentiality and harmful secrecy in a coven, with an example of each.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects people (who is a member, what others share, the coven's own rites). Secrecy that hides harm protects the person doing harm. No promise can require you to hide abuse, crime or danger. Ask: "Who does keeping this secret protect?"
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): explains that confidentiality protects members and the coven's private practice (1); explains that secrecy hiding abuse, crime or danger is never binding (1); gives a fitting example of each, such as not naming members vs. being told not to tell the police or a doctor (1).

questions.prompt: A practice has left you feeling anxious and unsettled for several hours. Describe what you would do, step by step.
questions.explanation: Stop the practice; ground yourself with food, water, feeling your feet and doing something ordinary; tell your mentor; seek medical or crisis help if it's severe or doesn't settle; rest from practice and return gently.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): stops the practice and grounds in a concrete way (1); tells the mentor (1); says they would seek professional or emergency help if it doesn't settle or if they feel unsafe, and returns gently or pauses (1).

quizzes.title: Energy: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on what practitioners mean by energy, the ways of understanding it, and how to perceive it safely and honestly. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: When practitioners of magic talk about "energy", what do they usually mean?
options: The physicist's energy, measured in joules
A felt sense of aliveness, force, mood or presence in the body, between people, in places and objects
Electricity from the body that instruments can measure
Only the energy that comes from food
questions.explanation: In magical practice, "energy" is an old, loose word for a felt sense of aliveness, force, mood or presence, which can be felt, raised, directed, released and grounded. It isn't the physicist's measurable quantity.

questions.prompt: Which of these are ways practitioners understand energy, as taught in this module? Choose all that apply.
options: A subtle life force that flows through living things
Presence and relationship with spirits, gods and the land
What it feels like when attention, imagination, emotion and the body work together
A proven physical force that guarantees results
questions.explanation: The three views are subtle energy, spirit and relationship, and the psychological view. Many practitioners hold a mix. None is a proven physical force guaranteeing results.

questions.prompt: You need to decide which view of energy is true before you can learn the practices.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The practices work the same way whatever you believe: slow down, pay attention, notice, and learn to shift what you notice. Your own view can grow from experience.

questions.prompt: After two weeks of practice, you still feel very little in your hands. What does this most likely mean?
options: You have no ability and should stop
Something is blocking you that needs removing
It's normal; attention is a skill that grows, and some people perceive more through images, moods or a sense of knowing
You should practise for hours at a time to force it
questions.explanation: Noticing little at first is completely normal. Keep practising gently, notice what you do perceive (images, moods, knowing), and talk to your mentor.

questions.prompt: During the four-count breath you start to feel dizzy and your lips tingle. What should you do?
options: Breathe faster to push through it
Hold your breath until it passes
Stop shaping the breath, breathe normally, and rest
Carry on; dizziness means energy is rising
questions.explanation: Dizziness and tingling around the lips are signs of over-breathing, which can bring on panic. Stop, breathe naturally and rest. Breath practices in this course are always gentle.

questions.prompt: In breath awareness, your mind wanders over and over. What's the right attitude?
options: You're failing at the practice
Noticing that you've wandered and coming back is the practice itself
Stop and try again when your mind is clear
Force your thoughts to stop
questions.explanation: No one's mind stops. Each time you notice you've drifted and return to the breath, you're doing the exercise. That's how attention is trained.

questions.prompt: The purpose of the body scan is to learn what your body normally feels like, so you can notice changes during practice.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The body scan gives you a baseline. Once you know what normal feels like, you can recognise the changes that come with grounding, raising energy and ritual.

questions.prompt: A body scan brings up panic and a feeling of being outside your body. Which of these are good responses? Choose all that apply.
options: Open your eyes and press your feet into the floor
Look around and name things you can see
Tell your mentor, so the practice can be adapted
Close your eyes tighter and keep scanning to get through it
questions.explanation: Stop, come back to the room through the senses and the body's contact with the floor, have some water, and tell your mentor. These reactions aren't your fault; they mean the method needs adapting.

questions.prompt: You can't picture images in your mind. How can you do the energy ball exercise?
options: You can't; energy work needs visualisation
Focus on a felt sense of warmth gathering, or a silent word with each breath, instead of a picture
Look at a photo of a ball instead
Skip all energy work
questions.explanation: Energy work doesn't depend on visualisation. Felt sense, breath and words work just as well, and many practitioners can't form mental pictures.

questions.prompt: Which journal entry best keeps perception and interpretation apart?
options: "The room had bad vibes."
"A spirit was in the room."
"My shoulders tightened when I walked in and I wanted to leave. Maybe the room holds the argument from yesterday."
"My aura was attacked."
questions.explanation: Write what you noticed in plain words first, then any interpretation separately and tentatively. Plain words keep you honest and make patterns visible.

questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you would do the "between the palms" exercise, and name three things you might notice.
questions.explanation: Breathe for a couple of minutes, rub the palms to warm them, hold them facing each other about thirty centimetres apart, and very slowly bring them close and apart again for a few minutes while breathing slowly. People notice warmth, tingling, pressure, a push or pull, or nothing at first. Finish by resting and shaking the hands.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): describes preparing (breath and warming or waking the hands) (1); describes the slow movement of the palms towards and away from each other without touching, with slow breathing (1); names three plausible sensations such as warmth, tingling, pressure, push or pull, or says that noticing little is normal (1).

questions.prompt: You sense a room in your home and it feels "heavy". Explain how you would work out whether this is perception or assumption.
questions.explanation: Check your own state first (your baseline), write the raw impression before explaining it, notice whether you expected it, return at other times and in other moods, and compare with someone else's impressions taken separately.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): mentions checking their own state or baseline (tiredness, mood) (1); mentions recording the raw impression before explaining it, or noticing whether it was expected (1); mentions checking consistency over time or comparing with another person's separate impression (1).

quizzes.title: Grounding, centring, shielding and cleansing: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on the four protective skills, when to use them, and what they can't do. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: Which best describes grounding?
options: Putting a protective boundary around yourself
Settling into your body and the present, letting excess energy drain to the earth and steadiness come in
Washing away what's clinging to you
Raising energy for a spell
questions.explanation: Grounding settles you: attention in the body and the present, excess drained away, steadiness drawn in. Shielding sets a boundary; cleansing clears what's clinging.

questions.prompt: What is centring?
options: Standing in the middle of the ritual space
Gathering your scattered attention and energy back to a still point in your body, such as the belly or chest
Balancing the four elements on the altar
Sending energy to the centre of the earth
questions.explanation: Centring gathers you in to your own middle, usually felt in the belly or chest, so you feel collected and balanced. It's normally done after grounding.

questions.prompt: Which are signs you need to ground? Choose all that apply.
options: Feeling spacey or "not quite here" after practice
Buzzing, jittery energy you can't settle
Clumsiness and bumping into things
Feeling calm, steady and present
questions.explanation: Spaciness, jitteriness, racing thoughts and clumsiness are classic signs you need grounding. Calm and steady is what grounding leads to.

questions.prompt: After a ritual you feel very floaty, and the roots visualisation isn't helping. Which is the best next step?
options: Do more energy work to use up the extra energy
Eat something substantial, drink water, press your feet into the floor, and name things you can see and hear
Drive home quickly before it gets worse
Go straight to sleep without grounding
questions.explanation: Physical grounding (food, water, firm contact with the floor, using your senses) is the fastest method when you're very spacey. Don't drive until you feel fully present.

questions.prompt: You must be able to visualise roots to ground successfully.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Physical grounding and breath-and-words methods work just as well. Use whichever suits you.

questions.prompt: Which of these can a shield NOT do? Choose all that apply.
options: Replace locking your door or leaving a dangerous situation
Replace saying no to someone who is mistreating you
Treat anxiety or depression on its own
Help you feel steadier in a crowded place
questions.explanation: A shield is a practice for your own steadiness. It doesn't give physical protection, replace real-life boundaries, or treat health conditions. It can help you feel steadier in busy places.

questions.prompt: Why do many practitioners prefer a mirror shield that sends things down into the earth, rather than back at the sender?
options: Because it's more powerful
So that nothing is returned to anyone with force: protect yourself without sending harm
Because mirrors only work facing downward
Because the earth needs feeding
questions.explanation: Most covens' ethics allow protecting yourself but not sending harm back. Sending things to the earth protects you without targeting anyone.

questions.prompt: Which are safe ways to cleanse yourself if someone in your home has asthma? Choose all that apply.
options: Ringing a bell or singing bowl around yourself
Washing your hands and face with intention
Burning a large bundle of herbs in a closed room
Breath and brushing down with your hands
questions.explanation: Smoke can trigger asthma, so choose smoke-free methods: sound, water, breath and brushing, shaking. If you do use smoke, ventilate and use small amounts, and not around anyone with breathing problems.

questions.prompt: What should you call burning herbs to cleanse, and what herbs should you use?
options: Smudging, with wild white sage
Smoke cleansing, with herbs grown locally or in your garden, such as garden sage, rosemary or lavender
Smudging, with palo santo
It doesn't matter what you call it or use
questions.explanation: "Smudging" names a particular practice of some Indigenous nations, and wild white sage is being overharvested. Call it smoke cleansing and use local or garden herbs or reliably sourced resins.

questions.prompt: If you feel under constant psychic attack and are spending more and more time on protection, the right response is to shield harder.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. That's a sign to pause magical practice and talk to your mentor, and to a doctor or mental health professional. Protection practices that take over your day need care, not more protection.

questions.prompt: Describe the two-minute grounding and centring sequence you'll use before and after practice, step by step.
questions.explanation: Three slow breaths; feel your feet and send roots down or press your feet into the floor; let tension and excess drain on the out-breath and draw steadiness up on the in-breath; hand on your centre and gather your attention in; one last breath and notice how you feel.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): includes slow breathing and contact with the floor or roots (1); includes releasing tension or excess downward and drawing steadiness in (1); includes gathering attention to a centre (belly or chest) and checking how they feel (1). Equivalent physical or verbal methods are fine.

questions.prompt: Give a short daily routine of grounding, shielding and cleansing that would fit your own life, saying when you'd do each part.
questions.explanation: A good routine grounds and centres in the morning, uses quick shields before demanding situations, quick grounds and cleanses during the day, and an evening cleanse and grounding, all fitted to real moments in your day.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): includes grounding (and ideally centring) at a named time (1); includes a shield at a named time or situation (1); includes a cleansing at a named time, with methods that are realistic and safe for their home (1).

quizzes.title: Raising, directing and releasing: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on the arc of a working, the methods of raising energy, directing and releasing it, grounding afterwards, and working in a group. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: What should you do before you raise any energy?
options: Decide your purpose in one sentence and check it against your ethics
Raise as much as you can, then decide what to use it for
Drink something alcoholic to relax
Ask the energy what it wants to do
questions.explanation: Know exactly what a working is for, check that it doesn't harm or override anyone, and pair it with practical action. Energy raised without a purpose tends to leave you unsettled.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order for the arc of a working?
options: Raise, prepare, ground, decide the purpose, release, record
Decide the purpose, prepare, raise, focus and hold, direct and release, ground the excess, record
Prepare, release, raise, record, ground
Ground, raise, keep it inside you, record
questions.explanation: Purpose, preparation (cleanse, ground, centre), raise, focus and hold, direct and release, ground the excess, record. Every working, alone or in a group, follows this arc.

questions.prompt: After releasing a working, it's best to keep checking on it and thinking about it so it stays strong.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Releasing is an act of letting go. Holding on tends to leave you jittery and keeps worrying at the working. Do your part, release it, ground, and move on.

questions.prompt: Which describes the breath method of raising energy safely?
options: Breathing as fast and hard as you can until your hands tingle
Holding your breath for as long as possible
Slow, slightly deepened breathing, gathering warmth and fullness in your centre with each breath
Breathing through a cloth to make it harder
questions.explanation: Raise with slow, comfortable breathing and imagery. Fast or forced breathing causes over-breathing, with dizziness, tingling lips and panic. Stop and breathe normally if those appear.

questions.prompt: Which are good ways to adapt raising energy if you live in a shared home and have limited mobility? Choose all that apply.
options: Whispering a chant, or chanting silently with moving lips
Swaying in your chair, building gradually
Tapping a rhythm softly on a cushion
Spinning on the spot as fast as you can
questions.explanation: Quiet chanting, seated movement and soft rhythm all work. Spinning risks falls and isn't needed; seated and quiet methods are fully valid.

questions.prompt: What does "charging" an object mean?
options: Plugging it in
Selling it
Filling it with energy and purpose so that it carries the working
Leaving it in sunlight for a day
questions.explanation: Charging means cleansing an object, raising energy with a clear purpose, and directing it into the object so it carries that purpose. Many people recharge objects regularly.

questions.prompt: A friend is going through a hard time but hasn't asked for help. What's the ethical way to work for them?
options: Send healing energy to them without telling them
Ask them if they'd like you to, or offer a general blessing that doesn't target them
Charge an object and hide it in their home
Do a working to change how they feel
questions.explanation: Direct energy at a person only with their consent. Ask first, or offer a general blessing such as "may all who suffer find ease". Healing work is always alongside medical care, never instead of it.

questions.prompt: Which are signs of overdoing energy work? Choose all that apply.
options: A headache or nausea that doesn't settle with grounding
Being wired and unable to sleep for hours
Feeling drained and flat the next day
Feeling calm and pleasantly tired after grounding
questions.explanation: Persistent headache, sleeplessness, exhaustion, irritability and spaciness are signs to rest, ground thoroughly, raise less next time, and talk to your mentor. Calm tiredness after grounding is normal.

questions.prompt: After a working you're still buzzing and restless ten minutes later. What should you do?
options: Raise more energy to use it up
Keep grounding: palms on the floor, eat and drink, then go for a walk, wash your hands or do something ordinary and physical
Ignore it and go to bed
Drive somewhere to clear your head
questions.explanation: Ground the excess: palms to the floor, food and water, the grounding sequence, then ordinary physical activity. Don't drive while you're not fully present.

questions.prompt: The "cone of power" story of witches in 1940 is well documented by independent historical evidence.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The story comes from Gerald Gardner and later accounts, with no independent evidence. Treat it as a story the tradition tells about itself. The image of the cone is still a useful one for group work.

questions.prompt: In a coven's circle dance, which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
options: Holding hands should be asked for, not assumed
You can step out and sit if you feel unwell
You should know the purpose of the working before you join in
Everyone must dance at full speed, whatever their body
questions.explanation: Group work rests on consent: to the purpose, to touch, and to taking part at all. Anyone can step out, and those who can't dance can drum, chant or hold the centre.

questions.prompt: Describe your first working (charging a candle for a purpose) from start to finish: your purpose, how you prepared, which method you used to raise energy, how you directed and released it, how you grounded, and what you noticed at each stage.
questions.explanation: A full working moves through purpose, safe preparation (space, cleansing, grounding and centring), raising with a chosen method while holding the purpose, directing into the candle, a clear release, lighting the candle safely, grounding the excess, and recording honestly.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): a clear, ethical one-sentence purpose (1); preparation including candle safety and grounding and centring (1); a named raising method described with the purpose held in mind (1); directing into the candle and a clear moment of release (1); grounding afterwards and an honest account of what they noticed, including if little happened (1).

questions.prompt: In a group working, what is the leader's role, and what is yours as a member?
questions.explanation: The leader sets the pace, keeps the group together, senses the peak and calls the release. Members follow the cues, keep the purpose in mind, put in full effort within their limits, release together, and ground afterwards.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): leader sets pace and keeps the group together (1); leader senses the peak and calls the release (1); member follows cues, holds the purpose, releases on the call and grounds afterwards, within their own limits (1).

quizzes.title: Sacred space: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on purification, why boundaries matter, how traditions differ, casting and closing a circle, and leaving safely. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: Which are reasons practitioners mark the boundary of sacred space? Choose all that apply.
options: To focus the mind and mark the change from everyday life
To be clean and fit to approach the gods
To hold what's raised until it's released, and keep out unwanted influences
To make sure nothing can ever go wrong in a ritual
questions.explanation: Boundaries help with focus, purity and respect, containment, protection and marking time. They don't guarantee anything, and safety still applies inside them.

questions.prompt: Every pagan tradition casts a circle before ritual.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The circle comes mainly from ceremonial magic and Wicca. Hellenic practice centres on purification with khernips and procession; Heathens may hallow the space; Druids open a grove; Christian folk practice uses prayer and blessing.

questions.prompt: What is khernips, in Hellenic practice?
options: A circle drawn with a knife
Lustral water made by plunging a burning brand into water, used to wash the hands and sprinkle the space and people
A Norse toast
A type of incense
questions.explanation: Khernips is purifying water: a lit match, twig or sprig is plunged into water and the water used to wash the hands and sprinkle. Purification, not a circle, is the heart of Hellenic sacred space.

questions.prompt: What comes first in nearly every tradition's way of making sacred space?
options: Calling the quarters
Purification of yourself and the space
Raising energy
Making an offering
questions.explanation: Purification is shared by almost every tradition: cleaning yourself and the space, physically and symbolically, before marking a boundary or approaching the gods.

questions.prompt: Which are safe ways to purify a small flat where someone has asthma and there's a cat? Choose all that apply.
options: Cleaning and sweeping with intention
Ringing a bell at the centre, corners and door
Sprinkling a little water around the edges
Burning a large amount of incense with the windows shut
questions.explanation: Sweeping, sound and water are all smoke-free. Smoke can trigger asthma and harm pets; if you use it at all, use a little, with good ventilation, and not around anyone with breathing problems.

questions.prompt: In the most common modern pattern, which element is linked with the east?
options: Air
Fire
Water
Earth
questions.explanation: East is usually air, south fire, west water and north earth. This pattern comes from the Golden Dawn and north-western European geography; many in the Southern Hemisphere swap north and south.

questions.prompt: The idea of four elements (air, fire, water, earth) goes back to the Greek philosopher Empedocles in the fifth century BCE.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Empedocles taught that everything is made of four "roots". The pairing of elements with the four quarters in modern witchcraft is much later, from the Golden Dawn.

questions.prompt: A pan catches fire in the kitchen while you're inside a cast circle. What do you do?
options: Cut a door in the circle carefully first
Close the circle formally, then deal with the fire
Leave immediately and deal with the fire; the circle doesn't matter
Stay in the circle, where you're protected
questions.explanation: Safety always comes first. In any emergency, just go. Nothing terrible happens to someone who leaves a circle in a hurry; you can recast or close it later.

questions.prompt: When closing a circle, in what order are the quarters usually thanked?
options: The same order as they were called: east, south, west, north
In reverse: north, west, south, east
Any order
Only the east is thanked
questions.explanation: Closing usually reverses opening: thank the quarters from the last called back to the first, then take up the circle widdershins (against the direction you cast).

questions.prompt: Which belong in closing sacred space? Choose all that apply.
options: Thanking the gods, spirits or quarters you invited
Grounding and eating something
Making sure every candle and incense is out or safely attended
Leaving the circle open overnight to keep working
questions.explanation: Closing thanks those invited, unwinds the boundary, grounds you, puts out flames and tidies. A space left open tends to leave people spacey and unsettled.

questions.prompt: Describe step by step how you make sacred space at home: either the simple circle from this module, or your coven's own form if it doesn't cast circles. Include purification, opening, what you did inside, and closing.
questions.explanation: A complete answer moves through purification of self and space, grounding and centring, marking the boundary (circle and quarters, or the coven's own opening), the work inside, then thanks, closing in reverse, grounding, putting out flames, tidying and recording.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): purification of self and space (1); grounding and centring (1); a clear opening, either circle and quarters with direction of walking or the coven's own form (1); thanks and closing in reverse, or the coven's closing (1); grounding afterwards, fire safety and tidying or recording (1).

questions.prompt: Why might a coven in the Southern Hemisphere cast its circle anticlockwise and place fire in the north? What does this tell you about the quarters?
questions.explanation: "Sunwise" means following the sun's apparent path: south of the equator it rises in the east, passes through the north at noon and sets in the west, so following it means turning anticlockwise, and the noon sun (fire) is in the north. The usual pattern comes from north-western Europe; quarters are conventions to be applied thoughtfully and consistently, not fixed laws.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): explains that sunwise follows the sun, which moves the other way as seen in the Southern Hemisphere (1); explains that the noon sun (fire) is in the north there (1); concludes that the common pattern reflects north-western European geography and that quarters are adaptable conventions, used consistently (1).

quizzes.title: Hellenic ritual: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on the shape of a Hellenic rite, khernips, sacred space, prayer, libation and offering, and closing. You need 80% to pass. Your mentor will score the written answers.

questions.prompt: Which order is right for the opening of a Hellenic rite?
options: Hestia last, khernips, procession
Procession, khernips, Hestia first
Prayer, procession, khernips
Libation, closing, khernips
questions.explanation: You walk to the altar with the offerings, purify with khernips, and then make the first offering to Hestia before turning to the other gods.

questions.prompt: How is khernips made?
options: By boiling water with salt
By plunging a burning leaf, brand or match into water
By leaving water in moonlight overnight
By blessing tap water with a prayer only
questions.explanation: Khernips is water into which a flame has been quenched. A bay leaf, herb sprig or match lit from Hestia's flame is plunged into fresh water.

questions.prompt: What should you do with used khernips?
options: Drink it to take the blessing inside
Pour it back into the kettle
Pour it on the earth, or down a drain if you have no outside space
Keep it in the bowl for next week
questions.explanation: Used khernips has carried away impurity, so it is not drunk or reused for food. Pour it on the earth, or down a drain with running water, and make fresh khernips each time.

questions.prompt: In Hellenic practice, sacred space is made mainly by casting a circle and calling the four quarters.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The Greeks made sacred space through the purity of the worshipper, the altar and the sacred precinct (temenos). Circles and quarter calls are modern witchcraft practices, which some covens add for magical work.

questions.prompt: You must leave a Hellenic rite at home for a few minutes. What should you do?
options: Carry on later without washing, since there is no circle
Make sure no flame is left unattended, step away, and wash again in khernips when you return
Start the whole rite from the beginning tomorrow
Leave the candle burning so the gods know you will return
questions.explanation: There is no circle to break, so you can pause. Never leave a flame unattended. When you return, wash in khernips again and carry on.

questions.prompt: Which are the three parts of a Greek prayer? Choose all that apply.
options: Invocation: naming the god with epithets
Argument: recalling the relationship or offering a reason to listen
Banishing: driving away hostile spirits
Request: asking plainly, or giving thanks
questions.explanation: Greek prayer names the god, reminds them of the bond (the argument, or hypomnesis), and then asks or thanks.

questions.prompt: What is the traditional gesture when praying to the heavenly gods?
options: Kneeling with the head bowed to the floor
Standing with both arms raised, palms up
Hands pressed together at the chest
Touching the earth with both palms
questions.explanation: Greeks prayed to the heavenly gods standing, arms raised. For chthonic powers and the dead, hands were lowered toward or onto the earth.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a sponde and a choe?
options: A sponde is wine; a choe is always water
A sponde is poured to the heavenly gods and may be shared; a choe is poured wholly away to the dead and powers below
A sponde is for women; a choe is for men
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Sponde is the libation to the heavenly gods, often shared with a sip. Choe is poured entirely away, often into the earth, for the dead and chthonic powers, and not drunk.

questions.prompt: After a festival rite to Apollo with a cake, what is the usual modern practice?
options: Give Apollo the first portion, then share and eat the rest
Bury the whole cake without eating any
Throw the whole cake away at once
Leave the whole cake on the shrine until it spoils
questions.explanation: Offerings to the heavenly gods follow the pattern of thusia, the shared offering: the god's portion is given away, and the rest is eaten with joy.

questions.prompt: It is acceptable to wrap an offering respectfully and put it in the bin when you cannot bury, compost or burn it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The gift was given in the rite. Composting or burying is preferred where possible, but respectful disposal in the bin is fine, and far better than leaving food to spoil.

questions.prompt: Which of these are safe practices with fire and offerings? Choose all that apply.
options: Using a charcoal disc on a heatproof base with a window open
Leaving a candle burning on the outdoor Deipnon supper overnight
Holding a burning bay leaf over the khernips bowl, with hair tied back
Keeping water nearby when burning offerings
questions.explanation: Charcoal needs ventilation and a heatproof base; burning leaves are held over the bowl with hair and sleeves clear; water should be close. Never leave a flame burning unattended, indoors or out.

questions.prompt: Write a short prayer of your own to a god of your choice, using the three-part shape. Label each part.
questions.explanation: A Greek prayer names the god with fitting epithets, recalls the bond or gives a reason to listen, and then asks or thanks plainly.
questions.rubric: Full marks: a clear invocation naming the god with at least one fitting epithet or description (1 point); an argument that recalls a relationship, past offering or promise appropriate to the trainee (1 point); a specific, modest request or thanks (1 point). Labels should match the parts.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between offerings shared with the gods, offerings wholly burnt, and offerings given to the dead, and say how you would dispose of each kind in your own home.
questions.explanation: Thusia was shared: the god's portion burned and the rest eaten. Holocaust offerings were burned whole and not eaten. Offerings to heroes and the dead were poured or placed into the earth and not eaten. Modern practice: share heavenly offerings after giving the god's portion; give underworld and Deipnon offerings away entirely; dispose by earth, burial, compost, safe burning or respectful binning.
questions.rubric: Full marks: describes thusia as shared, with the god's portion given and the rest eaten (1 point); describes holocaust or wholly given offerings as not eaten, linked to chthonic powers or purification (1 point); describes offerings to the dead or heroes as given into the earth and not eaten (1 point); gives a practical, safe disposal plan for their own home, mentioning animal safety or local rules (1 point).

quizzes.title: The altar and tools: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on what an altar is for, setting one up, tools, cleansing and consecrating, caring for an altar, and the app's altar. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: What can an altar be for? Choose all that apply.
options: A place to meet your gods, spirits or ancestors and make offerings
A focus for your attention and practice
A workbench for magical work
Proof to others of how advanced you are
questions.explanation: An altar is a place of meeting, a focus, a workbench and a record of your path. It isn't a status symbol; a simple shelf with a candle and one meaningful object is a real altar.

questions.prompt: You must own a full set of tools (athame, wand, chalice, pentacle) before you can practise.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. No tools are required. Your breath, body, attention and hands are enough. Tools are aids, and pressure to buy a set (especially from the person telling you) is a red flag.

questions.prompt: What is an athame traditionally used for?
options: Cutting herbs and cords
Directing energy: casting the circle, cutting a door, consecrating
Eating the ritual feast
Self-defence
questions.explanation: The athame is a ritual knife for directing energy, not for physical cutting; the boline does the practical cutting. Your finger or a wand does the same job as an athame.

questions.prompt: You want to take your ritual knife to an outdoor coven rite. What should you do first?
options: Carry it on your belt so it's ready
Check the law where you live; keep it at home or transport it only if it's legal, wrapped and out of reach, or use a wand or your finger instead
Nothing; religious tools are always exempt
Sharpen it
questions.explanation: In many places, carrying a knife in public without good reason is a crime, and a ritual purpose may not count. Check the law, keep knives at home, and use a wand or your finger for outdoor rites.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Hellenic tool, used for pouring libations?
options: A drinking horn
A phiale
A besom
A boline
questions.explanation: The phiale is a shallow libation bowl used in Hellenic practice (the Roman equivalent is the patera). The drinking horn is Heathen, the besom a broom, the boline a practical knife.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between cleansing and consecrating an object?
options: They're the same thing
Cleansing clears what the object carries from before; consecrating dedicates it to sacred use
Cleansing is for stones; consecrating is for metal
Consecrating clears the object; cleansing blesses it
questions.explanation: Cleansing clears an object's past; consecrating dedicates it to your practice. Charging, a third step, fills it with energy for a particular purpose.

questions.prompt: Which cleansing methods are safe for a silver pendant set with an opal? Choose all that apply.
options: Passing it through incense smoke
Ringing a bell over it
Burying it in salt overnight
Breath and visualisation
questions.explanation: Salt corrodes metal and can damage soft or porous stones like opal. Smoke, sound and breath are safe for everything.

questions.prompt: During a consecration, how should you use the candle flame for an object made of fabric?
options: Pass it quickly through the flame
Hold it well above the flame, or simply name fire while holding it near the candle
Burn a corner of it
Leave it on the candle overnight
questions.explanation: Never pass anything flammable through a flame. Hold it well clear, or name fire while holding it near the candle. Keep sleeves and hair back.

questions.prompt: Which are good ways to deal with old food and drink offerings? Choose all that apply.
options: Put food outdoors on the earth if it's safe for wildlife
Pour drink onto soil or into the garden
Compost or bin them respectfully if you can't put them outside
Leave them on the altar until they go mouldy
questions.explanation: Offerings are returned to the earth, composted or binned respectfully, following your tradition's custom. Avoid foods toxic to animals outdoors, and don't let offerings rot on the altar.

questions.prompt: If you can't keep a physical altar, the app's altar can be a real place of practice where you light candles, make offerings and tend daily.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Practitioners have long used images, words and imagination for sacred space. The app's altar can be used instead of a physical one, alongside it as a twin, for workings, or with your coven.

questions.prompt: Describe the altar you've set up (or the one you would set up): where it is, what's on it and why, and how you've made it safe.
questions.explanation: A good altar answer gives a safe, stable place; things chosen for meaning (a light, the elements, something for your gods or path, an offering dish, something from nature, something personal); and practical safety for flames, pets, children and plants.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): a suitable, stable location with a reason (1); at least three items with what each means or is for (1); at least one specific safety measure for flames, pets, children, plants or food (1).

questions.prompt: Describe how you cleansed and consecrated one object, step by step: what it was, which cleansing method you chose and why it was safe for that material, the steps of the consecration, and what you noticed.
questions.explanation: Choose a cleansing method safe for the material, then consecrate within sacred space by stating the object's purpose and blessing it by earth, air, fire (safely), water and spirit, or your coven's form; then use it, close and ground.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): names the object and a cleansing method (1); explains why the method is safe for that material (1); describes stating the purpose and consecrating by the elements or the coven's own form (1); handles fire safely and closes and grounds (1); honestly describes what they noticed, including if little (1).

quizzes.title: The Hellenic tradition: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on what Hellenismos is, its sources and values, its gods and other powers, Hekate, and how a Hellenic coven works. You need 80% to pass. Your mentor will score the written answers.

questions.prompt: What does UPG stand for, and what does it describe?
options: Universal Pagan Guidance: rules agreed by all Hellenic groups
Unverified personal gnosis: something you have come to believe through your own experience
Unwritten Practice of the Greeks: customs passed down in secret since ancient times
Upper Gods: the Olympians, as opposed to the chthonic powers
questions.explanation: Unverified personal gnosis is knowledge from your own experience: a dream, a feeling in prayer. It can be precious to you, but it is not evidence for anyone else, and it should be labelled honestly.

questions.prompt: Which of these are ancient sources for Greek religion? Choose all that apply.
options: Hesiod's Theogony
Sacred laws carved in stone
The Homeric Hymns
A popular website listing crystals for each god
Vase paintings of libation and procession
questions.explanation: Poems, hymns, inscriptions and art are all ancient evidence, each with its own strengths and blind spots. Crystal lists are modern correspondences: useful, but not ancient.

questions.prompt: The Orphic Hymns and the Homeric poems are both ancient. What should you remember when using them together?
options: They were written by the same poet
They are roughly a thousand years apart and come from different worlds
The Orphic Hymns are older and therefore more reliable
Only the Orphic Hymns may be used as prayers
questions.explanation: Homer is about the 8th to 7th century BCE; the Orphic Hymns are probably Roman-period, around the 2nd or 3rd century CE. Always ask who wrote something, when and where.

questions.prompt: Which best describes kharis?
options: A payment that obliges a god to grant your request
The goodwill that builds between a person and a god through a history of gifts and gratitude
A purification made by plunging fire into water
The Greek word for the household shrine
questions.explanation: Kharis is a bond of goodwill, closer to friendship than to a bargain. Regular small offerings and thanks keep it alive; the gods are never obliged.

questions.prompt: Xenia, the sacred duty of hospitality, means you must welcome anyone into your home even if they threaten you.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Xenia bound the guest as firmly as the host. You may refuse anyone who threatens you, and no group may use hospitality to pressure you into giving money, shelter or anything else.

questions.prompt: How were offerings to the dead and the underworld powers usually treated, and how do most modern practitioners treat them?
options: They were shared at a feast with the living
They were given away completely, often poured into the earth, and not eaten by the living
They were burned on high altars at noon
They were kept on the shrine for a year
questions.explanation: Offerings to the dead and chthonic powers, such as choai, were given away entirely. Most practitioners keep this rule: what is given to the dead is not eaten.

questions.prompt: In Hesiod's Theogony, how is Hekate described?
options: As a frightening crone who punishes the disrespectful
As a great goddess honoured by Zeus above all, with a share of earth, sea and sky, who helps people in many walks of life
As a minor spirit of crossroads with no other powers
As the mother of Persephone
questions.explanation: Hesiod's long praise of Hekate (Theogony 411 to 452) shows a generous, powerful goddess. Her links with crossroads, night and magic grew over later centuries; the Crone is modern.

questions.prompt: Which of these are modern additions to the picture of Hekate rather than ancient evidence? Choose all that apply.
options: Hekate as the Crone of a Maiden, Mother and Crone triple goddess
Small shrines to Hekate at house doors and crossroads
Suppers left for Hekate at the end of the month
Lists of crystals and colours sacred to her
questions.explanation: Door and crossroads shrines and the monthly supper are ancient. The Crone comes from 20th-century writing, and crystal and colour lists are modern correspondences.

questions.prompt: You leave a Deipnon supper for Hekate outdoors where dogs and cats roam. Which of these should you leave out?
options: Bread
A plain boiled egg
Garlic
A small honey cake
questions.explanation: Garlic and onion are toxic to dogs and cats. Garlic is a traditional offering to Hekate, so keep it indoors or clear it promptly, and leave only animal-safe food outside.

questions.prompt: If a message in prayer tells you a god wants you to stop your medication and give your savings to the coven, you should talk to your mentor and not act on it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. No god will ask you to harm yourself, give away money you need, isolate yourself or stop medical treatment. Stop, ground yourself and get support.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words the difference between something ancient, a modern reconstruction and personal gnosis, with one example of each from Hellenic practice.
questions.explanation: Ancient practices are attested in ancient evidence (khernips, libation). Reconstructions rebuild practice from that evidence, filling gaps (the monthly cycle as one household package). Personal gnosis comes from your own experience and is labelled as such.
questions.rubric: Full marks: defines all three layers clearly (1 point); gives a correct example of each, such as khernips or libation for ancient, the monthly Deipnon-Noumenia-Agathos Daimon cycle or modern correspondences for reconstruction, and a personal sense of a god's preference for UPG (1 point); shows why labelling matters, for example honesty with others or avoiding false "ancient" claims (1 point).

questions.prompt: Describe what a Hellenic coven gathering for a festival is likely to involve, from arrival to the shared meal, and name two rights every member keeps.
questions.explanation: A gathering usually runs: welcome, briefing, procession, khernips, Hestia first, prayer and offerings, the festival's heart, Hestia last, closing and a shared meal. Members can always say no, leave, know what a rite involves, and are never asked for sex, money beyond agreed costs or harmful secrets.
questions.rubric: Full marks: gives the main steps in a sensible order including procession, khernips, Hestia first and last, prayer with libation or offering, and a shared meal (2 points); names two rights, such as being told what a rite involves, saying no at any time, never being asked for sex, money or harmful secrets, or leaving with kindness (1 point); mentions how online gatherings work or what their own part might be (1 point).

quizzes.title: Hellenic devotion: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on household worship, daily and monthly practice, the Deipnon, offerings, ancestors, purification and discernment. You need 80% to pass. Your mentor will score the written answers.

questions.prompt: Which god receives the first and last offering in Hellenic household worship?
options: Zeus
Hekate
Hestia
Hermes
questions.explanation: Hestia, the hearth, receives the first and last offering. The Homeric Hymn to Hestia says wine is poured to her "both first and last".

questions.prompt: What is a kadiskos?
options: A jar for Zeus Ktesios, kept near the household stores and filled with small amounts of food
A torch carried for Hekate at the crossroads
A bowl for khernips
A cake offered at the Noumenia
questions.explanation: The kadiskos is a lidded jar for Zeus Ktesios, guardian of the household stores, described in an ancient guide quoted by Athenaeus. Modern practitioners feed it each month.

questions.prompt: In what order do the three monthly days come?
options: Noumenia, Deipnon, Agathos Daimon
Deipnon (last day), Noumenia (first day), Agathos Daimon (second day)
Agathos Daimon, Noumenia, Deipnon
All three fall on the full moon
questions.explanation: The Deipnon closes the old month at the dark moon, the Noumenia begins the new month with the crescent, and the Agathos Daimon follows on the second day.

questions.prompt: Which belong to keeping Hekate's Deipnon? Choose all that apply.
options: Cleaning the house and carrying out the sweepings
Leaving a supper at a crossroads or your threshold
Eating the supper together afterwards
Walking away without looking back
questions.explanation: The Deipnon combines household cleaning and purification with a supper for Hekate left at a crossroads or threshold. You walk away without turning back, and the supper is not eaten by the household.

questions.prompt: You want to leave Hekate's supper on a street corner where dogs are walked. Which offering is safest?
options: A chocolate cake
A bunch of grapes
A plain boiled egg and a piece of bread
A clove of garlic
questions.explanation: Chocolate, grapes, raisins, onion and garlic are toxic to dogs and cats. Plain bread and a boiled egg in small amounts are traditional and safe.

questions.prompt: If it is not safe to go out at night, leaving the Deipnon supper on your own doorstep and clearing it in the morning is a proper way to keep the rite.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The threshold is Hekate's place too. Your safety matters more than the exact location.

questions.prompt: What is the best approach to a vow made to a god?
options: Promise something large to make sure the god notices
Make it small, specific and certainly keepable, write it down, and tell your mentor if it is large
Keep it secret from everyone, including your mentor
Vows are not part of Greek religion
questions.explanation: Vows were common in Greek religion and votive offerings fill the sanctuaries. Because a broken vow damages the relationship, keep vows small, specific and achievable.

questions.prompt: Why do most modern practitioners keep an ancestor shrine separate from the shrine of the gods?
options: Because ancestors are jealous of the gods
Because Greek religion kept the deathless gods and the dead apart, with offerings to the dead given into the earth
Because ancestors must be honoured outdoors only
There is no reason; it is just tidier
questions.explanation: The gods are deathless; the dead have died. Greek religion kept them apart, and choai to the dead were poured wholly away into the earth. A separate shelf honours that distinction.

questions.prompt: Miasma is the Greek word for sin: it means you have done something morally wrong.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Miasma is ritual uncleanness, often from good and necessary acts like attending a birth or a funeral. It is removed by washing and time. Moral wrongs need amends, not khernips.

questions.prompt: Which of these messages are red flags that you should not act on, whatever their source? Choose all that apply.
options: Stop taking your prescribed medication
Give your savings to a particular person
Clean your shrine and pour a libation this evening
Cut off contact with your family and friends
questions.explanation: No god asks you to stop treatment, give away money you need or isolate yourself. Cleaning a shrine and pouring a libation is ordinary practice.

questions.prompt: Ancient writers distinguished healthy piety from deisidaimonia. What was deisidaimonia?
options: The most devout form of piety
Superstition: excessive fear of the gods, seeing danger everywhere
A festival of the dead
A kind of incense
questions.explanation: Theophrastus and Plutarch both mocked or criticised superstition, a fearful religion that sees divine anger behind every accident. Piety is not fear.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would keep the Noumenia at home, step by step, in a way that fits your real life.
questions.explanation: A Noumenia usually includes looking for the crescent, refreshing the shrine, khernips, Hestia first, incense and offerings to the household gods, a hope for the month, and Hestia last.
questions.rubric: Full marks: includes khernips and Hestia first and last (1 point); includes an offering to the household gods such as incense, a cake, or feeding the kadiskos (1 point); is realistic for the trainee's life, with a short version or timing, and includes a safe disposal of the offering (1 point).

questions.prompt: You feel strongly, during evening prayer, that a god wants you to make a large change in your life. Explain step by step how you would discern what to do.
questions.explanation: Write it down and label it, wait, compare it with the tradition, notice your own state, ask by divination without fishing for answers, talk to your mentor, and check it against the red flags before acting.
questions.rubric: Full marks: writes it down and labels it as personal experience (1 point); waits rather than acting at once, and checks it against the tradition and their own state (1 point); uses divination honestly and talks to their mentor (1 point); checks it against red flags such as harm, money, isolation or stopping treatment, and knows when to seek medical help (1 point).

quizzes.title: Dedication: test
quizzes.intro: Ten questions on what dedication means, how to prepare, the shape of the rite and aftercare. You need 80% to pass. Your mentor will score the written answers.

questions.prompt: What is an anathema in Greek religion?
options: A curse on an enemy
A gift dedicated to a god and left with them
A purification with water
A festival of the dead
questions.explanation: An anathema, "something set up", was a gift dedicated to a god. Once given, it belonged to the god and was not taken back or used for ordinary purposes.

questions.prompt: Which were ancient Greek ways of dedicating something of oneself at a threshold of life? Choose all that apply.
options: Girls dedicating toys or a lock of hair to Artemis before marriage
Young men dedicating a lock of hair to a river god or Apollo
Signing a lifelong contract with a priest
Craftspeople dedicating their tools on retirement
questions.explanation: Greeks marked life's thresholds by dedicating hair, toys, clothes or tools to the gods. Contracts with priests were no part of this.

questions.prompt: A devotee's dedication is the same as initiation.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Dedication is the first commitment to the coven's path. Initiation, if sought later, follows a year and a day of further study and service, with its own oath.

questions.prompt: Which is the wisest approach to dedicating yourself to a particular god, such as Hekate?
options: Do it after one strong experience
Honour them steadily for months, learn about them, discern, and talk to your mentor first
Do it secretly without telling anyone
Dedicate to them instead of Hestia
questions.explanation: A relationship built slowly is stronger than one built on a single intense experience. Dedication to one god never means neglecting Hestia and the household gods.

questions.prompt: Your words of dedication should include commitments that are:
options: As grand and sweeping as possible
Specific and things you can actually do
Secret from your mentor
Promises to stay in the coven forever
questions.explanation: Like a vow or an oath, a dedication is only as good as your ability to keep it. Two or three specific, keepable commitments are best.

questions.prompt: In the dedication rite, why does the leader ask the devotee questions such as "Do you come freely?"
options: To test their knowledge
So that the devotee's consent is spoken aloud before the gods and the coven
To embarrass them
Because the gods require it by law
questions.explanation: The questions make consent explicit. A dedication must be freely given.

questions.prompt: If you are unwell or in crisis as your dedication date approaches, it is right to postpone.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Dedication can wait; your wellbeing comes first.

questions.prompt: After dedication, which of these remain true? Choose all that apply.
options: You can still say no, ask questions, pause or leave
The coven or its leader now owns your time
Your life outside the coven still matters
You keep your household practice
questions.explanation: Dedication is a free commitment. You keep every right, your life outside matters, and your household practice continues. No one owns you.

questions.prompt: Write a draft of your words of dedication, following the steps in the lesson.
questions.explanation: Good words address the gods, recall the relationship, state what you give and will do, and ask simply for what you hope.
questions.rubric: Full marks: addresses Hestia and other fitting gods (1 point); recalls the relationship built over the devotee months, in the manner of a Greek prayer's argument (1 point); makes two or three specific, keepable commitments and a simple request (1 point).

questions.prompt: If, after dedicating, you found the path was not yours, how would you leave well?
questions.explanation: Leaving well means talking honestly, taking time unless there is harm, keeping confidences, returning coven property, thanking the gods and parting kindly.
questions.rubric: Full marks: describes honest conversation and keeping confidences (1 point); mentions a closing act with the gods or returning what belongs to the coven, and notes that leaving because of harm should be immediate with outside support (1 point).

programs.title: Hellenic: A year and a day to initiation
programs.summary: For devotees seeking initiation: deeper craft, the full year of holy days, service, oath and preparation.
programs.description: A year and a day of deeper study: correspondences, the moon and timing, divination, spellcraft, every holy day of the year, ritual craft and coven life, and the path to initiation itself: study, service, the oath and preparing for the rite your coven keeps.

stages.title: Correspondences
stages.intro: In this stage you learn the language of correspondences: colours, plants, stones, days and hours, and how to use them safely. You will study a few materials closely, start your own list, and plan a working.

tasks.title: What correspondences are, and colours
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “What correspondences are” and “Colours”.
2. Do the colour exercise at the end of “Colours”: five coloured things, one minute each.
3. In the answer box, write the five colours and your three words for each, and note where you agreed or disagreed with the list.

tasks.title: Herb, oil and incense safety audit
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Herb, oil and incense safety” in full.
2. Gather every herb, oil, resin and incense you own.
3. For each, look up its cautions in the Living Library or on its label and write one line in your Grimoire: what it is, what it is safe for, what to avoid.
4. Throw away anything unlabelled you can’t identify, and move anything dangerous out of reach of children and pets.
5. In the answer box, list what you found and anything you moved or got rid of.

tasks.title: Study a plant
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Twelve common plants”.
2. Choose one of the twelve that you have or can easily get. Check its cautions first.
3. Do the ten-minute correspondence study from “Building your own correspondences”, writing your notes before you look anything up.
4. Do this three times, with a different plant each time, or the same plant on three different days.
5. Log each session. In the answer box, write your notes for each session.

tasks.title: Meet a stone
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Seven common stones”.
2. Take one stone you own, or a pebble you have found. Check whether it can go in water or sun.
3. Cleanse it by a method safe for that stone, then sit with it for five minutes as the lesson describes.
4. Dedicate it to one purpose in a sentence.
5. In the answer box, write what stone it is, how you cleansed it, what you noticed and what you dedicated it to. If you would like your mentor to see it, add a photo description.

tasks.title: A week of days and hours
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Days of the week and planetary hours”.
2. Each day for seven days, open the app’s planetary hours and note the planet of the day and of the hour you looked.
3. Write one line in your journal on how the day felt.
4. Log each day. On the last day, write in the answer box whether you noticed any pattern (it is fine if you didn’t).

tasks.title: Start your own correspondence list
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read “Building your own correspondences”.
2. Choose one intention that matters to you now.
3. Gather from your home one colour, one plant or food, one stone or natural object, and one sound or song that feel like it.
4. Write them as the first page of your personal list in your Grimoire, marking each as traditional, coven or mine.
5. In the answer box, copy the page and add a line on why you chose each.
6. Send your mentor a message on this step if you would like to talk through your choices.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read any lesson you are unsure of.
2. Take the Correspondences test. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers.
3. You need 80 per cent to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, revisit the lessons and take it again.

stages.title: The Moon and the seasons
stages.intro: In this stage you get to know the real Moon and the turning year where you live, and learn how to time your magic by them without being ruled by them. It takes at least one full lunation, because you will watch the Moon through a whole month.

tasks.title: Read about the phases
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “The Moon’s phases”.
2. Check the app for today’s phase and the dates of the next new and full moons.
3. In the answer box, write which phase it is today, how the lit side should look from where you live, and when your coven holds its lunar gatherings (ask your mentor if you don’t know).

tasks.title: Keep a moon journal for a lunation
tasks.instructions:
1. For about a month, look for the Moon as often as you can.
2. Each time, write in your journal the date, time, where it was, its shape, and one word for how you felt. Note your mood, energy and sleep too.
3. If you can’t see it, write that down.
4. Log each entry here. Aim for at least twenty days in the month.
5. On your last entry, write in the answer box any patterns you noticed.

tasks.title: Keep the full moon
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Working with the phases”.
2. On or near the next full moon, do the full-moon practice from the lesson (about 20 minutes), keeping your candle safe.
3. Make a jar of moon water with the lid on, and use it over the next fortnight to cleanse your altar.
4. In the answer box, write your three thanks, what you named, and what you noticed. Send your mentor a message on this step if anything came up you would like to talk about.

tasks.title: Look further into the sky
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Signs, void-of-course and eclipses”.
2. On three days this week, open the app and note the Moon’s phase, sign, and the next void-of-course period.
3. Log each day, with one line on how the day felt.

tasks.title: Your seasonal spot
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “The Sun’s year and the seasons”.
2. Choose an outdoor spot (or a window view) you can visit weekly.
3. Visit four times, a week apart, for about five minutes each.
4. Each time, write three lines: what you saw, what changed, how you feel. Log each visit.
5. Keep visiting through the rest of the course if you can.

tasks.title: Plan a timed working
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “When timing matters, and when it doesn’t”.
2. Choose something you would like to work for.
3. In the answer box, write the intention three ways: plainly, for a waxing Moon, and for a waning Moon. Add the day and planetary hour you would choose, and one practical action you will take this week whatever the Moon.
4. Your mentor will read it and may reply on this step.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read any lesson you are unsure of.
2. Take the Moon and magical timing test. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers.
3. You need 80 per cent to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, revisit the lessons and take it again.

stages.title: Divination
stages.intro: In this stage you learn what divination is and isn’t, get to know the tarot deck, read for yourself every day, try another system, and learn how to read for others with care. It takes about a month, because daily practice is how readers are made.

tasks.title: What divination is
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “What divination is”.
2. Write three questions about your own life, each turned into a good open question.
3. In the answer box, write each question as you first thought of it, then as you rewrote it.

tasks.title: Meet the deck
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “The tarot deck”.
2. Using your own deck or the app’s cards, sort the deck into the Major Arcana and the four suits.
3. Then study one card a day: two minutes looking at the picture, then write what you see, read its meaning, and write what it means for you.
4. Log each card studied. Start with the 22 Major Arcana.

tasks.title: Daily draw
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “The daily draw and your reading journal”.
2. Each day, draw one card, look, read its meaning, and write two or three lines. In the evening, add a line on how it showed up.
3. Log each day. Aim for 21 days.
4. On the last day, review all your draws as the lesson describes, and write your monthly summary in the answer box.

tasks.title: Three-card readings
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Reading the cards: a three-card spread”.
2. Do three three-card readings for yourself on real questions, a few days apart, following every step.
3. Record each in your reading journal. Log each one.
4. In the answer box, write one of them out in full: question, spread, cards, what you saw, and your summary.

tasks.title: Try another system
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Runes, ogham, pendulum and scrying”, including the safety notes.
2. Choose one system and try it three times this fortnight.
3. Log each session. In the answer box, write what you did, what came, and how it compared with tarot for you.

tasks.title: Read for someone else
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Reading for others, ethically”.
2. Send your mentor a message on this step to agree who you will read for (a friend or fellow trainee who would like it).
3. With their consent and an open question, give a three-card reading, following the steps in the lesson.
4. Afterwards, ask them how it felt.
5. In the answer box, write how you agreed the question, what you read (without anything they asked you to keep private), how you gave any hard cards, and what you learned.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read any lesson you are unsure of.
2. Take the Divination test. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers.
3. You need 80 per cent to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, revisit the lessons and take it again.

stages.title: Spellcraft
stages.intro: In this stage you learn how a spell is made: shaping an intention, the structure every spell shares, the common forms, the ethics that keep magic honourable, and how to record and judge results honestly. You will plan, perform and follow up your own spells.

tasks.title: Shape an intention
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “What a spell is, and the heart of it: intention”.
2. Work through the eight steps for something you genuinely want to change.
3. In the answer box, write your first rough version and your final intention, and say what changed and why.

tasks.title: Ethics check
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “The ethics of spellcraft”.
2. Ask your mentor (send a message on this step) what your coven’s rules are on binding, banishing, cursing and doing magic for others.
3. Do the exercise at the end of the lesson: three imagined spells, checked for consent and harm, and rewritten where needed.
4. In the answer box, write your coven’s rules as you understand them and your three spells before and after.

tasks.title: A candle spell
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “The structure of a spell”, including the safety notes.
2. Plan a candle spell for your intention: timing, two or three components, and three or four lines of words. Show your mentor the plan first by sending it on this step if you would like a second opinion.
3. Perform it, following every step and never leaving the candle unattended.
4. Record it in your Grimoire using the list in “Recording results, and when nothing happens”.
5. In the answer box, write your plan and how it went.

tasks.title: Another form of spell
tasks.instructions:
1. Read “Common forms of spell”.
2. Choose one form other than a candle spell (a jar, charm bag, petition, knots, sigil or kitchen magic) and make it for an ethical intention, following every step and safety note.
3. Plan how you will dispose of it when it is done.
4. Record it in your Grimoire, and log it here. In the answer box, describe what you made and why. Add a photo description if you would like your mentor to see it.

tasks.title: Follow up your spells
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read “Recording results, and when nothing happens”.
2. One week after each spell, and again after a month, add a follow-up note in your Grimoire. Log each follow-up here.
3. On your last follow-up, write in the answer box what happened, what mundane action you took, and, if nothing seemed to happen, your answers to the questions in the lesson.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read any lesson you are unsure of.
2. Take the Spellcraft test. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers.
3. You need 80 per cent to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, revisit the lessons and take it again.

stages.title: The festival year
stages.intro: The Attic year turns through festivals of the city, the harvest, wine and theatre, the dead and the cleansing of sacred things. Here you keep each festival as it comes, reading its lesson ahead of time and writing up what you did. A full turn of the year takes a year; your mentor will help you plan.

tasks.title: Keep the Kronia
tasks.instructions:
1. A week or two before 12 Hekatombaion, in high summer, read the lesson on the Kronia (and "The Attic year" if you haven't yet). The app's calendar shows this year's date.
2. Plan how you will keep it: alone, with the coven, or both. Gather what you need.
3. On the day, keep it as the lesson describes, or in your coven's way.
4. Afterwards, write in the answer box what you did, what you noticed, what you learned about the festival's history, and one thing you'd do differently next year.
5. If you could not keep it on the day, keep a simple version within a few days and say so in your answer.

2. Plan how you will keep it: alone, with the coven, or both. Gather what you need.
3. On the day, keep it as the lesson describes, or in your coven's way.
4. Afterwards, write in the answer box what you did, what you noticed, what you learned about the festival's history, and one thing you'd do differently next year.
5. If you could not keep it on the day, keep a simple version within a few days and say so in your answer.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "The Attic year" and the lessons for any festivals you haven't kept yet.
