> **Try this:** Choose your outdoor spot this week and make your first visit. Write down what you notice. Keep visiting once a week through this course.

docs.title: When timing matters, and when it doesn’t
docs.summary: How to decide how much timing a working needs, why urgent needs should never wait for the Moon, and how to layer timing without becoming ruled by it.
docs.body:
## Timing is a tool, not a gate

Once people learn about phases, days, hours, signs and seasons, some begin to feel they can’t do anything without consulting a chart. That is a trap. Timing is one way to add meaning and focus to a working. It is never a reason to leave someone without help, to avoid acting in ordinary ways, or to feel your magic has “failed” because you got the date wrong.

## When timing matters more

Timing is worth thinking about when:

- **You are planning ahead.** A working for a new project next month can easily be set for a waxing Moon on the right day.
- **The working is large or important to you.** Extra layers of meaning help you focus and treat it seriously.
- **It is a coven rite.** Shared timing (full moons, festivals) brings a group together in a common rhythm, which has a strength of its own.
- **Your tradition asks for it.** Some traditions keep particular days for particular gods, or particular hours for particular rites.
- **You are learning.** Paying attention to timing trains you to notice the world.

## When timing matters less, or not at all

- **When something is urgent.** If you or someone you love needs protection, comfort or healing *now*, act now. Every phase can be worded to suit (as you learned in Working with the phases), and every day has an hour of every planet.
- **For daily devotion and simple practices.** Grounding, prayer, offerings, a daily card: do them every day, whatever the Moon is doing.
- **When the alternative is not doing it at all.** A working done at the “wrong” time with care is worth more than a perfect working that never happens.

> **Safety:** Magic never replaces ordinary action in a crisis. If someone is in danger, ill or in distress, contact emergency services, a doctor or a crisis line first. Do your magic as well, at any time, but never instead.

## Layering timing

When you do want to plan, here is a simple order that keeps it manageable:

1. **Start with the phase.** Waxing for growth, waning for release, full for power and thanks, new for seeds and rest.
2. **Add the day,** if it is easy: Friday for love, Thursday for luck, Saturday for boundaries.
3. **Add the planetary hour,** if you want to: the app finds the next one.
4. **Check the void-of-course Moon,** if you or your coven use it, for big new beginnings.
5. **Stop there.** If all the layers won’t line up for weeks, pick the most important one (usually the phase) and go ahead.

## A worked example

Sam wants to do a working to find a new job.

1. *Intention:* “I find a job that suits me and pays fairly.”
2. *Phase:* it is a waning Moon. Sam can wait about ten days for the waxing Moon, or reword the intention for the waning Moon: “All that keeps me from the right job falls away.” Sam decides to do both: a release working now, and a drawing-in working when the Moon is waxing.
3. *Day and hour:* for the waxing working, Sam chooses a Sunday (success) in the hour of Mercury (applications and interviews), found in the app.
4. *Mundane action:* every week, whatever the Moon, Sam sends applications and updates their CV. The magic supports the action; it doesn’t replace it.
5. *Record:* Sam writes down both workings with their dates, phases, days and hours, and notes what happens over the following weeks.

## Common traps

- **Waiting for perfect timing.** All the layers rarely line up. If you find yourself putting a working off week after week, choose the phase alone and begin.
- **Anxiety about getting it wrong.** Timing is meant to add meaning and confidence, not fear. If checking the sky makes you anxious, step back to the phases only, or set timing aside for a while.
- **Blaming the timing.** When a working doesn’t go as hoped, it is tempting to blame the void-of-course Moon or a retrograde. Look first at the intention, the effort and the ordinary action you took, as you will learn in Spellcraft.
- **Letting timing replace care.** No phase or hour is ever a reason to delay helping someone, seeing a doctor, or keeping yourself safe.
- **Copying someone else’s calendar.** A book written for another hemisphere or tradition may not fit you. Use your own sky and your own coven’s calendar.

## Recording and learning

The only way to know how much timing matters *for you* is to keep records. For every working, note the date, time, phase, day, hour (and sign and void-of-course status if you use them). After six months, look back. Did workings at certain times feel stronger? Did they turn out differently? Your records, honestly kept, will teach you more than any book, including this one.

> **Your coven:** Covens often have to meet when people are free, not when the sky is perfect. Many covens hold their full-moon rite on the nearest convenient evening. Ask your mentor how strict your coven is about dates, and why.

> **Try this:** Think of something you would like to work for. Write the intention, then write it twice more: once worded for a waxing Moon and once for a waning Moon. Add the day and hour you would choose. Then write one ordinary, practical action you will take towards it this week, whatever the Moon.

docs.title: What divination is
docs.summary: What divination is and isn’t, a short honest history, the different ways practitioners understand it, how to ask a good question, and how to choose a system.
docs.body:
## Seeking insight

**Divination** is any practice of seeking insight or guidance through a system of signs: cards, runes, the fall of lots, a swinging pendulum, the patterns in water or smoke, the flight of birds, dreams. The word comes from Latin *divinare*, “to foresee” or “to be inspired by a god”.

Divination is one of the oldest and most widespread human practices. Babylonian priests read the livers of sacrificed animals. Greeks travelled to the oracle at Delphi. Romans watched the flight of birds before public business (the *augurs*). The Norse and other Germanic peoples, according to the Roman writer Tacitus, cast marked strips of wood to learn the will of the gods. Chinese diviners used the *Yijing* (I Ching). It is found on every continent.

In a coven, divination is used to look at a situation more clearly, to ask the gods or spirits for guidance, to check whether a working is wise before doing it, to reflect on your own path, and sometimes to help others.

## What divination can and can’t do

Be honest with yourself and with anyone you read for.

Divination **can**:

- help you see a situation from new angles;
- bring to the surface what you already half know;
- prompt good questions and better decisions;
- give a sense of guidance, comfort or warning;
- in many traditions, be a way of listening to gods, spirits and ancestors.

Divination **can’t**:

- tell you fixed facts about the future, as if it were already written;
- diagnose illness, predict pregnancy, settle legal questions, or tell you whether to take a medicine;
- tell you for certain what someone else is thinking or doing;
- replace doctors, lawyers, counsellors, or your own judgement.

There is no scientific evidence that divination predicts events. Practitioners who find it valuable usually speak of it as insight and guidance rather than prediction.

## How might it work?

Practitioners hold different views. You don’t need to choose one.

1. **As a mirror.** The symbols prompt your own intuition and unconscious mind. A card shows you a picture; what you see in it, and what you feel about it, tells you something you didn’t know you knew. The psychologist Carl Jung’s idea of *synchronicity* (meaningful coincidence) is often mentioned here.
2. **As a conversation.** Gods, spirits, ancestors or your own deeper self guide the fall of cards or runes to say something. This is the oldest understanding: in most ancient divination, the gods were the ones speaking.
3. **As a tool for thinking.** Even if nothing beyond chance is at work, a random prompt breaks habits of thought and helps you consider options you had overlooked.

Many practitioners use all three at different times.

## Asking a good question

The quality of a reading depends heavily on the question.

1. **Make it open, not yes or no.** “What do I need to know about this new job?” works better than “Will I get the job?”
2. **Make it about you,** or about something you have a right to know. “How can I improve my relationship with my sister?” rather than “What is my sister secretly thinking?”
3. **Make it about the near future or the present.** Readings are clearest about the next weeks or months, and about the forces at work now.
4. **Make it one question.** If you have three questions, do three readings.
5. **Write it down** before you begin, so you can read it back later.

Good starting forms: “What do I need to know about…?”, “What would help me with…?”, “What is the best approach to…?”, “What am I not seeing about…?”

## Choosing a system

There are hundreds of divination systems. For a beginner, it is best to learn **one** system well before trying others. A good choice:

- **Tarot** is the most widely used in modern witchcraft, has a rich picture language that beginners can read straight away, and is taught in depth in the next two lessons. The app has a full tarot deck with meanings.
- **Oracle decks** are simpler picture decks with no fixed structure; each comes with its own guidebook. They are gentle to start with but vary greatly.
- **Runes** suit Heathen and Germanic-leaning practitioners, and are taught briefly in a later lesson.
- **Ogham** suits Celtic-leaning practitioners, also taught briefly later.
- **Pendulum** is good for simple yes-or-no questions.
- **Scrying** (gazing into water, a mirror or flame) suits people who see images easily.

Choose what draws you, what fits your tradition, and what you can get easily. You can use the app’s cards and runes before buying anything.

## A first reading, before you know anything

You can begin today, before learning a single meaning.

1. Sit quietly and take five slow breaths.
2. Write an open question about your own life.
3. Draw one tarot card (from the app or a deck) without looking up its meaning.
4. Look at the picture for three minutes. Describe aloud or on paper everything you see: who is there, what they are doing, the colours, the weather, the mood.
5. Ask: if this picture were an answer to my question, what would it be saying?
6. Write your answer down. Only then look up the card’s meaning and compare.

Many beginners are surprised how much they find in the picture alone. That is the heart of reading: looking closely and listening to what arises.

## Common difficulties at the start

- **“I feel silly.”** Most people do at first. It passes with practice.
- **“I don’t trust what comes.”** That’s healthy. Write it down and see how it looks in a week.
- **“I want to read about everything.”** Keep to one question a day for now. Too many readings blur together.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may favour one system, especially one tied to its tradition: runes in Heathenry, ogham in Celtic paths, lots and omens in Hellenic and Roman practice, Psalms and Bible-opening in Christian folk magic. Ask your mentor which the coven uses and whether it has a reader you can learn from.

> **Safety:** If divination ever makes you anxious, obsessive (reading again and again on the same question) or frightened, stop for a while. Ground yourself, talk to your mentor, and remember that a reading shows possibilities, not fate.

docs.title: The tarot deck
docs.summary: The structure of a tarot deck: the 22 Major Arcana, the four suits and their elements, what the numbers and court cards mean, and a short honest history.
docs.body:
## A short history

Tarot cards first appear in northern Italy in the fifteenth century, as luxury hand-painted decks for a card game called *tarocchi*. The game is still played in parts of Europe. There is no evidence that tarot was used for divination for its first three hundred years or so.

In 1781 the French writer Antoine Court de Gébelin claimed that the tarot held the lost wisdom of ancient Egypt. He was wrong (the Egyptian language hadn’t yet been deciphered, and nothing connects the cards to Egypt), but the idea caught on. In 1789 a French occultist known as Etteilla published the first deck designed for fortune-telling. In the late nineteenth century the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn linked the cards to astrology, the Hebrew alphabet and the four elements.

In 1909 the artist **Pamela Colman Smith**, working with the occultist A. E. Waite, painted a deck in which every card, including the numbered ones, shows a scene. This **Rider–Waite–Smith** deck is the most influential tarot of the twentieth century, and most modern decks follow its structure and imagery. The app’s tarot uses it.

So tarot is old as a deck of cards, and a little over two centuries old as a divination system. It is a living, creative tradition, with thousands of decks made every year.

## The structure

A tarot deck has **78 cards**, in two parts.

### The Major Arcana: 22 cards

*Arcana* means “secrets”. The 22 Major Arcana show large themes, turning points and spiritual lessons. They are numbered 0 to 21. Read through them slowly; the keywords are the app’s.

- **0 The Fool:** beginnings, trust, the open road.
- **1 The Magician:** will, skill, the tools to hand.
- **2 The High Priestess:** secrets, intuition, the inner voice.
- **3 The Empress:** abundance, nurture, fruitfulness.
- **4 The Emperor:** structure, authority, steadiness.
- **5 The Hierophant:** tradition, teaching, belonging.
- **6 The Lovers:** love, union, a true choice.
- **7 The Chariot:** will, direction, victory.
- **8 Strength:** gentle courage, patience, compassion.
- **9 The Hermit:** solitude, inner light, seeking.
- **10 Wheel of Fortune:** cycles, fate, a turning point.
- **11 Justice:** fairness, truth, cause and effect.
- **12 The Hanged Man:** surrender, pause, a new way of seeing.
- **13 Death:** endings, transformation, clearing. Almost never a physical death.
- **14 Temperance:** balance, moderation, patience.
- **15 The Devil:** attachment, temptation, the shadow.
- **16 The Tower:** upheaval, revelation, sudden change.
- **17 The Star:** hope, renewal, calm.
- **18 The Moon:** illusion, fear, the unconscious.
- **19 The Sun:** joy, success, vitality.
- **20 Judgement:** awakening, reckoning, a calling.
- **21 The World:** completion, wholeness, arrival.

Many readers see the Major Arcana as a story, sometimes called **the Fool’s Journey**: the Fool sets out (0), meets teachers and powers (1 to 5), makes choices and gains mastery (6 to 10), faces trials, surrender and endings (11 to 16), and finds hope, illumination and completion (17 to 21).

> **Note:** In older decks such as the Tarot of Marseille, Strength is 11 and Justice is 8. Waite swapped them. Neither is wrong; just know which your deck uses.

### The Minor Arcana: 56 cards

The Minor Arcana are like ordinary playing cards: four suits, each with cards from Ace to Ten and four court cards. They show the everyday events, people, feelings and choices of life.

The four suits, with the elements most modern readers give them (from the Golden Dawn):

- **Wands** (also rods, staves): **fire.** Will, energy, creativity, ambition, work, passion. Equivalent to clubs in playing cards.
- **Cups:** **water.** Feelings, love, relationships, intuition, dreams. Equivalent to hearts.
- **Swords:** **air.** Thought, truth, words, conflict, decisions, difficulty. Equivalent to spades.
- **Pentacles** (also coins, disks): **earth.** Money, work, the body, home, the material world. Equivalent to diamonds.

> **Note:** A few decks and readers swap Wands and Swords, giving Wands to air and Swords to fire. If your deck’s book does this, follow it.

### The numbers

Each number has a general meaning, which combines with the suit:

- **Ace:** a seed, a beginning, the pure gift of the suit.
- **Two:** balance, choice, partnership.
- **Three:** growth, first results, cooperation.
- **Four:** stability, structure, rest (sometimes stagnation).
- **Five:** conflict, loss, challenge, disruption.
- **Six:** harmony restored, generosity, moving on.
- **Seven:** assessment, testing, a choice or a challenge to hold your ground.
- **Eight:** movement, effort, mastery or being caught.
- **Nine:** near-completion, fulfilment or its anxieties.
- **Ten:** completion, the end of a cycle, sometimes too much.

So the **Ace of Cups** is a new love or emotional beginning; the **Five of Pentacles** is material hardship; the **Ten of Wands** is the burden of carrying too much work.

### The court cards

Each suit has four court cards: **Page, Knight, Queen, King.** They can show:

- **a person** in your life, with the qualities of that rank and suit;
- **a part of you** you need to use;
- **a way of approaching** the situation.

A general guide:

- **Page:** a learner, messenger, beginner, curiosity.
- **Knight:** action, movement, pursuit (sometimes too fast or too much).
- **Queen:** mature, inward mastery of the suit; nurturing, understanding.
- **King:** mature, outward mastery of the suit; leadership, responsibility.

The **Queen of Cups** might be a deeply compassionate person, or a call to listen to your own feelings with care. The **Knight of Swords** might be someone rushing in with sharp words, or a call to act quickly on a clear idea.

Court cards are traditionally hard for beginners. Don’t worry about getting them “right”; notice what they suggest.

## Reversed cards

Some readers read cards that come out upside down as **reversed**, with a changed meaning: often the energy of the card blocked, delayed, turned inward, or overdone. The app gives reversed meanings for every card. Reading reversals is optional. Many good readers never use them. As a beginner, you may prefer to turn every card upright and add reversals later.

## Getting to know your deck

1. **Choose a deck.** The app’s Rider–Waite–Smith cards are a good start. If you buy a deck, choose one whose pictures you like and that follows the Rider–Waite–Smith structure, with scenes on every card.
2. **Look through every card,** slowly, without reading the meanings. Notice what catches your eye.
3. **Sort them** into Major Arcana and the four suits, and lay out each suit from Ace to King.
4. **Study one card a day.** Look at the picture for two minutes. Write what you see: people, colours, objects, weather, mood. Then read its meaning and write what you think it means *for you*.

There is a myth that your first tarot deck must be given to you as a gift. It needn’t. Buy, borrow or use the app’s.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have a preferred deck, or readers who use a particular one. Some covens cleanse and consecrate decks as tools (as you learned in Altar and tools). Ask your mentor.

docs.title: The daily draw and your reading journal
docs.summary: How to keep a daily one-card practice and a reading journal, what to record, and how reviewing your readings over time makes you a better reader.
docs.body:
## Little and often

The single best way to learn any divination system is a **daily draw**: one card (or rune, or ogham stave) each day, read and recorded. It takes five minutes. Over a few months, you will meet every card many times in the context of real days, which teaches you more than any book.

## The daily draw, step by step

1. **Choose a time.** Morning works well, so you can carry the card through the day and see how it fits. Some people prefer evening, as a reflection on the day just gone. Be consistent.
2. **Ground briefly.** Three slow breaths.
3. **Ask a simple question.** For example: “What do I need to know today?”, “What energy will help me today?”, or “What should I pay attention to?”
4. **Shuffle and draw one card.** Use your own deck or the app’s draw.
5. **Look first.** Spend a minute with the picture.
6. **Read the meaning.** Look it up if you need to.
7. **Write two or three lines:** the card, what you see in it, and one guess about how it might show up today.
8. **In the evening, add a line:** did it show up? How?

## Learning a card through the day

A daily card is a small teacher. To get the most from it:

1. **Describe it in your own words** before reading anything. “A man carrying ten heavy sticks towards a town, bent over, can’t see where he’s going.”
2. **Find the keyword that fits the picture.** For the Ten of Wands the app gives burden, responsibility, overload. You can see it in the picture.
3. **Make one guess.** “Today I might take on too much at work.”
4. **Watch.** During the day, notice anything that echoes the card: a conversation, a mood, a sight, a choice.
5. **Reflect in the evening.** Perhaps you did take on too much; perhaps you said no to something and felt relief; perhaps nothing matched. Write it down either way.

Over months, each card gathers real memories: the day the Ten of Wands was the shopping you carried home in the rain, the day the Star was the message from an old friend. Those memories become your meanings, and they are far easier to recall than lists.

## A worked week

Here is a trainee’s first week, as she wrote it in her journal.

- **Monday, Page of Cups:** a young person looking at a fish in a cup, surprised. *Guess:* a pleasant surprise. *Evening:* a colleague brought cake for no reason. Small, but it fitted.
- **Tuesday, Five of Swords:** someone walking off with swords, others defeated. *Guess:* an argument. *Evening:* I nearly snapped at my brother and didn’t. Maybe a warning heeded.
- **Wednesday, The Hermit:** an old man with a lantern alone on a mountain. *Guess:* I need time alone. *Evening:* cancelled plans and read; felt much better.
- **Thursday, Eight of Pentacles:** someone carefully making coins at a bench. *Guess:* steady work. *Evening:* finished a dull report properly. Felt good.
- **Friday, Three of Cups:** three women dancing with cups. *Guess:* friends. *Evening:* drinks with friends. Easy one.
- **Saturday, The Tower:** lightning, people falling. *Guess:* something sudden. *Evening:* the boiler broke. Annoying, not a disaster.
- **Sunday, Four of Swords:** a knight lying still in a church. *Guess:* rest. *Evening:* slept all afternoon.

Notice how ordinary it is. The daily draw is not about drama. It is about learning the cards through real life, and noticing your days more closely.

## Common difficulties

- **Missing days.** Don’t worry; start again the next day.
- **Drawing the same card often.** Take notice. A card that keeps returning may be pointing at something.
- **Every card seems to fit, whatever happens.** That can happen, because cards are broad. Make your morning guess specific, and be honest in the evening about whether it fitted.

## What to record

Keep every reading, daily draws and larger spreads alike, in one place: your Grimoire in the app, the app’s reading log, or a notebook. For each reading, write:

- the **date and time**, and the **Moon’s phase** (you will learn something from this);
- the **question**;
- the **spread** and the **cards** in their positions (and whether any were reversed);
- **what you saw** in the pictures and **what you felt**;
- your **summary**: the answer in a sentence or two;
- later, a **follow-up note**: what actually happened, and how the reading looks now.

## Reviewing your readings

Once a month, at the same phase of the Moon if you like, read back over the month’s readings.

1. **Count.** Which cards came up most? Which suits? Were there many Major Arcana? Repeated cards often point to a theme in your life.
2. **Check.** Read your follow-up notes. Which readings seem apt now? Which seem off? Can you see why?
3. **Learn.** Pick one card that confused you and study it again, looking at the picture and the app’s longer Grimoire page.
4. **Write a short summary** of the month: themes, lessons, how your reading is changing.

## Honest record-keeping

It is natural to remember the readings that “came true” and forget those that didn’t. That is how all human memory works. Writing everything down, including the misses, keeps you honest, helps you learn which kinds of question your system answers well, and protects you from both over-trusting and dismissing it.

> **Note:** If a daily card is hard (the Tower, the Five of Pentacles), don’t dread the day. Take it as a gentle warning: be careful with plans, look after your money, check in with yourself. Most days, nothing dramatic happens. Notice how the card shows up in small ways.

> **Your coven:** Some covens share a monthly card or rune with the whole group, or draw one at each esbat. Ask your mentor if yours does.

> **Try this:** Start your daily draw today. Keep it for the rest of this stage, recording each draw, and review the whole set at the end.

docs.title: Reading the cards: a three-card spread
docs.summary: How to prepare, shuffle, lay out and read a three-card spread step by step, with a worked example, common difficulties, and how to know you are improving.
docs.body:
## What a spread is

A **spread** is a pattern for laying out cards, where each position has a meaning. The positions turn a handful of cards into an answer you can read. There are many spreads, from one card to the famous ten-card Celtic Cross. The best one to learn first is the **three-card spread**: simple enough to learn quickly, rich enough to say something real.

## Three ways to read three cards

Choose one before you lay the cards.

- **Past, present, future:** what led here, where things stand, where they are heading if nothing changes.
- **Situation, challenge, advice:** what is going on, what stands in the way, what would help.
- **Mind, body, spirit:** what is happening in your thoughts, your physical life, and your spiritual life.

“Situation, challenge, advice” is especially good for beginners, because it always ends on something you can act on.

## Reading step by step

Allow about twenty minutes.

1. **Prepare the space.** Clear a table. Some people lay a cloth. Light a candle if you wish (safely). Switch off notifications.
2. **Ground and centre,** as you learned in Grounding. Take five slow breaths: in for four, out for six.
3. **Write your question** in your journal. Keep it open and about you (see What divination is).
4. **Shuffle.** Hold the cards and shuffle in whatever way is comfortable: overhand, riffle, or spread them face down on the table and swirl them. While you shuffle, hold the question in mind. Stop when it feels right, or after a count of your choice.
5. **Cut** the deck if you like (many readers cut into three piles with the left hand and restack), then take the top three cards. Or fan them out and pick three that draw you.
6. **Lay them face down,** left to right: position one, two, three.
7. **Turn them over** one at a time.
8. **Look before you read.** For each card, spend a minute just looking. What is happening in the picture? What is the mood? What catches your eye? What do you feel?
9. **Add the meaning.** Now recall or look up the card’s keywords. How do they fit the picture and the position?
10. **Read the cards together.** Look at all three. Is there a story moving left to right? Are there many cards of one suit (lots of Cups suggests feelings are the heart of it)? Many Major Arcana (a big, significant time)? Do people in the cards face towards or away from each other?
11. **Sum it up in one or two sentences.** This is the answer to your question.
12. **Write it down:** the date, question, spread, cards, what you saw, and your summary. If you’re using the app, you can save the reading.
13. **Close.** Thank whatever you feel helped (your deck, your gods, your own intuition), put the cards away, and drink some water.

## A worked example

**Question:** “What would help me feel settled in my new home?”

**Spread:** situation, challenge, advice.

1. **Situation: Four of Wands.** Garlands, people dancing at the gate: celebration, homecoming. The picture says this home is a good thing, a real arrival.
2. **Challenge: Eight of Swords.** A blindfolded woman surrounded by swords, though the way out is open. Feeling trapped, mostly by thoughts. The challenge isn’t the home; it’s worry.
3. **Advice: Six of Cups.** Children sharing flowers in an old courtyard: memory, kindness, simple pleasures. Bring things that feel like home from the past; be gentle; perhaps invite an old friend.

**Summary:** “The home is right. What unsettles me is worry, which is less real than it feels. Fill the place with familiar comforts and people I love.”

Notice that the reading didn’t predict anything. It gave a fresh way of looking at the situation and something to do.

## Common difficulties

- **“I can’t remember the meanings.”** Normal. Look them up, every time, for months. Meanings stick through use, not memorising lists. Lean on the pictures; they were drawn to be read.
- **“The cards don’t make sense together.”** Read each card alone first, then ask: if these three were a sentence, what would it say? If it still doesn’t fit, write it down and come back in a week. Many readings make sense only in hindsight.
- **“I got a scary card.”** Death, the Tower and the Devil are dramatic, but not curses. Death is endings and change; the Tower is upheaval that clears the ground; the Devil is unhealthy attachment. They show what is happening so you can respond.
- **“I keep drawing again because I don’t like the answer.”** Stop. Re-drawing until you get the answer you want teaches nothing. Write down the first reading and sit with it. Give the question a few days, at least, before asking again.
- **“I read what I want to see.”** Everyone does at first. Writing your reading down and checking it later is the cure.

## How you’ll know it’s working

You will not wake up one day with second sight. Instead, over weeks, you will notice: the meanings come faster; you see more in the pictures; your summaries get clearer; and when you look back at old readings, more of them seem apt. That is real progress.

> **Safety:** Don’t read about your health, a pregnancy, someone’s death, or legal and financial decisions in a way that replaces professional advice. If a reading frightens you, put it away, ground yourself, and talk to your mentor.

> **Try this:** Do a situation, challenge, advice reading on a small, real question in your life this week. Follow every step above and write it all down.

docs.title: Runes, ogham, pendulum and scrying
docs.summary: A short, honest introduction to four other common systems: what each is, where it comes from, and a simple way to begin.
docs.body:
## Other ways of seeing

Tarot is not the only way. This lesson introduces four other systems you may meet in your coven. Each could fill a course of its own; this is a first taste. The app’s Grimoire has fuller pages on the runes and ogham.

## Runes

**Runes** are the letters of the old Germanic alphabets. The oldest, the **Elder Futhark**, has 24 runes and was used from roughly the second to the eighth century, carved on stone, wood, metal and bone. It is named after its first six letters: *f, u, th, a, r, k*. Each rune is a letter, a sound and a name with a meaning: **Fehu** (cattle, wealth), **Uruz** (aurochs, strength), **Thurisaz** (giant, thorn), and so on.

**History, honestly.** The Roman writer Tacitus, around the year 98, described Germanic peoples casting strips of wood marked with signs to learn the will of the gods, but he doesn’t say the signs were runes. The old rune poems (Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic, written down in the Middle Ages) give each rune a short verse, and these are the main old source for meanings. Most modern methods of rune divination, and nearly all reversed (“merkstave”) readings, are twentieth-century inventions. The “blank rune” in many sets was added in 1982 and has no historical basis.

**A simple start:**

1. Make or buy a set of 24 runes. You can paint them on pebbles or write them on card, or use the app’s.
2. Ground and centre. Hold a question in mind.
3. Draw one rune from a bag without looking.
4. Read its name and meaning, and look at its shape. What does it say about your question?
5. Write it down.

> **Note:** Runes are sacred in Heathenry, and some runic symbols have been misused by hate groups. Learn them respectfully, from good sources. Your coven’s tradition lessons may teach them more fully.

## Ogham

**Ogham** is an early medieval Irish alphabet of twenty letters (plus a few later additions), made of strokes cut along a straight line, often the edge of a standing stone. Several hundred ogham stones survive in Ireland and western Britain, mostly from the fourth to sixth centuries, recording people’s names.

**History, honestly.** Medieval Irish scholars, in texts such as the *Ogham Tract*, listed each letter with names and associations, including trees: *beith* (birch), *luis* (rowan), *fearn* (alder), and so on. Not every letter name originally meant a tree; the tree lists were partly a later learned scheme. There is no direct evidence that ogham was used for divination in early Ireland. The popular “Celtic tree calendar”, with each letter given a month, was invented by the poet Robert Graves in *The White Goddess* (1948). Modern ogham divination, usually with letters carved on wooden sticks (“few”), is a living modern practice built on these sources.

**A simple start:** as with runes, draw one stick or card, read its name, tree and meaning, and reflect on how it speaks to your question.

## The pendulum

A **pendulum** is a small weight on a chain or thread: a crystal, a ring, a key. You hold it still and ask a yes-or-no question, and it swings in a pattern you have agreed means yes, no or unsure.

**How it works, honestly.** In 1852 the physiologist William Carpenter described the **ideomotor effect**: tiny muscle movements you make without noticing, driven by what you expect or half know. Experiments show pendulums move this way. Some practitioners see this as exactly the point (it reveals what your deeper mind knows); others believe spirits or energy guide it too. Either way, it can only tell you what *something* in you or around you inclines towards. It is not a lie detector, a medical test or a way to choose numbers.

**A simple start:**

1. Sit with your elbow resting on a table and hold the chain between thumb and finger, the weight hanging still.
2. **Calibrate.** Ask it to show you “yes”, and wait. It may swing back and forth, side to side, or in a circle. Then ask for “no”, and then “unsure”. Write down each.
3. **Test.** Ask questions you know the answer to (“Is my name Alex?”) to check.
4. **Ask** simple, real questions about yourself, and treat the answer as one voice among many, not a command.

## Scrying

**Scrying** means gazing into a surface (still water, a dark mirror, a crystal ball, a candle flame, smoke) until images, impressions or ideas arise. The Elizabethan scholar John Dee used a polished obsidian mirror (now in the British Museum) and a crystal for his visionary work. Scrying is found in many cultures.

**A simple start: water scrying.**

1. In a dim room, fill a dark bowl with water. Put a candle (in a safe holder) where its light doesn’t reflect directly in the water.
2. Ground and centre, then hold a question gently in mind.
3. Gaze softly at the water’s surface, or just into it. Blink when you need to. Breathe slowly.
4. Wait. For ten minutes, notice any shapes, colours, pictures, words, memories or feelings that arise, in the water or in your mind’s eye. Many people see little for the first few sessions; that is normal.
5. Stop, write down everything, eat or drink something, and ground.

> **Safety:** Keep scrying sessions short (ten to fifteen minutes). Gazing can bring on a dreamy, spaced-out state. If you feel disoriented, frightened, or unsure what is real, stop at once, put the lights on, ground yourself firmly, and talk to your mentor. If you have a history of dissociation, psychosis or seizures, talk to your mentor and your doctor before scrying, and choose another method if in doubt. Never leave a candle unattended.

> **Your coven:** Your tradition may have its own forms of divination, taught in its own lessons. Ask your mentor which of these, if any, your coven uses.

> **Try this:** Choose one of these four systems and try it three times this fortnight. Write down what you did, what you asked, what came, and how it compared with tarot for you.

docs.title: Reading for others, ethically
docs.summary: How to read for another person with consent, care and honesty: what to read about and what not to, how to give hard news, confidentiality, money and red flags.
docs.body:
## A responsibility

Reading for yourself is practice. Reading for someone else is a responsibility. People often come to a reader when they are worried, grieving, lovesick or at a crossroads, and what you say can affect them deeply. Most covens expect members to read for others only once they are confident in their system, and always with care.

## Consent

1. **Read only for someone who has asked,** or who has clearly agreed when you offered. Never do an unasked-for reading “at” someone, and don’t announce what the cards say about people who didn’t ask.
2. **Don’t read about third parties** who haven’t consented, as if spying on them. “What is my ex doing?” or “Is my partner cheating?” invade someone else’s privacy and rarely help. Turn the question back to the person asking: “What do I need to know about how I feel after the break-up?”, “What would help me with my worries about trust?”
3. **The person can stop at any time.** Say so at the start.

## What not to read on

Some questions are not for divination, or should only be read alongside proper help. Gently redirect, and say why.

- **Health:** don’t diagnose, predict illness or recovery, or advise on medicine. Encourage them to see a doctor.
- **Pregnancy:** don’t predict whether someone is or will become pregnant, or the sex of a baby.
- **Death:** don’t predict anyone’s death, ever.
- **Legal and financial decisions:** don’t tell someone how a court case will go or whether to make an investment. Point them to a lawyer or adviser.
- **Mental health crises:** if someone is in crisis or talking about harming themselves, don’t read. Stay with them, listen, and help them contact a crisis line, a doctor or emergency services.

You can still read around these subjects in a supportive way: “What would help me cope while I wait for test results?” is a fair question; “Do I have cancer?” is not.

## How to give a reading

1. **Before you start,** agree the question together, and explain briefly how you read: that the cards show possibilities and advice, not fixed fate.
2. **Ground** yourself, and offer the other person a few slow breaths too.
3. **Read honestly but kindly.** Describe what you see. Use “this suggests”, “this might mean”, “how does that fit for you?” rather than certainties.
4. **Invite them in.** Ask what they see in the pictures. A reading is a conversation.
5. **Give hard cards with care.** Explain what they really mean (the Death card is change, not death), focus on what can be done, and never frighten someone.
6. **End with something they can act on,** and remind them that the choices are theirs.
7. **Check how they are** before they go. If they seem shaken, ground together, offer water, and stay a while.

## Words to open and close

It helps to have simple words ready. You might begin:

“Before we start: the cards show possibilities and advice, not a fixed future. You make your own choices. If anything feels uncomfortable, say so and we’ll stop. What would you like to ask about?”

And close:

“Those are the cards. What stands out most for you? Remember, this is one way of looking at things; you know your life best. How are you feeling?”

## Reading within the coven

Coven members often read for one another, and sometimes the coven asks a reader to divine for the group, for example before a working or at a festival. The same ethics apply: an agreed question, honesty with kindness, and confidentiality. When you read for the coven as a whole, report what you saw plainly and humbly, and leave decisions to the coven and its leaders. A reading is advice, not an order.

## Confidentiality

What someone tells you in a reading is private. Don’t share it with anyone, including other coven members, without permission. Don’t post readings about real people online. If you keep notes, keep them private and without full names.

The only exception is safety: if someone tells you they or another person, especially a child, is in danger, encourage them to get help, and talk to your mentor or High Priestess about what to do. Safety comes before confidentiality.

## Money, pressure and red flags

Some professional readers charge fairly for their time and skill, and that is fine. But divination is also used to exploit people. Watch for these red flags, whether in yourself, in other readers, or in anyone who reads for you:

- claiming a curse or “dark energy” that only an expensive working can remove;
- asking for more and more money, gifts, or secrets;
- making someone dependent, reading on the same question again and again;
- frightening someone so they come back;
- using a reading to pressure someone into a relationship, sex, or joining a group.

No genuine reader or coven will demand money, sex or secrets from you. If anyone does, stop, and talk to your mentor or High Priestess.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have its own rules on reading for others, for money, or for people outside the coven. Ask your mentor before you start.

> **Try this:** With your mentor’s agreement, offer a three-card reading to a friend or fellow trainee who would like one. Follow the steps above, with consent and an open question. Afterwards, ask them how it felt, and write down what you learned.

docs.title: What a spell is, and the heart of it: intention
docs.summary: What practitioners mean by a spell, how spells are understood, an honest word on what magic can and can’t do, and how to shape a clear intention.
docs.body:
## What is a spell?

A **spell** is a deliberate act of magic, done for a particular purpose. It usually combines words, actions and objects, gathered around a single **intention**, and is done in a focused, ritual way. Lighting a candle while asking for courage before a hard conversation is a spell. So is sewing a small bag of lavender and rosemary for a friend who can’t sleep (with their agreement), or writing what you want to let go of on paper and burning it safely at the waning Moon.

The word *spell* comes from Old English *spel*, “a story, a saying”: a spell was first something *spoken*. Charms, prayers, blessings and spoken formulas for healing, protection and luck are found in the folk practice of almost every culture, including the Anglo-Saxon charms of the tenth and eleventh centuries, Greek and Roman curse tablets and amulets, and the charms recorded by folklorists across Europe in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Modern witchcraft draws on all of these, and on Renaissance ceremonial magic, but most spells you will meet in books today were written in the last fifty years.

## How spells might work

As with energy and correspondences, practitioners hold different views. You met several of these in the earlier lessons on energy.

1. **Energy and intention.** You raise energy (as you learned in Raising and directing energy), shape it with intention, and send it out to affect the world.
2. **Relationship.** You ask gods, spirits, ancestors or the powers of plants and stones to help, and they do, or don’t, as they choose. A spell is like a well-made request.
3. **Psychology.** A spell focuses your mind, strengthens your resolve, and changes how you act and what you notice, which changes your results.

Most experienced practitioners would say a spell uses all three. You don’t need to settle the question to practise well.

## What magic can and can’t do

Honesty here protects you and the people you care about.

- Magic is a **practice and an experience**, not a guaranteed physical cause and effect. There is no scientific evidence that spells change the world directly.
- Many practitioners find that spells help: they feel clearer, braver, calmer, luckier, more connected, and things often move in the direction they worked for.
- Magic works **with** ordinary action, never instead of it. A money spell works best alongside job applications; a healing spell alongside a doctor’s care.
- Magic is **never** a substitute for medical treatment, psychological help, legal advice, or emergency services. If you or someone else is in danger or crisis, get practical help first.

## Intention: the heart of every spell

An **intention** is a clear statement of what you want a spell to do. Every part of a spell (the timing, the colours, the herbs, the words, the actions) serves the intention. A spell with a fuzzy intention is like a letter with no address.

### Shaping an intention, step by step

1. **Write down what you want, roughly.** For example: “I want things to be better at work.”
2. **Ask what “better” means.** Be specific. “I want to be less anxious in meetings and to be noticed for my work.”
3. **Choose one thing.** A spell works best for one aim. Here, perhaps: “I want to speak confidently in meetings.” Save the other for another spell.
4. **Make it about you,** or about something you have the right to affect. You can work for your own confidence; you can’t ethically work to make your manager like you against their will.
5. **Make it realistic.** Magic is said to follow the easiest path. “I win the lottery” has very few paths; “I find ways to bring in an extra hundred a month” has many.
6. **Make it positive where you can.** Say what you want rather than what you don’t: “I speak calmly and clearly” rather than “I don’t stammer.”
7. **Check it in your body.** Read it aloud. Does it feel right? Do you really want it? If you feel a twinge of doubt, explore it before you go on.
8. **Write the final version** at the top of a page in your Grimoire. This sentence will guide every choice that follows.

### Before and after

Some examples of rough wishes shaped into good intentions:

- “I want more money.” becomes “I find steady extra work that pays at least a hundred a month by the end of the season.”
- “I want him to notice me.” (about a particular person, without their consent) becomes “I am open to love, and I meet people who value me.”
- “I don’t want to be ill.” becomes “My body heals well, and I follow my doctor’s advice faithfully.”
- “Make my house feel better.” becomes “My home is peaceful, clean and welcoming.”

Notice how each “after” is specific, about one thing, about the person working, realistic, and positive.

> **Note:** Sometimes, while working out the intention, you realise what you really need is not magic at all: a conversation, a form filled in, a doctor’s appointment, a rest. That is a good outcome. Do that first.

## Prayer and spell

In some traditions, especially Christian folk magic and some devotional paths, the line between prayer and spell is blurred or absent: you ask God, a saint or a god for help, sometimes with candles, oils and psalms. In others, a spell is your own act and a prayer is a request. Your tradition’s lessons will say how it sees this.

> **Your coven:** Covens differ on what kinds of spell they do together and on whether trainees may do spells for others. Ask your mentor what your coven expects of you during training.

> **Try this:** Think of one thing you would genuinely like to change. Work through the eight steps above and write the final intention in your Grimoire. You will build a spell around it in the next lessons.

docs.title: The ethics of spellcraft
docs.summary: Consent, harm, love spells, healing others, binding and cursing, and why most covens forbid harmful work; plus how to protect yourself without harming anyone.
docs.body:
## Why ethics come first

If magic is real enough to be worth doing, it is real enough to be done responsibly. And even if you see magic mostly as psychology, *trying* to harm or control someone is a harmful act in itself: it shapes your character and your relationships. Every responsible coven teaches ethics alongside spellcraft.

Different traditions express ethics differently. This lesson sets out the common ground most covens share. Your tradition’s lessons will add its own teaching.

## Some well-known principles

- **The Wiccan Rede:** “An it harm none, do what ye will.” Its best-known form is from a 1964 speech by Doreen Valiente, a founding figure of modern Wicca. It is usually understood as: you are free to act, *as long as* you harm no one, including yourself. Some read it as a strict rule, others as an ideal to weigh choices against.
- **The Threefold Law** (or Law of Return): the idea that whatever you send out returns to you three times over. A form of it appears in Gerald Gardner’s novel *High Magic’s Aid* (1949), and it was popularised by later Wiccan writers. Many witches treat it as a moral teaching rather than a literal law.
- **Other traditions** frame ethics through virtues (such as honour, hospitality and courage in Heathenry), piety and right relationship with the gods (in Hellenic and Roman practice), or Christian teaching (love of neighbour). They arrive at much the same place: act honourably, keep your word, and don’t abuse your power.

You don’t have to adopt any one of these to see their common sense: **take responsibility for what you do, and don’t harm or control others.**

## Consent

**Never do magic on or for another person without their consent.** This includes:

- **Healing spells.** Even with good intentions, ask first: “Would you like me to light a candle for your recovery?” People have the right to refuse, for religious or personal reasons. If someone can’t be asked (for example, they are unconscious), many practitioners send healing “for their highest good, to use or not as they choose”, or pray for them, rather than working directly on them.
- **Protection and blessings for adults.** Ask.
- **Children.** Parents and guardians may bless and protect their own young children. Don’t work on other people’s children without their parents’ agreement.
- **Pets and animals in your care:** blessings and protection are generally fine.

## Love spells

Spells to make a **particular person** love you, return to you, or leave their partner are manipulation: they try to override someone else’s free will. Most covens forbid them.

Ethical love magic is about **you**: becoming more open to love, healing old wounds, loving yourself, attracting a partner who is right for you (without naming who), or strengthening a relationship where both of you have agreed to the working.

## Binding, banishing and cursing

These words are often confused.

- **Banishing** means sending away an unwanted influence, habit, or energy from yourself or your home: clearing out, as at the waning Moon. It is part of ordinary practice and harms no one.
- **Binding** means trying to restrain a person from acting, usually to stop them harming you or others. It is controversial. Some traditions allow it in serious cases of protection; many covens forbid it, because it works directly on another person’s will without consent.
- **Cursing** (hexing) means trying to harm someone. Curses existed in the ancient world (archaeologists have found hundreds of Greek and Roman curse tablets) and in folk practice. **Most covens forbid cursing and any work meant to harm**, for ethical reasons, for the sake of the practitioner’s own character, and because it so often reflects anger that would be better dealt with in other ways.

> **Your coven:** Your coven will have clear rules on binding, banishing and harmful magic. Ask your mentor what they are, and follow them strictly during your training. If you are ever unsure whether a working is allowed, ask before you do it.

## When someone is harming you

If someone is threatening, harassing, abusing or stalking you, your first protection is **practical**: tell people you trust, keep records, contact the police, a domestic abuse service, or a support line, and make a safety plan. Magic can support you, but it is never a substitute for real-world safety.

Ethical protective magic focuses on **you and your space**: shielding yourself (as you learned in Grounding), warding your home, strengthening your courage and boundaries, drawing helpful people to you, and cutting your *own* emotional ties to the person. These protect you without trying to control them.

## Harm to yourself

Ethics includes how you treat yourself. Don’t do magic in ways that endanger your health: fasting dangerously, using harmful substances, depriving yourself of sleep, or spending money you don’t have. Don’t let spellcraft become a compulsion, such as repeating the same working over and over from anxiety. If that happens, pause, ground, and talk to your mentor.

## Money, pressure and red flags

Be wary of anyone, in or out of a coven, who:

- offers to do expensive spells for you, especially to “remove a curse”;
- tells you that you must do harmful magic, or that ethics are for the weak;
- pressures you to do magic you’re uncomfortable with;
- asks for money, sex, or secrets in exchange for magic or teaching.

No legitimate coven or teacher will demand any of these. If it happens, step back and talk to your mentor or High Priestess, or to someone outside the group if they are involved.

> **Try this:** Write down three spells you can imagine wanting to do: one for yourself, one for someone you love, one about someone who has hurt you. For each, ask: whose consent is needed? Could it harm anyone? How could I word it so it focuses on me and harms no one? Rewrite any that need it.

docs.title: The structure of a spell
docs.summary: The stages of a well-made spell from preparation to closing, how to choose timing and components, how to word it, and a complete candle spell to follow step by step.
docs.body:
## The shape of a spell

Spells vary enormously, but most well-made ones share the same basic shape. Once you know it, you can understand any spell you read, adapt it, and write your own.

1. **Intention.** Decide exactly what the spell is for (the previous lesson).
2. **Planning.** Choose the timing, the components and the words.
3. **Preparation.** Gather what you need, clean the space, and cleanse yourself.
4. **Opening.** Ground and centre; make sacred space if your practice uses it.
5. **The working.** Charge the components, say the words, raise energy and focus it.
6. **Release.** Let the energy go to do its work.
7. **Grounding and closing.** Ground any excess, give thanks, close sacred space.
8. **Afterwards.** Dispose of or keep what remains, eat and drink, record the spell, and take ordinary action.

You learned the skills behind steps 4 to 7 in Grounding, Raising and directing energy, and Sacred space. This lesson puts them together.

## Planning: timing

You learned about timing in the Moon and magical timing module. In short:

- **Phase:** waxing for growth and drawing in; waning for release and banishing; full for power and thanks; new for seeds.
- **Day and hour:** match the planet to your intention if it is easy.
- **Urgency first:** if the need is urgent, work now and word it to suit the phase.

## Planning: components

**Components** are the physical things in a spell: candles, herbs, stones, paper, cord, water, salt, oil, images. You learned how to choose them in Correspondences.

1. **Choose two or three things whose meanings match your intention.** More is not better.
2. **Prefer what you have and know.**
3. **Check every component for safety:** fire, skin, pets, children, pregnancy, allergies.
4. **Have a plan for disposal** before you start (more on this in the next lesson).

## Planning: wording

Words focus the mind and carry the intention. They can be spoken aloud, whispered, thought, sung or written.

- **Say it as if it is already true,** or happening now: “Courage fills me when I speak” rather than “I hope I will be brave.”
- **Be clear and specific.** Name what you want, and when if that matters: “by the end of this month”.
- **Be positive** where you can.
- **Keep it short enough to remember.** Three or four lines is plenty.
- **Rhyme and rhythm are optional.** They help many people remember and feel the words, and they have a long history in charms. If rhyming makes you giggle or freeze, speak plainly.
- **Many practitioners add a safety clause,** such as “for the good of all, harming none” or “in a way that is right for me and harms no one”. It reminds you of your ethics and guards against unintended results.
- **End with a closing phrase** that marks the words as done: “So it is”, “So mote it be” (a phrase from Freemasonry, taken up by Wicca), “Amen”, or whatever your tradition uses.

## A complete candle spell for courage

This simple spell can be adapted for almost any intention by changing the colour, herb and words. Allow about forty minutes, plus time for the candle to burn.

**You will need:** a small candle (a chime or tea light) in red, orange or white, in a heat-proof holder on a heat-proof plate; a pinch of dried thyme or basil; a little plain cooking oil; a pin or cocktail stick; paper and pen; matches or a lighter; water nearby.

1. **Plan.** Write your intention, for example “I speak with courage at the meeting on Thursday.” Choose a waxing Moon or a Tuesday or Sunday if you can; if not, any time.
2. **Prepare.** Clear and clean your space. Wash your hands. Turn off your phone. Put the candle on its plate, away from anything that can burn, with the water within reach.
3. **Open.** Ground and centre. If you cast a circle or make sacred space in your practice, do so now.
4. **Carve.** With the pin, gently scratch a word or symbol for your intention into the candle: “courage”, your initials, or a simple sign that means courage to you.
5. **Anoint.** Put a drop of oil on your fingers and rub it onto the candle from the middle to the top and from the middle to the bottom, thinking of your intention. (Many practitioners rub *towards* themselves to draw something in and *away* to send something out. Choose one and be consistent.) Wipe your hands.
6. **Dress.** Sprinkle a pinch of thyme or basil on the plate around the base of the candle, not on the candle itself, where it could catch fire.
7. **Charge.** Hold the candle (unlit) in both hands. Close your eyes and imagine, as vividly as you can, the moment you want: you, at the meeting, speaking clearly and calmly. Feel how it feels. Breathe slowly. Raise energy as you learned, with breath, a hum or a chant, and feel it flow into the candle.
8. **Light and speak.** Put the candle down and light it. Say your words, for example: “Flame of courage, burn in me. When I speak, my words fly free. Clear and calm, for good of all. So it is.” Say them three times, more strongly each time.
9. **Release.** At the peak of your focus, let go: breathe out fully, open your hands, and imagine the energy going out into the world to do its work.
10. **Watch.** Sit with the candle for a few minutes, gazing at the flame and holding the image of success.
11. **Ground and close.** Put your hands on the floor and let any excess energy drain away. Give thanks to anything you called on. Close sacred space if you made it.
12. **Let it burn.** Either let the small candle burn down completely while you stay in the room, or snuff it and relight it each day until it is gone. Never leave it unattended.
13. **Afterwards.** Eat and drink something. Write the spell in your Grimoire. Then prepare for the meeting in ordinary ways: write notes, practise what you’ll say.

> **Safety:** Never leave a burning candle unattended, even for a moment. Keep herbs and paper away from the flame. Candles in glass can crack if they burn down too far; put them out before the last centimetre. Keep hair and sleeves back.

> **Your coven:** Your tradition may open and close spells in its own way: with a circle and quarters, a prayer to a patron, an offering, or a particular closing phrase. Use your coven’s forms when you have learned them.

> **Try this:** Using the intention you wrote in the last lesson, plan a spell using the eight-part shape: timing, two or three components, and three or four lines of words. Write the plan in your Grimoire.

docs.title: Recording results, and when nothing happens
docs.summary: How to record a spell, what counts as a result and how long to wait, how to evaluate honestly, what to do when nothing happens, and why mundane action matters.
docs.body:
## Why records matter

Experienced practitioners keep records of their spells. Records let you see what works for you, learn from what doesn’t, notice patterns you would otherwise miss, and stay honest with yourself. They turn spellcraft from guesswork into a craft you get better at.

## What to record

For every spell, write in your Grimoire (the app’s works well, or a notebook):

- **Date and time,** Moon phase, day and hour.
- **Intention,** word for word.
- **Form** (candle, jar, sachet, petition, knots, sigil, kitchen).
- **Components** and why you chose them.
- **Words** you used.
- **What you did,** step by step, briefly.
- **How it felt:** your focus, energy, mood; anything unusual.
- **Mundane actions** you are taking alongside it.
- **Time frame:** when you expect to see results.

Then add **follow-up notes**: one week later, one month later, and at the end of your time frame.

Here is a sample record:

- **When:** Tuesday 4 March, 8 pm, waxing crescent, hour of Mars.
- **Intention:** “I speak with courage at the meeting on Thursday.”
- **Form:** candle spell.
- **Components:** red chime candle (courage), thyme (quiet courage), olive oil.
- **Words:** “Flame of courage, burn in me…” three times.
- **How it felt:** nervous at first, then focused; a warm feeling in my chest while charging; slight tiredness afterwards.
- **Mundane action:** wrote three points to make; practised them aloud twice.
- **Time frame:** Thursday.
- **Follow-up, Thursday:** made two of my three points; voice shook at first, then steadied. Manager asked a follow-up question. Partial success; felt braver than usual.
- **Follow-up, one month:** have spoken up in two more meetings since. The spell seems to have started something.

## What counts as a result

Results can take many forms. Some are obvious, some subtle.

- **The thing happens.** You get the job; you speak confidently at the meeting.
- **A path opens.** Someone mentions an opening; you meet a helpful person; an idea arrives.
- **You change.** You feel calmer, braver, clearer, and act differently.
- **Something partial happens:** some of what you wanted, or a version of it.
- **Something unexpected happens,** related but not what you asked for. This is common, and is often a sign the intention needed to be clearer.
- **Nothing happens** that you can see.

## Evaluating honestly

It is easy to see every good thing as proof that a spell “worked” and to forget the ones that didn’t. Every human mind does this. To keep yourself honest:

1. **Set a time frame** in advance, and look back at the end of it.
2. **Write down what you expected** before you know the result.
3. **Note other causes:** what you did in ordinary ways, what other people did, plain luck.
4. **Record the misses** as carefully as the hits.
5. **Look across many spells,** not just one. Patterns over months tell you more than any single result.

This isn’t about proving or disproving magic. It is about knowing your own practice well.

## When nothing happens

Every practitioner does spells that seem to do nothing. When it happens, work through these questions:

1. **Has enough time passed?** Some things take weeks or months.
2. **Was the intention clear?** Vague intentions bring vague results. Was it really one thing?
3. **Was it realistic?** Were there enough ways for it to happen?
4. **Did I take ordinary action?** A job spell with no applications has little to work with.
5. **Did I really want it?** Mixed feelings often show up as mixed results.
6. **Was I focused?** Were you rushed, distracted, or anxious during the spell?
7. **Was it the right approach?** Perhaps a divination reading beforehand would have suggested another way.
8. **Was the answer “no” or “not yet”?** In devotional traditions, the gods may simply decline. Sometimes, looking back, people are glad a spell didn’t work.

Then decide: rework it with a clearer intention, try a different form or timing, take more practical action, or let it go.

> **Note:** Don’t repeat the same spell over and over in quick succession out of worry. Most practitioners do a spell once (or as a set series, such as seven days of candle-burning) and then let it work, perhaps renewing it monthly. Repeating from anxiety tends to feed the anxiety, not the spell.

## Mundane action

This is the most important practical teaching in spellcraft: **back up your magic with ordinary action.**

- A spell for a job: apply for jobs, polish your CV, practise for interviews.
- A spell for health: see a doctor, follow their advice, rest, eat well.
- A spell for money: budget, look for extra work, ask for advice on debt.
- A spell for love: go where people are, be open, be kind.
- A spell for protection: lock the doors, tell trusted people, contact support services.

Many practitioners describe magic as opening doors and ordinary action as walking through them. Without the walking, the doors don’t help.

> **Safety:** If a spell is about your health or safety, the practical action must come first: a doctor, a counsellor, the police, a crisis line. Magic supports care; it never replaces it.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may keep a shared record of group workings and ask members to report back on them. Ask your mentor how your coven follows up on its work together.

> **Try this:** Do the spell you have been planning through this module. Record it fully, and add a follow-up note after one week and again after a month.

docs.title: Common forms of spell
docs.summary: Step-by-step introductions to jars, charm bags, petitions, knot magic, sigils and kitchen magic, with the safety and disposal notes for each.
docs.body:
## Many shapes, one structure

You have learned the structure of a spell. Here are the most common forms it takes. Each follows the same eight-part shape: intention, planning, preparation, opening, working, release, grounding and closing, afterwards. Only the working changes.

## Spell jars

A **spell jar** (or witch’s jar) is a small jar filled with components that all serve one intention, sealed and kept. It is a long, slow spell: it keeps working as long as it is kept. A related folk object, the **witch bottle**, was buried by people in England from the sixteenth century onward for protection; many have been found by archaeologists.

1. Choose a small clean jar with a lid.
2. Write your intention on a slip of paper, fold it towards you (to draw in) or away (to send away), and put it in first.
3. Add components one at a time, saying what each is for: “Salt for protection. Rosemary for clarity. Bay for success.”
4. Close the lid. If you seal it with drips of candle wax, do so over a plate, carefully.
5. Hold it, charge it, release, ground.
6. Keep it on your altar, by the door, in a cupboard, wherever suits the intention.

**Disposal:** when the work is done, thank it, empty the plant matter into compost or the garden waste, rinse the jar and recycle or reuse it.

## Charm bags and sachets

A **charm bag** (or sachet) is a small cloth bag of herbs, stones and other items, carried with you or kept in a particular place.

1. Use a small bag or a square of cloth tied up with thread, in a colour that suits the intention.
2. Add two or three herbs and a small stone or token, naming each.
3. Tie it closed with three knots, saying your intention once for each knot.
4. Charge it and carry it in a pocket or bag, or hang it somewhere.
5. Refresh it about once a month by holding it and restating your intention.

## Written petitions

A **petition** is a written request or intention. It may be kept, put under a candle, folded into a jar, or burned safely.

1. Write your intention in your own words, clearly and specifically. Some people write it three times, or sign it.
2. Fold it, place it under your candle, inside your jar, or on your altar.
3. If you burn it, hold it with tongs over a fire-safe bowl containing sand, with a window open and water nearby. Let it burn out completely, and make sure the ash is cold before disposing of it.

## Knot magic

Tying knots in a cord to “bind in” a spell is one of the oldest forms of magic, found in many cultures.

1. Take a length of cord or thread in a suitable colour.
2. Tie a series of knots (often three, seven or nine), saying a line of your intention with each one.
3. Keep the cord. Some practitioners untie the knots one by one to release the spell when it is needed, or when it is done.

## Sigils

A **sigil** is a symbol you design to stand for an intention. The modern method was developed by the English artist Austin Osman Spare in the early twentieth century and is now widely used.

1. Write your intention as a short sentence: “I SLEEP DEEPLY.”
2. Cross out repeated letters, and (in Spare’s method) vowels, leaving a handful of letters: S, L, P, D.
3. Combine the remaining letters into a single design, overlapping, turning and simplifying them until the result no longer reads as letters and pleases your eye.
4. Charge the sigil: gaze at it while raising energy, then release.
5. Many practitioners then put it away, burn it safely, or hide it, and try to forget it, so the conscious mind doesn’t interfere. Others draw it on candles or carry it.

## Kitchen and household magic

Everyday tasks become spells when done with intention: stirring a soup clockwise while thinking of health, sweeping the house from the back to the front door to clear it out, baking bread for abundance, simmering a pot of water with rosemary, orange peel and cinnamon to bless the home. The app’s craft pages have many of these. They are gentle, practical and easy to fit into a busy life.

> **Safety:** Never leave a simmer pot or anything on the stove unattended, and don’t let it boil dry. Only eat what is ordinary food in ordinary amounts.

## Disposal and the environment

What you do with the remains of a spell matters, magically and practically.

- **Plant matter:** compost, bury, or put in the garden waste.
- **Candle wax:** let it cool and put it in the household rubbish, or keep a jar for remnants. Don’t pour hot wax down the sink.
- **Ash:** when completely cold, scatter on soil or put in the bin.
- **Salt:** don’t pour it on soil or plants you want to grow; put it down the sink with running water, or in the bin.
- **Jars, stones and cords:** cleanse and reuse, or recycle.
- **Never** leave glass, plastic, wax, foil or non-native plants in rivers, the sea, woods or parks, even as an offering. If you leave something outdoors, it should be biodegradable and harmless to wildlife.

Some practitioners dispose of the remains of banishing spells away from home, at a crossroads or in a public bin, to “send them away”. That is fine, as long as you follow the same rules.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have its own preferred forms, materials, or ways of disposing of remains. Ask your mentor.

> **Try this:** Choose one form from this lesson (not a candle spell) and make it for the intention you have been working on, following every step and safety note. Record it.

docs.title: Kronia
docs.summary: The festival of Kronos in high summer, when masters and the enslaved ate at the same table in memory of the Golden Age, and how to keep it today as a feast of equality.
docs.body:
## The day

The Kronia falls on 12 Hekatombaion, in high summer, in the first month of the Athenian year. The app's calendar shows this year's date.

## Whom it honours

Kronos is the Titan who ruled the world before Zeus, with his consort Rhea. In the myth, Kronos swallowed his children for fear one would overthrow him; Rhea saved the youngest, Zeus, who did overthrow him. But the Greeks also remembered Kronos's reign as the Golden Age. In Works and Days, Hesiod describes it: people "lived like gods without sorrow of heart, remote and free from toil and grief", and "the fruitful earth unforced bare them fruit abundantly and without stint".

The Kronia remembers that lost age of plenty, when no one served anyone.

## What we know

The Kronia was one of Athens's older festivals. Demosthenes mentions it as a day when the Council did not sit. The Roman writer Macrobius, quoting the Athenian historian Philochorus and the poet Accius, tells us its most famous custom: at the Kronia, heads of households ate together with the people they enslaved, and even served them. Accius says the Greeks kept this custom long before the Romans kept the Saturnalia, the similar Roman festival of Saturn.

Kronos and Rhea had a sanctuary in Athens near the great temple of Olympian Zeus. The festival came just after the grain harvest, and Kronos was often shown with a sickle, so the Kronia was also a harvest-home feast.

## What we don't know

We know very little about any public sacrifice or temple rite at the Kronia. Even ancient writers explained the festival in different ways. Whether the reversal of roles was a real, widespread practice in every household or something done by some is not clear.

## Its meaning today

Ancient Athens kept enslaved people, and the Kronia's day of equality did not change that. Modern practitioners keep the festival as a day of shared food and equality, and many use it to think about justice, labour and who serves whom in our own world. It is a festival that asks: what would a fair world look like, and what could I do toward it?

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Plan a meal.** Invite friends, family or housemates, or simply cook for yourself with care. Make the best food you reasonably can: summer fruit, bread, honey cakes, figs.
2. **Begin with khernips and Hestia.** Light Hestia's flame, make khernips, and give her the first offering.
3. **Pour to Kronos and Rhea.** Pour a little wine, juice or water: "Kronos and Rhea, rulers of the Golden Age, I remember the time when the earth gave freely and no one served another. Let there be enough for all."
4. **Read Hesiod's Golden Age passage** (Works and Days, lines 109 to 126), aloud if you are with others.
5. **Reverse the roles.** Let the person who usually cooks or serves be served. If you live alone, cook for someone else, or give a meal to a stranger.
6. **Eat at one table**, with no head and no ranks; sit people at random.
7. **Name one thing** you will do to share more fairly this year.
8. **End with Hestia.**

A further offering many practitioners make: a day's pay or a day's work for a cause that supports workers or people in poverty.

## Words for the day

A prayer you can use, in the three-part shape of Greek prayer:

"Kronos, ancient king, and Rhea, mother of the gods: in your age the earth gave freely and no one was master or servant. I remember that time, and I have laid this table for all who come to it. Let there be enough for everyone, and let me do my part to share it."

Say it with arms raised, then pour your libation.

## Common difficulties

- **"I have no one to serve."** Serve a stranger instead: buy someone a meal, give to a food bank, or cook for a neighbour. The festival is about turning the usual order over, not about having a household.
- **"Kronos ate his children. Why honour him?"** The Greeks honoured Kronos for the Golden Age while telling dark stories about him. You can hold both, or honour the Golden Age itself and Rhea, who saved her children.
- **"It feels like charity, not religion."** For the Greeks, how you treated people was religion. Pour your libation first, and let the meal be the rite.

## Keeping it with a coven

A coven Kronia is a feast. Members bring food; the leaders cook and serve; everyone eats at one table. A reading of Hesiod, a libation to Kronos and Rhea, and conversation about fairness make a full rite. It is a good festival for welcoming new members and guests, in the spirit of xenia.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may hold its Kronia with a community meal, a donation, or an act of service. Ask your mentor what is planned, and offer to help serve.

> **Safety:** If you host, think about guests' allergies and diets. Keep alcohol optional. If you give to a cause, give what you can afford; generosity that puts you in hardship is not what the festival asks.

## Reflect

- Who serves you in your daily life, often unseen? How could you honour them?
- What does "enough for all" mean to you?
- The Golden Age myth looks backward. Can a festival of the past also be a hope for the future?

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** the date, the feast with the enslaved, the link with the Golden Age and harvest, a sanctuary of Kronos and Rhea.
- **Modern:** the focus on social justice and labour, giving to causes, and the household feast of equality as a festival rite.

docs.title: The Attic year
docs.summary: How the ancient Athenian calendar worked, why modern Hellenists use it, how the app dates the festivals, and how to keep a festival well as a beginner or a coven.
docs.body:
## A year of festivals

Ancient Athens kept more festivals than any other Greek city: by some counts, well over a hundred days a year had a public festival or sacrifice. Modern Hellenic polytheists mostly follow the Athenian calendar, called the Attic calendar after Attica, the region around Athens, because it is the best recorded. The app's Hellenic calendar holds thirteen of its great festivals, and this module gives one lesson to each.

## How the Attic calendar works

The Attic year was lunar. Each month began at the Noumenia, when the first crescent of the new moon was seen, and ran for 29 or 30 days. Twelve lunar months make about 354 days, eleven short of a solar year, so every few years an extra month was added to keep the festivals in their seasons.

The year began with the first new moon after the summer solstice. The months, with roughly where they fall in the northern year, are:

1. **Hekatombaion** (July to August): the Kronia and the Panathenaia.
2. **Metageitnion** (August to September).
3. **Boedromion** (September to October): the Eleusinian Mysteries.
4. **Pyanepsion** (October to November): the Pyanepsia and the Thesmophoria.
5. **Maimakterion** (November to December).
6. **Poseideon** (December to January): the Haloa.
7. **Gamelion** (January to February): the Lenaia.
8. **Anthesterion** (February to March): the Anthesteria.
9. **Elaphebolion** (March to April): the City Dionysia.
10. **Mounichion** (April to May): the Mounichia.
11. **Thargelion** (May to June): the Thargelia and the Plynteria.
12. **Skirophorion** (June to July): the Skira.

Festivals were dated by the day of the month, so they move against our calendar from year to year, as Easter does. You do not need to calculate any of this. The app's calendar works out each year's dates from the moon, and you can see the coming festivals in your calendar and on Today.
