stages.title: Sharing the work and leading through hard times
stages.intro: No head can do everything, and every head meets a crisis. In this stage you plan what to delegate, prepare for crises, and build a way of leading that can last. Then you take the module’s test.

tasks.title: A delegation plan
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Delegating".
2. List every task you (or your head) did for the coven in the last month. Mark each D (delegate), S (share) or K (keep).
3. For three of the D’s, write who you would ask, the outcome you’d describe, and which position or power in the app they would need.
4. Write a "who can do what" list for the coven, and note any role with only one person able to do it.
5. Write it all in the answer box.

tasks.title: A crisis plan
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Leading through a crisis".
2. Write a one-page crisis plan: the emergency number where the coven meets, two crisis lines, who the head calls first, who steps in if the head is involved, and the steps for each of the four kinds of crisis.
3. Write it in the answer box.
4. Send your mentor a message on this step to arrange a conversation. Talk through one of the four kinds of crisis as if it were happening.

tasks.title: Log your time for the coven
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Burnout and keeping it sustainable".
2. For seven days, each time you do something for the coven (messages, planning, conversations, rites), note it and the minutes it took.
3. Log each day here.
4. At the end of the week, add it up.

tasks.title: Your sustainability check
tasks.instructions:
1. Using your week’s log, answer the five questions in the sustainability check at the end of "Burnout and keeping it sustainable".
2. Write down one task you will hand on this season, and one rite you will attend without leading.
3. Write it in the answer box.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Read over the lessons in this module.
2. Take the test. The choice questions are scored at once; your mentor or the coven’s head scores the written answers.
3. You need 80% to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, talk to your mentor, and take it again.

stages.title: The coven over time
stages.intro: A head is a steward: you hold the coven for its members, its tradition and those who come after. In this stage you plan for succession, hiving and closing, grow the coven’s trainers, look at its health and lineage, and its place among other covens. Then you take the module’s test.

tasks.title: A succession plan
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Succession and handing over".
2. With your head’s permission, look at Members and see where Hand on leadership appears (don’t tap it).
3. Write a succession section for your coven’s rules: who steps in if the head can’t lead, how a successor is chosen and prepared, how the handover happens (including in the app), and what the former head does afterwards.
4. Write it in the answer box, and send your mentor a message on this step to talk it through.

tasks.title: Plan an imagined hiving
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Hiving off a daughter coven".
2. Imagine your coven needs to hive in two years. Write who might lead the daughter coven, what would be carried and what would not, how members would choose, how the two covens would stay in touch, and the shape of the hiving rite.
3. Draft the daughter coven’s one line and description, naming where it comes from.
4. Write it all in the answer box. Don’t found a coven for this task.

tasks.title: Bring on a mentor
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Training the trainers".
2. List the elders who mentor or could mentor, with one strength and one area to grow for each.
3. With your head’s agreement, choose one elder to bring on (or support one already mentoring). Meet them at least twice over the coming months to talk about their mentee and their scoring.
4. Log each meeting here, and in the answer box write what you noticed and the feedback you gave.

tasks.title: A health check and lineage page
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "The coven’s long-term health and lineage".
2. With your head’s agreement, ask three or four members the two or three questions in the yearly health check, and look at the members’ record if you may.
3. In the answer box, write the coven’s signs of health, signs of trouble, and two or three changes you’d suggest for the coming year.
4. Draft an "Our lineage" page. If your head agrees, suggest it for the coven’s Book (members only); otherwise write it in the answer box.

tasks.title: Closing well
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Closing a coven well".
2. Write a short "closing well" section for your coven’s rules: who decides, how members are told, what happens to trainees’ progress, the coven’s material and any shared money, and the shape of a final rite.
3. Write it in the answer box.

tasks.title: Reach out to the wider community
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Working with other covens and the wider community".
2. Re-read the coven community guidelines from your coven profile in the app.
3. Find two other covens, moots or Pagan groups near you or in your tradition online. With your head’s agreement, contact one of them, or go to one of their open gatherings.
4. In the answer box, write who you contacted or visited, what you learned, and one thing in your coven’s rules that should mention the community guidelines.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Read over the lessons in this module.
2. Take the test. The choice questions are scored at once; your mentor or the coven’s head scores the written answers.
3. You need 80% to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, talk to your mentor, and take it again.

stages.title: Hellenic high priesthood
stages.intro: You are preparing to lead a coven: to succeed its present head, share its leadership, or found a daughter coven. Here you learn how the Greeks held priesthood, write your coven's sacred laws, plan the whole year, lead divination for the coven, and face the ethics of leading worship. Your current High Priestess or High Priest will guide and sign off this work.

tasks.title: Priesthood, ancient and modern
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Priesthood in ancient Greece" and "High priesthood today".
2. In the answer box, write two pages: how the Greeks chose, used and held priests to account, and what your own authority as a coven leader will and will not include.

tasks.title: The coven's sacred laws
tasks.instructions:
1. Gather your coven's written and unwritten customs with the current High Priestess or High Priest.
2. Draft the coven's sacred laws under headings such as calendar, purity, procedure, membership, costs and conduct, marking which are ancient and which are the coven's own.
3. Share the draft with the elders for comment.
4. Put the draft in the answer box, and add the agreed version to the coven's book.

tasks.title: Plan the year
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Leading the whole year".
2. With the current High Priestess or High Priest, plan the coven's next Attic year: which festivals together, which household, which monthly days, any added festivals, leads for each, resources and rest.
3. Write the plan in the answer box, and publish it to the coven in the app once agreed.

tasks.title: An open rite
tasks.instructions:
1. With the coven's agreement, plan and lead one rite open to guests or the wider community, following the steps in "Leading the whole year".
2. In the answer box, write what you did, how you practised xenia, what went well and what you'd change.

tasks.title: Lead the coven's divination
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Oracles and divination in a leading role".
2. At a coven festival or planning meeting, lead divination for the coven: agree the question, purify, ask once, record, and interpret together.
3. In the answer box, write the question, method, answer and the coven's interpretation. Later, add a note on how it proved.

tasks.title: The ethics of leading worship
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "The theology and ethics of leading worship".
2. In the answer box, write honestly: how you will handle speaking for the gods and your own gnosis, one inclusion question your coven must decide, how you will handle money and accountability, and your own signs of hubris and remedies.
3. Talk it through with the current High Priestess or High Priest.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read any lesson you're unsure of.
2. Take the test. The choice questions are scored at once; the written answers are scored by the current High Priestess or High Priest or a mentor they choose.
3. You need 80% to pass. If you don't pass, look at the questions you missed, talk it through, and try again.

docs.title: Spiritual authority and accountability
docs.summary: What a head’s authority is and is not, how guru dynamics grow and how to avoid them, and how to stay answerable to the coven.
docs.body:
## What this module is for

You have been an elder: you have led rites, taught, mentored and cared for people. Leading a whole coven is a different kind of work. An elder serves inside a structure someone else holds. The High Priestess or High Priest (in this course, "the head", since covens use many titles) holds the structure itself: its purpose, its rules, its people, its safety and its future. This module teaches that work, practically and step by step, beginning with the thing that makes it possible and the thing that most often goes wrong: authority.

## What spiritual authority is

In a coven, **authority** is the trust a group gives one person to make certain decisions and to speak for it in certain moments. It is not a quality you possess. It is a relationship, and like any relationship it is given, kept and can be withdrawn.

People describe where a head's authority comes from in different ways, and you need not choose only one:

- **The tradition.** In lineaged traditions such as some forms of modern Wicca, a High Priestess holds her role because she was initiated and trained in a line that recognises her. The lineage is a real chain of teaching, though no modern lineage can honestly claim to reach back unbroken to antiquity; most go back to the twentieth century revival.
- **The gods or powers.** Many heads feel called, and some describe their role as service to a deity. That call is real to them, but it is personal experience, and it cannot be used as proof to others.
- **The coven's consent.** In every case, the members chose to join, chose to stay and accept the head's decisions. Without that, there is no coven to lead.

The practical point is the third one. Whatever you believe about the first two, you only lead people who are free to leave, and you must lead in a way that keeps them genuinely free.

## What authority is for, and what it is not for

Authority in a coven exists for a small number of jobs:

1. Keeping the circle safe, physically, emotionally and spiritually.
2. Holding the coven's purpose and tradition steady over time.
3. Making decisions when a decision is needed and the group can't or shouldn't make it together.
4. Recognising people's growth (dedication, initiation, elders) honestly and fairly.
5. Speaking for the coven to others when someone has to.

It does **not** extend to members' private lives, money, relationships, bodies, medical choices, jobs, votes, families or friendships. A head may say, "In our circle we don't drink before ritual." A head may not say, "You should leave your partner," or "Your doctor is wrong," or "Give me your savings for the temple." The Salt & Sovereignty community guidelines say the same: no one may pressure a member for money, gifts, secrets, private photographs, sexual contact, an address or obedience, and no one may tell a member to cut off family or friends, stop medical or mental-health care, or harm themselves.

## Guru dynamics: how good leaders go wrong

A **guru dynamic** is a pattern in which a leader comes to be treated, and to treat themselves, as the source of truth, beyond question and beyond ordinary rules. It rarely starts with a bad person. It usually grows slowly from good intentions and grateful students. Watch for these signs in yourself and in the coven:

- Members ask your permission for ordinary life decisions.
- Disagreement with you is described as a spiritual failing ("Your ego is resisting").
- You have special rules for yourself: you can be late, drink, date students or skip the agreements.
- Gossip flows towards you, and you enjoy knowing everyone's secrets.
- The coven's language changes so only you can interpret its teachings.
- Leaving is treated as betrayal, and those who leave are spoken of badly.
- Your needs (praise, money, attention) quietly shape what the coven does.
- No one has told you that you were wrong in a long time.

> **Safety:** Romantic or sexual relationships between a head (or any teacher) and a student they have power over are the commonest path to serious harm in magical groups. Consent is not freely given where one person controls another's progress. If attraction arises, step back from teaching that person and talk to someone outside the coven before anything else happens. Many covens forbid such relationships outright, and you are wise to.

## Being answerable: accountability in practice

**Accountability** means that someone besides you can ask what you did and why, and that it matters what they think. A head who is answerable to no one is in danger, however good their heart. Build accountability in on purpose:

1. **Write down what you may and may not do.** Put the head's powers and limits in the coven's rules (the next lesson shows how). Members then have something to point to.
2. **Have at least two other people with real voices.** Elders, a council, a co-leader. Give them permission, in so many words, to tell you when you are wrong, and thank them when they do.
3. **Explain decisions.** You needn't put everything to a vote, but say why. "I've decided we'll meet monthly instead of fortnightly, because three of us are struggling to come and I'd rather fewer, fuller rites."
4. **Keep a way to complain that doesn't go through you.** In the app, reports go to the Salt & Sovereignty moderators, never to the coven's leaders. Tell members this, plainly and kindly, and mean it.
5. **Have an outside friend.** A head of another coven, a former teacher, a counsellor: someone who knows you and owes the coven nothing.
6. **Review yourself yearly.** Ask your elders, and perhaps members anonymously on paper, three questions: What do I do that helps? What do I do that hurts? What should I stop?

## Holding authority well, day to day

- **Say "I don't know".** It makes your "I do know" believable.
- **Separate roles.** When you are a friend at the pub, you are not the head; when you are leading ritual, you are not a friend asking for favours.
- **Use the lightest touch that works.** A quiet word before a formal warning; a warning before a pause; a pause before removal.
- **Be the first to keep the rules.** Sign the agreements, arrive on time, ground after ritual, log your own practice.
- **Don't collect secrets.** If a member tells you something about another member, ask whether it's theirs to tell.
- **Give credit away.** Name who wrote the rite, who cleaned up, who welcomed the seeker.

> **Try this:** Write the words "In this coven I may decide…" and list five things. Then write "In this coven I may never…" and list five more. Keep both lists; you will use them when you write the coven's rules.

## When you are wrong

You will make mistakes: a bad decision, a sharp word, a broken confidence, a promise not kept. How you handle them teaches more than any lesson.

1. Notice it, or hear it when someone tells you. Thank them, whatever you feel.
2. Say plainly what you did, without excuses or long explanations.
3. Say what you'll do to put it right, and then do it.
4. If it touched the whole coven, tell the whole coven.
5. Learn the lesson and, where useful, change a rule or habit so it happens less.

An apology from a head is not weakness. It is the clearest sign to the coven that the authority they gave you is safe in your hands.

> **Your coven:** Each tradition speaks about the head's authority in its own words: a High Priestess as the Goddess's representative in circle, a gothi or gythia as one who speaks for the folk, a priest or priestess who serves the god's household. Ask your coven's head how your tradition understands it, and what limits it places on that role.

docs.title: Vision and the coven’s documents
docs.summary: Finding the coven’s vision, and writing and keeping its creed, rules, requirements and agreements in the app.
docs.body:
## Why a coven needs a vision

A **vision** is a short, honest statement of what the coven is for and how it wants to be. Without one, a coven drifts: towards whatever the most forceful member wants, or towards whatever the head happens to be interested in this year. With one, people can decide whether they belong, and the head has something other than personal taste to steer by.

A vision need not be grand. "A small, friendly circle keeping the Wheel of the Year in the hedge-witch way, for people who want depth without dogma" is a perfectly good vision. So is "A Hellenic household cult honouring the theoi of the hearth and city, with monthly devotions and the major festivals."

## Finding the vision, step by step

If you are succeeding a head, the vision already exists, written or not. Your first task is to find it, not replace it. If you are founding a daughter coven, you will write one fresh. The steps are much the same.

1. **Listen first.** Ask five or six members, separately, three questions: Why did you join? What would make you leave? What do you hope we're still doing in five years? Write down their words.
2. **Look at what the coven actually does.** List the last year's gatherings. What did you keep, what did you skip, what drew people?
3. **Draft three sentences.** One for what the coven is (tradition, practice). One for who it is for. One for how it behaves (its spirit).
4. **Test the draft.** Read it to your elders. Does anything make them wince? Is anything missing that they'd fight for?
5. **Revise and settle it.** Put it in the coven's description and its creed (below). Revisit it every year or two, not every month.

## The coven's documents

The app gives every coven a set of pages, which you find on the coven's page under **Manage**, then **Creed, rules and agreements**. When a coven is founded, it starts with four: an empty creed ("Our creed"), empty rules ("Coven rules"), an empty page of requirements ("What we ask of members"), and a starter member agreement that every member signs. Each page has a **kind**: Creed, Rules, Requirements, Agreement or Other.

Think of the kinds this way:

- **Creed:** what the coven holds sacred and believes, in its own voice. Not a test of belief for members, but an honest statement. Keep it short enough to read aloud.
- **Rules:** how the coven runs. Meetings, roles, decisions, confidentiality, conduct, how disagreements and complaints are handled, the head's powers and limits.
- **Requirements:** what membership and each step of it ask of people: attendance, study, practice, time.
- **Agreement:** what every member signs and commits to. Short, clear, and only what you'd truly hold people to.
- **Other:** anything else worth reading: a welcome, a short history, a reading list.

## Writing good documents

Good coven documents share some qualities:

- **Plain words.** Write as you'd speak to a thoughtful newcomer. Define any term of art the first time.
- **Honest about history.** If your rite is a 1970s creation, say so with pride; don't call it ancient.
- **Fair and enforceable.** Every rule should be one you'd actually apply to everyone, including yourself.
- **Consistent with the community guidelines.** The Salt & Sovereignty guidelines say coven rules can add to them but can't override them. A rule that requires members to share secrets, give money as a condition of belonging, or obey without question is not allowed, and would be wrong anyway.
- **Short.** People sign what they read. A three-page agreement is not read.

A sound set of **rules** usually covers:

1. Who leads and what they may decide; who the elders are and what they do.
2. How decisions are made: by the head, by the elders, by the whole coven, and which is which.
3. How people join, rise and leave (and that anyone may leave at any time without explaining).
4. Confidentiality, and its limits (safety always comes first).
5. Conduct in ritual and in the chat; alcohol and substances; consent to touch.
6. How complaints are made, including against the head, and that reports through the app go to the site's moderators.
7. Money, if any: shared costs only, never a condition of belonging or of rising.
8. How the rules themselves change.

## Doing it in the app, step by step

You need the **Leads the coven** power, which the head has, and which anyone in a position that carries it has too.

1. Open your coven from the Coven tab and tap **Manage**, then **Creed, rules and agreements**. The list shows each page with its kind and notes such as "to be signed", "members only" or "draft".
2. Tap a page to edit it, or **Add a page** for a new one.
3. Give it a **Title**, choose its **Kind**, and write the **Words**. Pages can be long (up to twenty thousand characters), but long is rarely better.
4. Choose **Who can read it**: "Everyone, before they join" or "Members only". Pages everyone can read help seekers decide whether the coven is for them, so put your creed, rules and requirements there unless there's a real reason not to.
5. Set the **Order** (lower numbers come first).
6. Tick **Members must sign this** for an agreement. An agreement must be readable by everyone, because seekers sign it before they join; the app won't save it otherwise.
7. Untick **Published** to keep a page as a draft while you work on it with your elders.
8. Tap **Save** (or **Add**).

> **Safety:** Changing the title or words of a page members sign creates a new version, and asks every member to sign it again before they can speak in the chat or tend the altars. That is right for real changes; it is disruptive for a typo. Gather changes up, tell the coven what's changing and why before you save, and give people a week or two.

Deleting a page takes its signatures with it. Prefer unpublishing to deleting while you're unsure.

## Keeping the description honest

Under **Manage**, then **The coven**, you set the coven's **Name**, its **One line about the coven**, **Who you are and how you practise**, its **Tradition or path**, **When you gather** and **Tags**. This is the first thing a seeker reads. Make it match the vision. If the coven has changed (smaller, quieter, more devotional) change the description too.

> **Try this:** Open your coven's pages and read them as if you were a stranger. Mark anything vague, anything you wouldn't actually enforce, and anything that sounds grander than the coven really is. Bring your notes to your mentor.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions hold their deepest material as oath-bound and keep it out of public pages entirely; others publish openly. Ask your head what may be written in the public pages, what belongs in "Members only", and what belongs only in the coven's Book or in speech.

docs.title: Running the coven in the app: its shape and its people
docs.summary: The head and the powers, setting up positions and open positions, joining, invitations, reviewing applications and requests to advance, and members’ positions.
docs.body:
## Running the coven in the app

The next three lessons walk through every part of a coven in the app, as the head sees it. Read them with the app open on your own coven if you can, and tap through as you go (looking changes nothing; only saving does). If you don't yet hold the powers, sit with your head and have them show you each screen.

Two places hold almost everything:

- **The coven's page**: Messages, Rituals and rites, Altars, Book of Shadows, Petitions, Initiation & training, Members and (if shown) Paths in the coven. Those with the powers also see **Review** and **Manage** here.
- **Manage**: the coven's settings: The coven, Creed, rules and agreements, Positions, Invite people, Questions for applicants, Practice calendar, Gathering notifications, Who runs training, Ritual participation, and archiving.

## The head and the powers

In the app, the coven's **head** is the person who founded it, or to whom it was handed on. The head always has every power, and only the head can do a few things: hand on leadership, archive the coven, choose who sees ritual participation and who keeps the members' record, and choose the position people reach by finishing a program.

Everyone else's powers come from their **position**. Each position can carry any of these powers:

- Reviews applications and requests to advance.
- Moderates the gathering (removes messages, pauses or removes members).
- Leads the coven's rituals (plans them, gives out their steps, begins them).
- Puts rites on the coven's calendar.
- Chooses who hears about the coven's gatherings.
- Writes in the coven's Book of Shadows (drafts go for approval).
- Approves pages for the coven's Book of Shadows.
- Manages initiation and training (designs programs, chooses who takes them, assigns mentors, signs off work).
- Sees everyone's initiation and training progress.
- Starts new altars for the coven.
- Tends the coven's altars outside rituals.
- Keeps the coven's altars (chooses who tends each one, locks them, clears them away).
- Talks in the coven's chat.
- Leads the coven (edits its pages, positions and details).

A new coven starts with five positions: Seeker (where new members begin), Dedicant, Initiate, Elder (reviews and moderates) and the founder's own title (leads the coven). You can rename, change or remove all of them.

## Setting up positions, step by step

1. Tap **Manage**, then **Positions**. Each position shows its level, whether new members begin there, whether it is open to apply for, and its powers.
2. Tap a position, or **Add a position**.
3. Give it a **Name** and a **Seniority** from 1 to 99. Higher is more senior. Seniority matters: people can only act on (raise, pause, remove) those below them.
4. Write **What this position is** in a sentence or two.
5. Write **What it asks of someone**. This is shown to members who apply for it, so make it concrete: "Has completed the devotee program, kept the eight festivals for a year, and served as a quarter-caller at least four times."
6. Tick **New members begin here** for your entry position (only one should).
7. Tick **Members can apply to rise to it** to make it an **open position**: members will see it under My standing, under "Rise to a higher position".
8. Tick its **Powers**. Give the fewest powers the role needs. Starting altars and talking in the chat are on by default; untick them if you need to.
9. Tap **Save**.

Deleting a position leaves anyone who held it as a member without a position until you give them another, so move people first.

> **Note:** Reviewers can raise members only to positions below their own that carry no powers. Those who lead the coven can give positions up to their own level. Only the head can act on everyone.

## Joining: how people come in

Under **Manage**, then **The coven**:

- **How witches join**: "Open to join" (sign the agreements and you're in), "By application" (the coven's reviewers decide) or "Not taking members".
- **Directory**: "Listed" or "Unlisted (link only)".
- **Most members**: a number from 2 to 1,000, or empty for no limit.

The coven's address can't change, so links keep working.

Under **Manage**, then **Questions for applicants**, you can set up to twenty questions, each marked **Required** or not. Applicants answer them after signing the agreements. Ask what you truly need to know: why they're drawn to this coven, their experience, their availability, anything about safety ("Is there anything we should know to make ritual safe and comfortable for you?"). Don't ask for more personal detail than you need.

## Invitations, step by step

Tap **Invite** on the coven's page (or **Manage**, then **Invite people**).

1. **To share a link:** under "Share an invite link", choose **How long it lasts** and **How many people can use it**, add a note for yourself if you like, then tap **Make a link**, and **Share** or **Copy link**. Anyone with the link can join without applying once they've signed the agreements, even if the coven isn't listed.
2. **To invite someone by name:** under "Invite someone in the app", search for the name they use in covens, tap them, add a message if you'd like, and tap **Send invitation**.
3. Below, **Invite links** and **Invitations waiting** list what is still open. **Revoke** takes one back.
4. Under **Who may invite**, the head and those who lead choose whether **Members may invite people**. Those who lead or review can always invite.

Short-lived, single-use links are safest. A link posted publicly is an open door.

## Reviewing applications and requests to advance

Tap **Review** on the coven's page. The number beside it is how many are waiting.

1. Under **Applications to join**, read each person's answers and note. Add a **Note to them** if you'd like, then **Approve** or **Decline**. A kind, specific note matters most when you decline.
2. Under **Requests to advance**, you'll see who asked, which position, what that position asks, and their statement. Approve, or decline with a note saying what they still need.
3. If an application worries you (someone may be under 18, or is pressuring, or offensive) use **Report**, which goes to the site's moderators.

Turn on notifications for new applications in Settings, under Notifications & reminders, then Covens.

## Members and their positions

Tap **Members**. Tap a person to see what you can do: change their **Position**, pause their messages, remove or ban them (if you moderate), see their record (if you keep it), report or block them. The head also sees **Hand on leadership** here; that belongs to the stewardship module.

> **Try this:** With your head's permission, sketch on paper the positions your coven would have if you founded it tomorrow: names, seniority, what each asks, which are open to apply for, and the powers each carries. Compare it with the coven's real positions and talk through the differences with your mentor.

> **Your coven:** Many traditions have degrees (first, second, third) or titles (Maiden, Summoner, Gothi) with their own meanings. Positions in the app are simply the way to give each one its powers; the names and meaning are your coven's.

docs.title: Running the coven in the app: training and gatherings
docs.summary: Programs and mentors, the practice calendar, rites, meetings, gathering notifications and ritual participation, step by step.
docs.body:
## Training: programs and mentors

The coven's training lives under **Initiation & training** on the coven's page. Everyone sees their own programs there; those who manage programs also see **Design and assign** and everyone's progress.

### Who runs training

Under **Manage**, then **Who runs training**, the head chooses, person by person, who **Manages programs** (designs programs, chooses who takes them, assigns mentors, signs off work) and who **Sees everyone's progress**. Positions can carry the same powers. Give these powers to the elders who actually teach, and no wider.

### Starting a program, step by step

1. Open **Initiation & training**, then **Design and assign**.
2. Under "Start a program", tap a ready-made program (those for your coven's practice calendar are shown first), or **Make your own initiation** or **Make your own training**.
3. Give it a **Title**, a line, and **About the program**.
4. The head may choose a position under **Those who finish it become**. Finishing the program then raises people to it.
5. Tick **Any member may begin it themselves** if it is open to all; otherwise only those you assign take it.
6. For each stage, set the **Least time in the stage** (366 for a year and a day) and **Who confirms it's passed**: their mentor, a program manager or themselves.
7. For each task, set its **Kind**, **Instructions**, **Times to do it**, how long it takes, **Signed off by**, whether they **write a response**, whether it is **Optional**, and a holiday if it belongs to one. You can link pages of the coven's Book.
8. **Save as draft** while you work; **Save and open** when it's ready.

### Assigning and mentoring

1. On the program, tap **Assign** and choose a person, or a whole position. Assigning a position enrols everyone in it now, and anyone who takes it later.
2. Under **Mentors**, tap a member and choose their mentor. A mentor sees their mentee's progress and signs off the tasks and stages left to mentors.
3. To follow someone, open their progress: you can sign off work, confirm a stage (with a note), **Pass the stage early** where it's right, **Pause** or **Withdraw** them.

Archive old programs rather than deleting them: deleting a program deletes everyone's progress in it.

## The practice calendar

Under **Manage**, then **Practice calendar**, tick the calendars the coven keeps, choose single holidays if you only keep some (leave all unticked to keep them all), and add **The coven's own days** with a name, date and meaning. Tap **Save the calendar**. The holidays show on the coven's page and members' Today, the ritual planner suggests dates from them, and ready-made programs for them are suggested first.

## Rites, step by step

Open **Rituals and rites**. Those who lead rituals see **Plan a ritual** under Planning.

1. Tap **Plan a ritual**, choose "A rite", and start from a ready-made template, one of the coven's own templates, a copy of an earlier coven rite, one of your own rituals, or an empty outline.
2. Tap the title row to fill in the **Details**: its name, **Intention**, **What members should know or bring**, **Occasion** (full moon, new moon, esbat, sabbat or other) and its name, and the date and time. Suggested moons and holidays appear as chips you can tap.
3. Work through the outline: **Roles** (give each to a person or a position), **Before the rite** (a checklist), **Afterwards**, **Sections**, and each step: what happens, the words, and what it does at the altar.
4. Tap **Read it through** to check the whole script.
5. Tap **Save it on the coven's calendar** (if you may put rites on the calendar) or **Save as a draft**.
6. Members answer **Will you be there?**: Going, Maybe or Can't make it.
7. On the day, open the rite and tap **Start the ritual**. Move with **Skip to the next step** or **Back a step**, and close with **End the ritual**.
8. Afterwards, those who lead can correct **Who was there** ("Was there in person", "Wasn't there", "Excuse the absence"), and save the rite or its record to the Book.

**Cancel the rite** tells those going that it's off; you can put it back later.

## Meetings, step by step

Business, planning and study belong in meetings, which the app treats as a gathering of their own.

1. In **Rituals and rites**, tap **Plan a meeting**.
2. Fill in the details as for a rite.
3. Open **Who it's for, and how it runs**: choose **Who it's for** (everyone, or kept to some, such as the elders), **The Chair** and **The Secretary**, when **The meeting's chat opens**, how long **It runs for**, and who **The minutes are read by**.
4. Build the agenda as steps. Steps can hold motions and votes.
5. Put it on the calendar. During it, the Chair steers, votes are cast and closed, and afterwards the minutes are written and can be saved to the Book.

A meeting kept to some only ever reaches them.

## Gathering notifications

When a rite or meeting goes on the calendar, moves or comes off it, the people it's for get a note on their phone. Under **Manage**, then **Gathering notifications** (or **Choose who hears** in Rituals and rites), those the head allows choose who hears:

1. Rites and meetings each have a rule. With no rule, everyone a gathering is for hears.
2. Under **Add a rule for an occasion**, add a rule for a kind (full moon, Samhain, an officials' meeting) or for a name you use in the planner (such as Deipnon), and choose who hears about it.
3. A single gathering can choose otherwise in its own details ("For this one"). Its own choice comes first; then the closest rule.

Each member can still turn these off for themselves under Reminders. Notifications are a courtesy, not a substitute for telling people in person about something important.

## Ritual participation

Under **Manage**, then **Ritual participation**, the head chooses who else may see, for each step that asks people to write, place or do something, how many have done it and who has and hasn't. They never see what anyone wrote, and private contributions stay sealed. Keep this to those who genuinely need it.

> **Try this:** With your head's permission and an elder alongside, plan a simple full-moon rite in the app from start to finish and save it as a draft. Then plan a short elders' meeting with an agenda of three items. Don't put either on the calendar unless your head agrees.

> **Your coven:** Some covens keep every gathering in person and use the app only for planning; some meet mostly online. Ask your head how your coven uses rites, meetings and notifications, and what it never puts in the app.

docs.title: Running the coven in the app: the Book, altars, records and safety
docs.summary: The coven’s Book and who may open it, altars and their keepers, members’ records and standing, moderation and reports, and a weekly rhythm for the head.
docs.body:
## The coven's Book of Shadows

The coven's **Book of Shadows** is its shared grimoire: sections and pages, with shelves for Rites, Ritual records, Meeting minutes and Study material. Members' own grimoires stay private.

Who may open, write in and approve each part is set per book, section and page:

1. Open **Book of Shadows**. Those who approve for the whole book see **Who can open the whole book**; each section and page has **Who can open it** for those who approve it.
2. For each of **open**, **write** and **approve**, choose whether it follows the level above (the coven's own powers, the whole book, or its section) or is **chosen here** for particular positions and people.
3. "Open" means only those named see it at all: it's left out of contents, searches, links and the ritual builder for everyone else. Use this for oath-bound or degree material.
4. **Save**.

Members who can't write suggest pages and changes, which wait under **Waiting for approval**. Those who approve can **Approve**, **Edit first**, **Send back** with a note, or **Decline**. Pages keep their **History**.

Good practice: make sure at least two people can approve every part of the Book, so material isn't stuck when one person is away.

## Altars

Open **Altars**. The coven's main ritual altar comes first, kept by the head; members may start more. Each altar's keepers (the head, those whose position keeps altars, and whoever started it) open its settings to:

1. Name it.
2. Choose **Who tends it, outside rituals**: everyone, chosen positions and people, or only its keepers.
3. Tick **Locked** so only its keepers can change it, even in a ritual's steps.
4. **Archive** it (kept, and can be restored) or delete it for good.

During a ritual, the ritual's steps decide who may act on the altar. Petitions each get their own small altar, which the asker or a moderator closes when it's answered.

## Members' records and standing

The **members' record** shows who has been taking part. Open **Members**, then **Members' record**.

- Everyone is listed least active first: rituals they came to, when they last took part, their studies and their mentor.
- Gentle flags show where someone may need a word: missed rituals in a row, a study that hasn't moved, no mentor check-in, a long quiet spell.
- Tap someone to see every ritual, their studies, their mentoring, and private **Leaders' notes** that only the record's keepers read.

At the foot of the record, the head chooses **Who also sees the record**, and whether mentees read their mentor's check-ins.

Every member sees their own record under **My standing**, then **Your record**, without the leaders' notes. Treat the record as a pastoral tool, not surveillance. A flag means "check in kindly", never "punish". Write leaders' notes as if the person might one day read them: factual, fair and brief.

The head also sees **Paths in the coven**: what share of members practise each way and honour each deity, never who. Anything fewer than three share is grouped as "Other", and nothing shows until five have shared. The head can show it to the whole coven.

## Moderation and reports

Moderation keeps the gathering safe. Those who moderate can:

1. **Remove a message**: press and hold it in the chat and choose "Remove message".
2. **Pause a member's messages** for an hour, a day or a week, from Members (tap them) or their record. Lift the pause early if it's resolved.
3. **Remove** someone from the coven (they can apply again later) or **ban** them (they can't rejoin or apply). On their record you can note why; it stays with the record.
4. **Lift a ban** from "Former members".

Use the lightest step that works, and talk to the person first whenever it is safe to.

**Reports** are different. Every message, member, application, Book page and coven has a **Report** button. Reports go to the Salt & Sovereignty moderators, **never** to the coven's leaders, and the person reported isn't told who reported them. The reasons include harassment, pressure for money, secrets, photos or obedience, hate, sexual content, someone who may be under 18, someone who may be at risk of harm, scams and spam.

As head, you should:

- Tell members, plainly, that they may report anything, including you, and that you won't ask who did.
- Report yourself anything you can't handle inside the coven: someone who may be under 18, threats, coercion, hate.
- Never punish anyone for reporting.

The site's moderators can read every coven's pages, chat and altars, remove messages, pause members, pause or archive a coven and ban accounts from all covens.

## Archiving

Under **Manage**, at the foot, the head can **Archive the coven**. It leaves the directory, and its chat and altars become read-only. Only the site's moderators can reopen it. This belongs to the stewardship module's lesson on closing a coven well, and should never be done in haste.

## A weekly rhythm for the head

The app is easiest to run with a small, steady habit. Once a week, perhaps on the same evening:

1. Open **Review** and answer anything waiting.
2. Glance at **Initiation & training** for work waiting for sign-off.
3. Look at the next fortnight in **Rituals and rites**: is everything planned, with roles filled?
4. Read the members' record flags and choose one or two people to message kindly.
5. Check **Book of Shadows** for suggestions waiting.
6. Look at the chat for anything unresolved.

Fifteen minutes a week saves hours of catching up.

> **Safety:** The app holds people's spiritual lives, studies and private notes. Lock your phone, don't let others use your account, and don't screenshot or share what members write. The community guidelines ask the same of every member.

> **Try this:** Sit with your head (or, if you already hold the powers, on your own) and walk through each screen named in this lesson. In your answer box, list anything that surprised you and anything you'd set up differently.

> **Your coven:** Covens differ in what they record. Some keep a full Book in the app; some keep the Book on paper and only minutes in the app. Ask your head what lives where.

docs.title: Delegating
docs.summary: What to hand on and what to keep, how to delegate step by step, and how to use positions and powers to share the work.
docs.body:
## Why a head must delegate

**Delegating** means handing a task, with the authority to do it, to someone else, and then trusting them with it. Heads who don't delegate burn out, and their covens stall: elders never grow, members never learn to lead, and everything stops when the head is ill or away. Delegation is not laziness. It is how a coven outlives its head.

## What to delegate, and what not to

Delegate:

- Routine work: setting up the space, the chat, the calendar, the Book's tidying, welcoming newcomers.
- Teaching within someone's competence: a mentor for each trainee, an elder for each subject.
- Leading rites, by turns, so that several people can do it well.
- Projects with a clear end: planning the Samhain feast, rewriting the reading list.

Keep, as head (or share only with a co-leader):

- Final responsibility for safety and safeguarding.
- Decisions about removing or banning members, except in emergencies.
- Changes to the creed, rules and agreements.
- Initiations and other recognitions your tradition reserves for the head.
- Handing on the coven.

## How to delegate well, step by step

1. **Choose the person for the task.** Ask: who is ready for this, who would grow from it, who has time? Not always the most willing.
2. **Describe the outcome, not every move.** "I'd like the Imbolc rite written and cast by the end of the month, with parts for everyone who wants one." Let them choose the how.
3. **Give the authority with the task.** If they're leading rites, give them a position (or a power) that lets them plan rites and put them on the calendar. Responsibility without authority is a trap.
4. **Agree the limits.** Budget, dates, what they must check with you first.
5. **Agree how you'll check in.** "Let's talk Thursday week" is better than hovering.
6. **Stand back.** Let them do it their way, even if it isn't yours.
7. **Thank them in public, correct them in private.** Afterwards, talk about what went well and what to change.

## Delegation in the app

The app is built around delegation. Use it on purpose:

- **Positions carry powers.** Make a position for each real role: "Ritual lead" with "Leads the coven's rituals" and "Puts rites on the coven's calendar"; "Scribe" with "Writes in" and "Approves pages for" the Book; "Warden" with "Moderates the gathering". Give each role only the powers it needs.
- **Who runs training.** Under Manage, choose the elders who manage programs and who see progress.
- **Mentors.** Assign mentors under Initiation & training, Design and assign, Mentors.
- **Gathering notifications.** Let a trusted officer choose who hears, through the "Chooses who hears about the coven's gatherings" power.
- **Altars.** Give an altar keeper "Keeps the coven's altars".
- **The record.** Let one or two elders keep the members' record, so pastoral check-ins don't all fall to you.
- **Roles in a rite.** In the planner, give roles to positions ("whoever is Maiden") rather than always to people, so the rite still works when someone moves on.

## A worked example

Rowan leads a coven of nine. She writes every rite, moderates the chat, mentors four trainees and keeps the Book. She is tired. Here is how she delegates over one season:

1. She asks Ash, an initiate who loves liturgy, to write and lead the spring equinox rite. She describes the outcome ("a rite of balance, about forty minutes, with a part for anyone who wants one"), gives Ash a "Ritual lead" position with the powers to plan rites and put them on the calendar, and agrees to look at the draft a week before.
2. She asks Hazel, a steady elder, to share chat moderation. Hazel's Elder position already carries "Moderates the gathering". They agree that Hazel removes anything against the rules and pauses only in an emergency, and that removals or bans are talked over first.
3. She moves two of her mentees to Elm, who has finished the initiate program and has time, under Design and assign, Mentors, and meets Elm monthly to talk about them.
4. She makes Birch the Scribe, with powers to write in and approve the Book, and asks Birch to tidy the sections by Beltane.

At the season's end, Ash's rite was different from Rowan's style, and the coven loved it. Rowan has five hours a week back.

## Delegating to a co-leader

Sharing the head's work with a co-leader is the deepest kind of delegation. It needs more than a position with powers:

- **Agree who decides what.** Write it down: perhaps one of you leads ritual and the other leads training; perhaps you decide together on anything to do with membership.
- **Agree how you disagree.** Privately, never in front of the coven. If you can't agree, who has the final word, or whom do you ask?
- **Speak with one voice in public.** Members should never be able to play one of you against the other.
- **Meet regularly.** A short call each week keeps you in step.

## When delegation goes wrong

- **The task isn't done.** Ask what got in the way before you assume anything. Often it was too big, or the authority wasn't given.
- **It's done differently from how you'd do it.** If it's safe and in keeping with the tradition, let it be. Different is not wrong.
- **It's done badly or unsafely.** Talk privately, specifically and kindly. If needed, take the task back, with honesty about why.
- **Someone misuses a power.** Remove the power first (change their position), then talk. Safety before feelings.

## Growing leaders on purpose

Delegation is also teaching. Over a year, aim for:

- At least two people besides you who can lead each of your regular rites.
- At least two who can moderate the chat.
- At least two who can approve Book pages.
- A mentor for every trainee, and no mentor with more than three mentees.

Write this down as a "who can do what" list and keep it in the Book (members only). Review it each season.

> **Try this:** List every task you (or your head) did for the coven in the last month, however small. Mark each one D (delegate), S (share) or K (keep). For three of the D's, write who you'd ask, what outcome you'd describe, and what power in the app they'd need.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions give particular tasks to particular offices (a Maiden who assists, a Summoner who calls the coven together, a Handmaiden, a Steward). Ask your head which offices your coven has, and which tasks belong to each.

docs.title: Leading through a crisis
docs.summary: Principles for any crisis, and what to do when a member is in crisis, leaders are in conflict, something happens in public, or there is a safeguarding concern.
docs.body:
## Crisis leadership

A **crisis** is any situation where someone may be harmed, or the coven may break apart, unless it is handled well and soon. Every head meets them. You can't prevent all of them, but you can prepare, and preparation is most of what makes the difference.

This lesson covers four kinds: a member in crisis, conflict among leaders, a public incident, and a safeguarding concern. The principles are the same for all.

## The principles

1. **Safety first.** Before reputation, feelings, tradition or the rite, ask: is anyone in danger now?
2. **Slow is fast.** Except where someone is in immediate danger, take time: an hour, a night, a conversation with someone you trust. Hasty decisions in crises are the ones regretted.
3. **You are not a professional service.** A coven is not a crisis line, a therapist, a doctor or the police. Your job is to care, to connect people with the right help and to keep the circle safe.
4. **Write it down.** Keep a brief, factual note of what happened, what was said, what you did and when. Keep it private and secure.
5. **Tell the right few, not the many.** Confidentiality protects people, but it has limits: safety always comes first.
6. **Look after yourself and the helpers.** Crises are draining. Ground, rest and talk to someone outside it.

> **Safety:** If anyone is in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number first. Everything else comes after. The Sanctuary in the app lists support lines for many situations.

## A member in crisis

A member may be in distress: grief, a breakdown, suicidal thoughts, abuse at home, a frightening spiritual experience that won't settle.

1. **Listen first.** Find somewhere private (or a one-to-one conversation in the app). Let them talk. Don't rush to fix, interpret or reassure.
2. **Ask directly about safety.** If you are worried about suicide, ask plainly: "Are you thinking about ending your life?" Asking does not put the idea in someone's head; it opens the door to help.
3. **If they're in danger now**, stay with them (in person or on the phone) and contact emergency services or a crisis line together.
4. **Connect them to proper help.** A doctor, a counsellor, a crisis line, a domestic abuse service. Offer to help them make the call.
5. **Be clear that magic is not a substitute for care.** Ritual, prayer and the coven's love can support someone alongside professional help, never instead of it. Don't diagnose spiritual causes ("It's a curse", "You're being attacked") for what may be illness.
6. **Pause practice if it's harming them.** Gently suggest they step back from intense work, trance or fasting, and keep grounding practices only.
7. **Agree what is shared.** Ask them who in the coven may know, and what. Respect it, unless safety demands otherwise, and tell them if it does.
8. **Follow up.** A message the next day, and the next week. Note it in their record, briefly, if you keep one.

## Conflict among leaders

Two elders who can't stand each other, a co-leader who disagrees with every decision, an elder who undermines the head in private. Leadership conflict splits covens more than anything else.

1. **Keep it off the main stage.** Don't argue in front of the coven or in the coven's chat. Use a private conversation or a meeting kept to those involved.
2. **Meet in person or by call, not by long messages.** Text loses tone and invites escalation.
3. **Each speaks; each listens.** One speaks without interruption; the other summarises what they heard before replying. Then swap.
4. **Separate the issue from the person.** "We disagree about whether to take new members this year" is solvable. "You always undermine me" is not, until it's turned into specifics.
5. **Look for what's shared.** Nearly always, both want the coven to thrive.
6. **Decide how it gets decided.** Your rules should say who decides what. If they don't, agree now, and write it in.
7. **Bring in a third person** if you're stuck: a respected elder from another coven, or a professional mediator.
8. **Know when to part.** Sometimes the healthiest outcome is that one leader hives off or steps down. Part kindly, without a public narrative of villains.

## A public incident

Something happens that people outside will see: a member posts the coven's private chat online, a rite in a park draws a complaint, a former member writes about the coven publicly, a news story mentions you.

1. **Pause.** Don't respond publicly in the first hours.
2. **Find out the facts.** What actually happened? Who is affected?
3. **Protect members first.** Is anyone's name, face or address exposed? Help them; report doxxing to the site's moderators, and to the platform where it was posted.
4. **Decide whether to respond at all.** Often the best public answer is none.
5. **If you respond, be brief, factual and kind.** No attacks, no secrets, no excuses. Correct errors calmly.
6. **Tell the coven** what happened and what you're doing, in a meeting or a short message, so rumours don't fill the gap.
7. **Learn from it.** Do the rules on confidentiality need to be clearer? Did a public rite need a permit or more care?

## A safeguarding concern

**Safeguarding** means protecting people, especially those at risk, from abuse, exploitation and harm. In a coven, safeguarding concerns include: someone who may be under 18; a member being coerced for money, sex, secrets or obedience; a member abusing another; a vulnerable adult being exploited; or a leader (including you) misusing their position.

1. **Take it seriously.** Listen. Don't promise to keep it secret; promise to handle it carefully.
2. **Don't investigate like the police.** Ask only enough to understand what's alleged and whether anyone is at risk now. Don't confront the person accused before you've thought it through; it can put people in danger.
3. **Act on immediate danger** by contacting emergency services.
4. **Report through the app.** Use the **Report** button on the member or message (reasons include "Someone may be under 18" and "Pressure for money, secrets, photos or obedience"). Reports go to the Salt & Sovereignty moderators.
5. **Contact the proper authorities** where the law or the situation requires it: the police, or adult or child protection services in your area. Laws differ by country; if you are unsure, ask a local safeguarding helpline for advice.
6. **Protect the coven while it's resolved.** You can pause someone's messages or remove them from the coven. Do it calmly, without public accusation.
7. **Record what you know and did**, factually, with dates.
8. **If the concern is about you**, step back from that person and from leading while it is looked at, and let an elder or the site's moderators handle it. That is what accountability means.

> **Note:** Covens on Salt & Sovereignty are for adults only. If you believe someone in a coven is under 18, report them; the moderators remove under-18 accounts from covens.

## After any crisis

Hold a short, private review with your elders. What happened? What helped? What would we do differently? What needs to change in our rules, our habits or our app settings? Then rest.

> **Try this:** Write a one-page crisis plan for your coven: emergency numbers for where you meet, two crisis lines, who the head calls first, who steps in if the head is involved, and the steps to take for each of the four kinds of crisis. Keep it somewhere you'd find it in a hurry.

> **Your coven:** Some covens have a named welfare officer or "warden" for pastoral care and safety. Ask your head whether yours does, and how the coven's rules say concerns are raised.

docs.title: Burnout and keeping it sustainable
docs.summary: Recognising burnout, why heads burn out, and how to build a coven, and a leadership, that can last.
docs.body:
## What burnout is

**Burnout** is a state of physical, emotional and spiritual exhaustion that comes from long-term demands without enough rest or return. It isn't the same as being tired after a big rite. It builds over months, and it is very common among coven leaders, who often give far more than they receive and feel they can't stop.

Common signs:

- Dreading gatherings you used to love.
- Irritation with members over small things.
- Practice that feels empty, or that you've stopped doing for yourself.
- Trouble sleeping, frequent illness, headaches.
- Feeling that everything depends on you, and resenting it.
- Avoiding messages, letting things slide, then over-working to catch up.
- Cynicism about the tradition, the gods or the people.

Noticing a few of these sometimes is human. Noticing many for weeks is a warning.

## Why heads burn out

- **Everything goes through them.** No delegation, no co-leader.
- **No boundaries on time.** Messages at midnight, crises every week.
- **Pastoral overload.** Being everyone's counsellor, with no training and no support.
- **Losing their own practice.** Leading rites for others, never sitting in one.
- **Conflict without resolution.** Old disputes left to fester.
- **Unrealistic ambition.** Too many gatherings, too many programs, too many members.
- **No outside life.** The coven becomes all of their social and spiritual world.

## Building a sustainable coven, step by step

1. **Set a sustainable rhythm.** Count honestly how many gatherings a year you can lead well. A rich monthly rite is better than a tired weekly one. Write the rhythm into the coven's description ("When you gather").
2. **Share leadership.** A co-leader, or a rota of ritual leads. In the app, give a trusted elder a position with the powers they need.
3. **Set message hours.** Tell members when you're reachable ("I read coven messages in the evenings, not at work, and not on Sundays") and turn off notifications outside them. For a real emergency, members should contact emergency services, not you.
4. **Cap your mentees.** Two or three at most. Assign other mentors.
5. **Keep your own practice.** Daily devotion or meditation that is just yours. At least some rites a year where someone else leads and you simply take part.
6. **Have support outside the coven.** Another coven's head, a friend, a therapist, a spiritual director. Leaders need someone to bring their troubles to.
7. **Take a sabbatical.** Every few years, or when you need one, step back for a season. Hand the coven to your co-leader or elders for that time, with clear agreements about what they decide. A coven that can't survive three months without you is fragile.
8. **Say no.** To the extra program, the fifth newcomer this month, the public festival. A good no protects your yes.
9. **Close the loop on conflict.** Unresolved disputes drain more energy than resolved ones.
10. **Rest after big rites.** Plan nothing for the day after a festival.

> **Safety:** Burnout can tip into depression. If you feel hopeless, can't function, or have thoughts of harming yourself, step back from leading at once and talk to a doctor or a crisis line. Your coven will survive your absence; it needs you well more than it needs you present.

## Signs a coven is too big or too busy

- New members never get to know the head.
- Mentors have more mentees than they can check in with.
- The members' record shows many people quiet for months.
- Rites feel like events to be managed rather than worship.
- The head is the only one who can do most things.

Responses: close to new members for a season (under Manage, The coven, "Not taking members"), set a limit under "Most members", run fewer, better gatherings, train more leaders, or begin planning a daughter coven (see the stewardship module).

## Taking a sabbatical, step by step

1. **Decide the length and dates**: a season, three months, or from one festival to the next.
2. **Choose who leads while you're away.** Usually a co-leader or a senior elder. In the app, make sure their position carries the powers they'll need: leading the coven, leading rituals and putting rites on the calendar, reviewing, moderating, managing programs.
3. **Write down what they decide alone**, and what (if anything) waits for your return, such as removing a member or changing the agreement.
4. **Tell the coven** who is leading and how long you'll be away. Ask members to bring things to the acting leader, not to you.
5. **Hand over your mentees** to other mentors for the time.
6. **Turn off the coven's notifications on your phone** in Settings, under Notifications & reminders, then Covens.
7. **Actually rest.** Practise for yourself. Visit another coven's open rite. Read.
8. **Come back gently.** Meet the acting leader first, hear what happened, thank them in front of the coven, and don't undo their decisions lightly.

## Stepping back is not failing

There is a quiet pride in heads that says "I must hold on." It isn't humility, and it isn't service. Knowing when to rest, to share or to hand on is part of leadership. Many traditions teach that the priestess or priest serves something larger than themselves, and something larger than themselves will continue when they step back.

## A sustainability check

Every season, answer honestly:

1. How many hours a week does the coven take from me? Is that what I want to give?
2. When did I last take part in a rite I didn't lead?
3. Who could lead if I were ill tomorrow?
4. What one task could I hand on this season?
5. What gives me joy in this work? Am I making room for it?

> **Try this:** For one week, log every time you do something for the coven: messages, planning, conversations, rites. Note the minutes. At the end of the week, add it up and write what you notice.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions speak of the head as "wedded" to the coven; others have fixed terms for leaders, or rotate leadership among elders each year. Ask your head how your coven thinks about the length of a head's service and about rest.

docs.title: Succession and handing over
docs.summary: Choosing and preparing a successor, sharing leadership in the app, handing on the coven step by step, and stepping back well.
docs.body:
## Stewardship: leading for the long term

A **steward** looks after something that isn't entirely theirs, so that it can be handed on in good order. That is the right way for a head to think about a coven. It belongs to its members, its tradition and its gods (however you understand them) as much as to you. This module is about the coven over years: who comes next, how it grows and divides, how it trains its teachers, how it keeps its health and story, how it ends if it must, and how it lives among other covens.

## Why succession needs planning

**Succession** is the passing of leadership from one head to the next. It happens in only a few ways: planned, when a head chooses to step back; sudden, through illness, a move or death; or forced, after a crisis. Planned succession is far kinder to everyone, and it should start years before it's needed.

A coven with no succession plan is fragile. If the head disappears tomorrow, who can open the coven's settings? Who knows the rites? Who will the members trust?

## Choosing and preparing a successor

1. **Look for character before charisma.** The best successors are trusted, steady, fair and humble. They keep confidences, admit mistakes, turn up and do the dull work. Charisma without those is a risk.
2. **Ask the elders.** Succession that the elders support holds; succession imposed on them often splits the coven. Ask each elder privately whom they would trust, and why.
3. **Ask the person.** Being head is a heavy commitment. Ask whether they want it, and give them time to say no without loss of face.
4. **Train them in the open.** Let the coven see the successor taking on more: leading major rites, chairing meetings, sitting in on difficult conversations. This module and the one before it are part of that training.
5. **Share leadership first.** In the app, give the successor a position that carries "Leads the coven", so they can edit pages, positions and details and act on members below them, while you remain the head. A season or a year of shared leadership shows both of you, and the coven, whether it works.
6. **Name a deputy for emergencies.** Even before a successor is ready, name in the rules who steps in if the head is suddenly unable to lead.

## Sharing leadership in the app

The app has one **head** for each coven: the founder, or the person to whom it was handed on. The head always has every power. Others share leadership through their **position**: any position that carries "Leads the coven" lets its holders edit the coven's pages, positions and details, give positions up to their own level, and act on members below them.

A few things stay with the head alone: handing on leadership, archiving the coven, choosing who sees ritual participation and who keeps the members' record, and choosing the position people reach by finishing a program. If two of you lead together, decide in your rules which of you is the head in the app, and what each of you decides.

## Handing over, step by step

When the time comes:

1. **Agree the timing with your successor and elders.** A festival or the turn of the year can be a fitting moment.
2. **Tell the coven before the change, not after.** Explain why, what will change and what will stay the same. Give people the chance to speak with you and with the successor.
3. **Prepare a handover file.** Put it in the coven's Book (members only, or opened only to the successor): the vision, a "who can do what" list, current trainees and their mentors, open concerns (without needless private detail), the calendar for the coming year, and anything only you know how to do.
4. **Hold a rite or a meeting to mark it.** Many covens hold a simple rite of passing: the old head blesses the new, the coven affirms them, the old head steps back to the circle.
5. **Make the change in the app.** Open the coven, tap **Members**, and tap your successor. Under the options, tap **Hand on leadership**. The app asks, "Make (their name) the coven's leader?" and explains that they become its founder, with every power over the coven, and that you stay a member in your current position. Tap **Hand on**. Only the head (or a site moderator) can do this, and the new leader must be an active member.
6. **Sort out your own position.** You keep the position you held before. If that position carries "Leads the coven", you still have those powers. Agree with the new head what position you should now hold, and let them change it. Many outgoing heads take an "Elder" or honorary position with no managing powers, so the new head truly leads.
7. **Check the coven's settings together.** The new head should look through Manage: Who runs training, Ritual participation, the members' record's keepers, Gathering notifications. Some of these were chosen by you for your way of leading.

> **Safety:** Handing on leadership in the app can't be undone by you afterwards; only the new head could hand it back. Make sure it is the right person and the right time, and that you have talked it through, before you tap the button.

## After the handover

The hardest part comes afterwards. A former head who stays in the coven must truly step back:

- Don't countermand the new head, in public or in private.
- When members come to you with complaints about the new head, send them to the new head, or to the coven's complaints process.
- Offer advice when asked, and mostly only then.
- Consider stepping away from the coven entirely for a season, so the new head can find their feet.

If you are the successor, honour what came before, change things slowly, and say thank you often.

## When succession is sudden

If a head dies or becomes unable to lead without having handed on, no member can take over the coven's head role in the app by themselves. Those who hold "Leads the coven" through their position can keep most things running. Contact the Salt & Sovereignty moderators through the app; site moderators can hand on a coven. Have this possibility written into your rules so that the coven knows who should step forward.

> **Try this:** Write a short succession section for your coven's rules: who steps in if the head can't lead, how a successor is chosen, and how the handover happens in the app. Discuss it with your mentor.

> **Your coven:** In some lineaged traditions, only someone of a particular degree may lead a coven, and the line of succession matters greatly. In others, the coven chooses its leader. Ask your head what your tradition requires of a successor.

docs.title: Hiving off a daughter coven
docs.summary: What hiving is, good and less good reasons, planning it step by step, and founding the daughter coven in the app.
docs.body:
## What hiving off is

**Hiving off** is when part of a coven leaves, with blessing, to form a new coven of its own: a **daughter coven**. The word is borrowed from bees, which swarm out of a full hive with a new queen. In modern Wicca, especially British Traditional lines from the mid-twentieth century onwards, it describes a High Priestess (usually of a senior degree) leaving her teacher's coven to found her own, while staying connected to it. Other traditions use other words, but the pattern is common.

Hiving off is a sign of health, not of failure. A coven that trains good leaders will, in time, have more leaders than one circle needs.

## Good reasons, and less good ones

Good reasons to hive off:

- The coven has grown too big for a close circle (many find that ten to thirteen active members is a natural limit).
- An elder is ready to lead and has a calling the current coven can't hold.
- Members live far apart, and a second circle closer to some of them makes sense.
- A distinct focus has grown up (a devotional circle, a study group) that deserves its own space.

Less good reasons, which call for care:

- Conflict with the head. Sometimes parting is the right answer, but call it what it is, and part honestly rather than dressing a split as a hiving.
- Wanting status. Leading a coven is service, and it is hard.

## Planning a hiving, step by step

1. **Talk with the head first, privately.** If you are the elder who wants to hive, ask your head's view before you tell anyone else. If you are the head, raise it with the elder you see as ready.
2. **Agree the relationship.** Will the daughter coven keep the same tradition, rites and Book? Will its trainees be able to come to the mother coven's festivals? Will the heads meet? Write it down.
3. **Agree who goes, and let people choose freely.** No one should feel pressured to go or to stay. Members can belong to more than one coven in the app, so some may stay in both for a while.
4. **Agree what is carried.** Which rites, teachings and Book pages may go with the new coven? Oath-bound material may need the head's specific blessing.
5. **Set a date and a rite.** Many covens hold a rite of hiving: a blessing, the gift of a candle or flame lit from the mother coven's altar, and a farewell.
6. **Found the new coven** (below).
7. **Keep in touch.** A shared festival each year, a call between heads each season.

## Founding the daughter coven in the app

1. Open the Coven tab, choose **Find a coven**, and tap **Found a coven**. Make your coven profile first if asked.
2. Fill in the **Coven name**, its **Web address** (this can't change later, so choose with care), **One line about the coven**, and **Who you are and how you practise**. In the description, say honestly where the coven comes from ("A daughter of the Thistle & Moon Circle, hived in 2026").
3. Add its **Tradition or path**, **When you gather** and **Tags** if you like.
4. Choose **How witches join** and whether it is **Listed** in the directory. Many new covens start unlisted and by invitation, while they settle.
5. Write **Your title as leader**.
6. Agree to lead it by the community guidelines, and tap **Found the coven**.

The app sets up starting positions (Seeker, Dedicant, Initiate, Elder and your own title), empty creed, rules and requirements pages, and a starter member agreement. Then:

1. Under **Manage**, write the creed, rules, requirements and agreement. You may adapt the mother coven's, with permission.
2. Set the **Practice calendar**.
3. Set up **Positions** and their powers.
4. Invite the members who are coming, with an invitation in the app or a single-use link from **Invite**.
5. Begin the programs your new coven will use under **Initiation & training**, **Design and assign**, and assign mentors.
6. Carry over Book material by writing it into the new coven's Book, or by suggesting pages from your own grimoire to it, only where the mother coven has agreed.

The app has no built-in link between a mother and daughter coven. Record the relationship yourself: in the description, in the creed or an "Our lineage" page, and in both covens' Books.

> **Note:** If you were the mother coven's head and are leaving to found the daughter, hand on leadership of the mother coven first (see the lesson on succession). The head can't leave a coven they lead.

## Hiving when it's hard

Sometimes a hiving comes out of disagreement. It can still be done well:

- Agree a short, kind account that both covens give ("We've grown in different directions, and the circle is dividing with blessing").
- Don't recruit. Let people choose.
- Don't take material that wasn't agreed.
- Don't speak ill of the other coven, in person, online or in the coven's chat.
- After some time, reach out. Many hard partings soften into friendship.

## After the hiving

The first year of a daughter coven is fragile. If you lead it:

- Keep it small and simple at first.
- Lean on your mother coven's head for advice.
- Begin training leaders at once.
- Review your rules after six months.

> **Try this:** Imagine your coven needs to hive in two years. Write down who might lead the daughter, what would be carried and what would not, how members would choose, and the rite you'd hold. Discuss it with your mentor.

> **Your coven:** Some lineaged traditions honour a High Priestess whose covens have hived as a "Witch Queen", and keep formal rules about who may hive and what they carry. Ask your head what your tradition expects.

docs.title: Training the trainers
docs.summary: Growing elders into mentors and teachers: shadowing, assigning mentees, supervision, fair scoring and feedback, and looking after trainers.
docs.body:
## Training the trainers

A coven that only the head can teach is limited to what one person can give. A healthy coven has several **trainers**: elders who mentor, teach, lead rites and sign off work. Training those trainers is one of the head's most important tasks, and one of the longest.

## What a trainer needs

An elder who mentors or teaches needs:

- **Knowledge** of the material they're teaching, and honesty about where it comes from.
- **Skill** in explaining step by step, in listening, and in giving feedback.
- **Judgement** about when someone is ready, when to slow down, and when to refer on.
- **Boundaries**: not becoming a counsellor, a parent or a guru to their mentee.
- **Fairness**: holding every trainee to the same standards, and scoring tests and written answers against the rubric, not their feelings about the person.
- **Support**: someone they can bring difficulties to.

## Step by step: growing a mentor

1. **Choose them.** Look for elders who are patient, reliable and kind, and who have finished the training they'll be helping with.
2. **Let them shadow.** For a few months, they sit in on your mentoring conversations (with the mentee's consent) and read the work you sign off.
3. **Give them one mentee.** Choose someone who is likely to do well. In the app, open **Initiation & training**, **Design and assign**, then **Mentors**, tap the mentee and choose the new mentor.
4. **Give them the powers they need.** A mentor signs off tasks and stages left to mentors without any extra power. If they'll also design programs or see everyone's progress, the head can give that under **Manage**, then **Who runs training**, or through their position.
5. **Meet regularly.** Once a month, talk with each mentor about their mentees: what's going well, what's hard, any concerns. These conversations are a kind of supervision.
6. **Look at their scoring.** Read a few test answers they've scored. Are they fair and consistent with the rubric? Too generous or too harsh?
7. **Widen their role slowly.** A second mentee; teaching a session; leading a rite; then perhaps managing a program.

## Teaching trainers to give feedback

Good feedback is specific, kind and useful. Teach trainers a simple pattern:

1. Say what was done well, specifically. "Your account of grounding was clear, and you named three methods."
2. Say what is missing or wrong, specifically. "You didn't say what to do if someone feels dizzy after raising energy."
3. Say what to do next. "Read the section on grounding the excess again and add two sentences."

Avoid vague praise ("Lovely!"), vague criticism ("Not quite there") and comments about the person rather than the work.

## Keeping standards consistent

When several people teach, standards can drift. Help keep them steady:
